#5552. Sunlight, Weather and Childcare: A Year of New Data on Redfin Home Listings

In 2026, Redfin added information about sunlight, weather, childcare access and more to home listings. Here is everything you need to know about what’s new.

A home listing has always been good at telling you about a house: the square footage, the year it was built, the number of bedrooms. Historically, it has been less good at telling you what living there is actually like. Does the kitchen get morning sunlight? How hot are the summers? Is there a daycare within walking distance?

Those are the questions we set out to answer this year. Multiple new data sets arrived on Redfin in 2026, and they now sit alongside other information that was already there, including scores about a property’s walkability, transit access and climate.

Sunscore shows exactly how much sunlight a home gets

Natural light is one of the hardest things to judge from listing photos or a single showing, and it matters more than you might expect. In a recent Redfin survey, nearly 70% of people said the amount of sunlight in their home affects their satisfaction with where they live, and 11% said it is non-negotiable when searching for a home.

Sunscore is a property-level rating from 0 to 100 that shows how much sunlight a home gets. We co-created it with Shadowmap, a sunlight analysis platform, using 3D modeling that tracks how shadows fall across a home throughout the day and across the seasons. Here are the score breakdowns:

Each score accounts for the home’s 3D shape and structure, surrounding buildings, trees and terrain, the sun’s position throughout the day, and seasonal changes across the year. In other words, it catches the things you would only discover after moving in—like a neighboring building that blocks the afternoon light in winter.

And it is not only about comfort and aesthetics. A home’s sun exposure also says something about its solar potential, which can translate into real savings on energy costs over time.

Weather data helps predict precipitation and heat

Weather turns out to be one of the biggest reasons people move. In a recent Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos, 22% of Americans planning to move to another state said better weather was motivating the move—the most cited reason out of nearly 30 options, ahead of affordability, job opportunities and moving closer to family. Another 21% said concerns about climate change or natural disasters were shaping where they wanted to live.

In July, we partnered with The Weather Company, owner of The Weather Channel app and weather.com, to bring historical weather data to every for-sale listing on Redfin. As our exclusive historical weather provider, it supplies the same data hundreds of millions of people check every month.

Each listing shows ZIP code-level averages for:

Consider this information the difference between the weather on the day you tour a home and the climate you might actually live in.

Childcare data displays daycare and preschool options

For families with young children, childcare access can determine a neighborhood’s fit as much as school boundaries do. However, it’s historically been missing from the home browsing experience. Redfin is the first major real estate portal to partner with Winnie, the largest marketplace for childcare and early education in the U.S., to bring local childcare information to for-sale listings.

Nearby daycare and preschool options now appear on for-sale home listings with details that determine whether a spot is realistic for your family, such as:

Location scores capture everything from wellness access to noise

While Walk Score, Bike Score and Transit Score already existed on home listings, Redfin has expanded these location scores to capture more information about a neighborhood’s vibe using Local Logic data.

Start exploring homes on Redfin.com or the Redfin app to learn everything you’d want to know about a property. Need a place to start? Use Redfin’s conversational search to begin your homebuying journey.

#5551. Hedra’s new Model Factory cranks up the production volume for physical AI model training

Autonomous artificial intelligence agents have been a massive hit in the digital realm, and now a startup called Hedra Inc. is hoping to take the next step with physical AI systems that can automate tasks in the real world too.

The company today announced the Hedra Model Factory, a new post-training and inference platform that enables the recursive self-improvement of AI models, or RSI for short, designed specifically to power autonomous robots and other machines.

Hedra says that physical AI requires a very different and more specialized form of intelligence that can enable robots and other real-world hardware systems to perform very specific tasks, such as packing irregular-shaped parcels onto palettes. One of the main challenges of physical AI is that each robot and each task it performs requires a different model.

But training all of those models is not feasible, given the vast amounts of data required to create them. That’s why Hedra wants to use RSI to adapt existing models to new tasks.

RSI is a relatively new technique in AI that describes systems that can autonomously evaluate, train and then improve their own architectures. There has been a lot of research into these systems in frontier AI labs, but until now no one has managed to apply that continuous loop to the physical world.

The challenge is that physical AI models require massive volumes of multimodal data inputs, from sources such as high-resolution video, sensor feeds and 3D simulations. Running RSI against such enormous data environments simply is not practical given the staggering compute costs such an operation would incur.

Hedra says its Model Factory changes that. It’s an autonomous training pipeline offered as a service that’s designed for robotics, manufacturing, biology and defense workloads, pairing Hedra’s in-house research teams with AI agents that orchestrate the training runs, curate the data and iterate autonomously according to the customer’s specifications.

Hedra founder and Chief Executive Michael Lingelbach (pictured) told SiliconANGLE that RSI has already had a major impact on the way frontier models are developed. He believes that the next big frontier is physical AI, where the data primarily comes from video feeds, sensor readings and simulations. “Hedra Model Factory gives robotics, manufacturing, biology and defense teams the infrastructure to post-train, deploy and keep improving their own models,” he promised.

Lingelbach, a former reinforcement learning researcher for visual and physical systems at Stanford University and Nvidia Corp., said what his company has developed is basically an end-to-end production platform for physical AI models. The customer provides the base model, uploads their proprietary simulation and video data, which is then provisioned within a flexible graphics processing unit sandbox environment powered by its proprietary inference engine.

The RSI process then begins, with Hedra’s researchers keeping close tabs on its progress. Lingelbach said they use vision-language models to score data and provide live reinforcement learning feedback in order to continuously optimize the model to perform the task specified by the customer. Once done, customers can then deploy the model on-premises in their own systems, or with one of Hedra’s cloud data center partners.

The models can also be distilled to run on edge systems for lower-latency workloads. Once they’re up and running, they feed data back into the customer’s sandboxed environment, creating an autonomous flywheel that continuously optimizes the model, making it better over time.

Hedra has worked hard to validate the system. For instance, it retrained MiniMax Group Inc.’s open-weight H3 video model to enhance its physical consistency, creating a distilled version that bumped up its score on the Physics-IQ benchmark from 30.3 to 34.9. In another training run, the startup was able to distill the Krea 3 2K image generation model from 30 sampling steps to just 14 while reducing latency from 22 seconds to just 3.6 seconds, a sixfold speed boost that took just one week to achieve.

Lingelbach said Hedra’s ultimate goal is to help create the thousands of bespoke, cost-effective models needed to usher in the physical AI revolution by optimizing training as much as possible. With RSI, sometimes it’s possible to bypass the retraining process altogether. In one example, Hedra demonstrated that it was able to swap out a robot’s gripper with a new one and restore its task success rate to 100% without any additional training, simply by mapping the new hardware’s reach and grasp metrics to the robot’s wrist camera view.

The Hedra Model Factory service is available today, giving enterprises the option to bypass compute-intensive training and quickly develop the specialized autonomous systems needed to bring intelligence into real-world environments.

#5549. Inflation Hotter Than Economist Expectations, Raising Odds of 2027 Rate Hikes

Inflation picked up speed in October, as the latest Consumer Price Index (CPI) from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) accelerated faster than predictions from economists.

The October CPI saw the all-items index grow 0.4%, a slight decrease from last month’s 0.6% rise, but “hotter than expected,” according to Navy Federal Chief Economist Heather Long. Original forecasts were at 0.2% to 0.3% increases, as noted by Realtor.com® Senior Economist Jake Krimmel.

Inflation’s jump this month was due to increases in shelter inflation (up 0.3%), contributing to over 30% of the increase. Food inflation also advanced in October by 0.5%. Energy inflation, which decelerated in October, still saw a rise of 0.7%.

This month’s data does not include annual inflation numbers as the BLS noted it did not collect data in October 2025 due to the government being shut down at the time. As a result, it cannot calculate 12-month percent changes.

With the data available, Long said October’s increase “implies about a ~4% inflation rate for the past year.”

The index for all items less food and energy—core inflation—grew by 0.3% in October, the same rate of growth it saw in both September and August. Indexes that contributed to increase include household furnishings and operations, recreation, medical care, motor vehicle insurance and education.

Long said this month’s data “underscores why so many Americans voted the way they did in the mid-term elections,” speaking of the “blue wave” that overtook the elections last week.

“The same supply-side and geopolitical pressures are still at work, with energy playing an important role and tariff-driven goods inflation not going away,” added Krimmel. “These are the costs most salient to consumers and voters, as we saw, yet the Fed has less direct control over them.”

He noted that for the Fed outlook, a “December hike now looks almost certain, with odds jumping to 99% this morning.”

“Additional hikes in early 2027 look more in play as well, with the 10-year Treasury up 9 basis points just 25 minutes after the CPI report release,” Krimmel continued.

Looking at housing, Krimmel said that near-term there could be “upward pressure on mortgage rates again” due to rising Treasury yields and the potential of a rate hike from the Fed.

Claudia Larsen is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5548. A Looming Nor’easter Threatens Millions of Homeowners With First Snow of the Season

A potential nor’easter impacting the Northeast and New England is being forecasted for later this week, with millions of homeowners bracing for possibly the first snow of the season.

Meteorologists are predicting that as early as Wednesday evening, a deep plunge in temperatures combined with a low pressure system moving across the Midwest will make for wet conditions for Louisville, KY, all the way up to Maine.

While snow in these areas this time of year is not unheard of, some locales are prepping for a volatile winter ahead, given the Super El Niño conditions.

So is this just a taste of what’s to come?

Cold air sweeps across the East late in the week, setting the stage for winter weather, according to The Weather Channel.

By Thursday night, a secondary low-pressure system is expected to form off the Eastern Seaboard. As cold air filters in, rain could begin mixing with or fully changing over to wet snow across interior parts of the Northeast.

Friday into the weekend presents the greatest potential for snow, depending on the storm’s exact track, which meteorologists are still unclear on.

If the system tracks close to the coast, it could wrap heavy inland snowfall into the Northeast alongside coastal rain, strong winds, and flooding.

A track farther out to sea would result in much lighter snow accumulations across inland areas.

Homeowners in places like Buffalo, NY, and Burlington, VT, are among those who should prepare for the snow shovels and salt for a snowy weekend.

However, if the temperatures dip low enough, it wouldn’t be unthinkable to see snow in places like Washington, DC, Philadelphia, and New York City as well.

Speaking of New York City, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced ahead of the nor’easter a citywide mobilization to prepare Manhattan for winter weather. This includes a $25 million investment in an expanded Code Blue system and a supercharged snow- and ice-clearing operation.

“We have spent the past year preparing for any challenge winter throws our way. We have trained our workers, readied our equipment and strengthened our protocols because keeping New Yorkers safe can’t begin when the first storm hits,” Mamdani said in a press release.

“This winter, we’re doing things differently—we’re expanding Code Blue to reach more New Yorkers in need, equipping New York’s Strongest to clear snow and ice faster and leaving no stone unturned when it comes to protecting our neighbors from the cold. No New Yorker should face the dangers of winter alone, and no part of our city should be left behind.”

These initiatives come at a time where New York and much of the surrounding states are bracing themselves for the final months of the Super El Nino, which, according to the latest forecasts from the World Meteorological Organization, is projected to be the strongest on record and likely to persist through February 2027.

According to the NOAA, an El Niño system tends to be strongest during the winter months. But because of the strength of the system being tracked this year, there are plenty of variables at play.

“Every El Niño is not the same; each one is unique with its own imprint on our weather,” says Ken Graham, director of NOAA’s National Weather Service (NWS). "Advanced monitoring and an improved understanding of El Niño patterns allow the NWS to better predict and better prepare the public and our core partners for what is to come.”

With that in mind, the Farmers' Almanac 2026–'27 winter outlook outlines a season defined by sharp contrasts and volatile conditions across the United States, driven largely by an active El Niño pattern.

In the Northeast, it predicts a season dominated by wet conditions, both rainy and snowy. In fact, much of the country will need to contend with wetter than usual conditions, but whether snow develops will depend largely on the temperatures.

#5547. October Marks the First Month in 3 Years With a Decline in U.S. Home-Sale Prices

For three years, U.S. home-sale prices rose from a year earlier every single month, even as mortgage rates climbed and would-be buyers pulled back. That streak has ended.

The median home-sale price declined 0.4% year over year to $388,634 in October. That’s  the first decline since May 2023 and a sharp slowdown from the 2.5% gain just two months earlier. With Americans’ wages growing about 4% year over year, even a slight dip in prices can improve affordability. Sale prices have risen nearly every single month for the last 13 years; the only exception was a handful of months in 2023.

With the total number of homes for sale at its highest level since early 2020 and demand cooling, homebuyers’ negotiating power keeps increasing–and that’s finally showing up in sale prices.

Home-sale prices fell nationwide, but they rose in more than half of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas. San Francisco led the nation by a wide margin, with the median sale price rising 16.8% year over year. That’s the biggest increase since 2018. Next comes New Brunswick, NJ, with a 7.7% gain. Two other NYC-area metros also had price increases ranking in the top six; the median sale price rose 4.4% in both New York City and Nassau County.

In San Francisco, AI wealth is fueling competition for scarce inventory; active listings were down 7% from a year earlier. In the New York City area, years of limited homebuilding have left buyers competing for relatively few homes in a region with a strong job market.

Home-sale prices fell most in Austin, TX, where they declined 6.5% year over year. It’s followed by Seattle (-5.1%) and Nashville, TN (-4.9%). Austin and Nashville are among the biggest buyer’s markets in the U.S., and Seattle’s shaky tech job market is curbing demand.

National sale prices are losing steam because fewer Americans can afford to buy a home. U.S. pending home sales fell 3.6% from a month earlier in October on a seasonally adjusted basis to their lowest level since 2013, with the exception of April 2020.

This is a real-time indicator of the state of the housing market; fewer homes went under contract in October largely because mortgage rates averaged 7.33%, a three-year high and up from 6.86% the month before.

All figures in this report are seasonally adjusted, with the exception of median sale price data and mortgage rate data. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

“It’s a buyer’s market, but not many people can afford to buy,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economics. “That could start to shift a bit, now that sale prices are closer to reflecting the shape of the market. House hunters in most of the country should know that the price they see on a listing may very well be a starting point; they should try offering below the asking price, and negotiating for closing costs, repairs and maybe even mortgage-rate buydowns. If you can’t get the price or monthly payment you want on one house, move on to the next one–with a big pool of inventory sitting on the market, buyers can afford to be picky.”

Pending home sales declined in all of the most populous U.S. metros. That’s the second month in a row that has happened; before September, the last time was three years earlier.

The biggest declines were in Seattle and San Diego, both places where pending sales fell more than 20% year over year. Those West Coast metros are some of the priciest in the U.S., so 7%-plus mortgages hit house hunters’ monthly payments there hard. In Seattle, an uncertain local job market is also curbing demand.

Closed home sales fell to their lowest level in nearly 3 years. They declined 2.1% month over month in October to their lowest level since December 2023; before that, the last time sales dropped that low was 2014. Many of the deals that closed last month went under contract in August and September, when rates were already climbing and economic uncertainty was deterring a lot of house hunters.

With homebuying demand falling, supply is building. The total number of homes for sale rose 0.9% from September to its highest level since early 2020; that’s the biggest monthly gain since May 2025.

More supply gives buyers more homes to choose from and more leverage:

“Buyers are nervous about rates, the economy, and everything they’re seeing in the news– so they need the house and the price to line up perfectly before they’ll make an offer,” said Callie Kimmel, a Redfin Premier agent in Philadelphia. “I’m advising sellers to price just below current market value from day one–and not comps from six months ago, but homes that are listed right now. Otherwise, the home is likely to end up sitting on the market for a bit and selling for less than they hoped. There are a few exceptions: Move-in ready homes in the most desirable neighborhoods are still competitive; in those cases, sellers have the upper hand.”

While total housing supply is growing, fewer sellers are adding new inventory to the pool. New listings of homes for sale fell 1% month over month to the lowest level in more than two years. Would-be sellers are pulling back as homebuying demand slows and sale prices lose steam.

The figures below are based on a list of the 50 most populous U.S. metropolitan areas. Some metros may be removed from time to time to ensure data accuracy. Refer to our metrics definition page for explanations of metrics used in this report. All changes below represent year-over-year changes.

#5546. SUSE points Rancher Prime’s AI agents at virtual machines and updates its enterprise Linux

Open-source enterprise software company SUSE S.A. today extended the artificial intelligence troubleshooting agents in its SUSE Rancher Prime platform from Kubernetes clusters to virtual machines.

The company released version 16.1 of its SUSE Linux Enterprise Server operating system at the same time. The updates are pitched at enterprises trying to run AI workloads next to existing applications in hybrid environments.

Research sponsored by SUSE found that information technology leaders rank Kubernetes management as their top investment priority, with AI second, and 24% named AI-assisted troubleshooting as one way to make Kubernetes easier to manage.

Thomas Di Giacomo, SUSE’s chief technology and product officer, said companies moving from AI experiments to deployment at scale need infrastructure that can take on the new workloads alongside the applications they already run. He said SUSE’s commitment to open infrastructure lets organizations adopt AI “on their terms, without being locked into a single technology stack or vendor.”

The troubleshooting agents report to Liz, the Rancher Prime assistant SUSE first shipped as a tech preview in November 2025. Virtual machines come within their reach through a new integration with SUSE Virtualization. Peter Smails, SUSE’s general manager of cloud native, told theCUBE in March that customers could also bring agents of their own to Liz. SUSE said nothing the agents propose gets carried out until someone approves it.

New OAuth2 support lets Liz connect to Model Context Protocol servers. SUSE has also introduced an AI-first version of the Rancher command-line interface, and operators can use its server-side dry run to see what a command would change before it takes effect.

Further down the stack, SUSE Rancher Prime Virtual Clusters gains a hosted control plane mode so platform teams can offer Kubernetes as a service on SUSE’s RKE2 distribution. Stateful workloads run up to 10 times faster on the v2 data engine in SUSE Storage, according to the company.

Version 16.1 of SUSE Linux Enterprise Server pulls in deployments that previously needed separate SUSE products. Customers on the immutable SUSE Linux Enterprise Micro or on SUSE Linux Enterprise Real Time can migrate to it, according to the release notes, and keep everything on one support lifecycle.

The release also carries an on-box MCP framework for AI-assisted diagnostics. Support for accelerated infrastructure from Nvidia Corp. is included, as are expanded live patching and preparation for post-quantum cryptography.

The security updates run from the components AI applications are built on through to the workloads in production. SUSE Application Collection now holds more than 1,000 Python libraries built from verified sources, each shipped with a software bill of materials and provenance information that developers can use to assess dependencies.

The upcoming SUSE Security 6.0 release will add SUSE Security Vulnerability Scanner to find and rank flaws in deployed workloads and cluster nodes. Its Runtime Enforcer component will detect anomalous workload behavior and block it.

SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.1 is available now, with its MCP framework in tech preview. The AI-first Rancher command-line interface and the hosted control plane mode for Virtual Clusters are in open beta, and the remaining Rancher Prime features will ship on their own release schedules.

#5545. Russell Brand Filed To Put $6.6 Million Home in His Wife’s Name—6 Weeks Before 10-Year Prison Sentence

Russell Brand reportedly changed the ownership of his $6.6 million Oxfordshire family home to his wife, Laura Brand—just six weeks before he was convicted of rape and sexual assault and sentenced to over 10 years behind bars.

On Nov. 5, a London court found Brand, 51—who was previously married to pop star Katy Perry, and now shares three children with Laura—guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, and not guilty of two additional counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Four days later, during sentencing, Judge Joel Bennathan said, "The total sentence is one of 10 years, six months."

Now, it has been revealed that just over one month before he was convicted, Brand transferred the ownership of his cottage, putting the property under his wife's name, as first reported by the Daily Mail.

The disgraced actor's conviction and sentencing came more than a year after he relocated his entire family to Florida to escape "attacks" by the "media, government, and judiciary."

Following an April 2025 arrest by Metropolitan Police, Brand denied all charges, sharing a video statement on his X account, in which he insisted that he has "never engaged in non-consensual activity," while conceding that he had acted like "a fool" when he was "young and single."

"I've always told you guys that when I was young and single, before I had my wife and family, who were just about a shot over there, my beautiful children, I was a fool, man," he said in the video, which appears to have been shot in Florida.

The alleged offenses are understood to involve six women and took place between 1999 and 2009. Police interviewed Brand about the allegations—which were first brought to light in 2023, when The Sunday Times and Channel 4, two British media outlets, released an expose in which Brand's accusers claimed they had been assaulted or raped by the comedian.

Brand vehemently denied all accusations of "non-consensual activity" at the time.

He is understood to have moved his family from their home in Oxfordshire in favor of a rental property in the Sunshine State, where he is reportedly living in a $2.5 million home in Santa Rosa Beach.

Although he has not revealed when exactly he moved, it has been reported by multiple outlets that he relocated shortly before the 2024 presidential election. Images taken of the comedian show him enjoying public events in the Santa Rosa Beach area as early as October of that year.

The Times reported in 2025 that Brand, his wife, and their three children had been living in a $3.3 million home in the U.K. before their move. It is unclear if they have since sold it.

In the lead-up to his move, the comedian and "Forgetting Sarah Marshall" star had been making efforts to connect with members of President Donald Trump's inner circle, interviewing Donald Trump Jr. at his Florida home in 2024 and attending a black-tie dinner at Mar-a-Lago, where he received a Global Defender of Freedom Award.

In April 2025, Brand sat down for an in-depth interview with Fox News host—and newly minted Florida resident—Sean Hannity, during which he opened up about his past addictions and his Christian faith.

Since moving to Santa Rosa Beach, the comedian has reportedly been seen attending church services, as well as yoga sessions, with one local telling The Sun that Brand "always says hello" when they see him.

It is not the first time that Brand has resided in the U.S., having previously owned multiple properties in Los Angeles—including a $6.5 million Mediterranean-style home in the Hollywood Hills, which he shared with Perry, his wife at the time.

Before that, he was reported to have been living in a 1920s abode nearby, which he purchased for $2.2 million in 2013.

Most recently, he snapped up a three-bedroom, five-bathroom Spanish-style property, also in the Hollywood Hills, this time paying $3 million.

The home, which Brand bought in 2019, was built in 1956. The original listing noted that it had since undergone several renovations. He put that property on the market for $3.5 million in the summer of 2024.

Bitcoin treasury stocks are set to react sharply to Tuesday’s US CPI release, as these companies’ share prices track Bitcoin closely and Bitcoin has grown more sensitive to inflation data as a macro asset.

The Consumer Price Index (CPI), published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, measures the monthly change in prices paid by urban consumers for a fixed basket of goods and services. Headline CPI includes food and energy; core CPI excludes those volatile categories.

Markets and the Federal Reserve watch it closely because sustained readings above the Fed’s roughly 2% target influence rate decisions, liquidity, and risk appetite. The October 2026 data drops on Tuesday, November 10, at 8:30 a.m. ET.

Key Events This Week:1. October CPI Inflation data – Tuesday 2. OPEC Monthly Report – Wednesday3. Initial Jobless Claims data – Thursday4. October Existing Home Sales data – Thursday5. October PPI Inflation data – Friday 6. Total of 17 Fed Speaker Events This WeekWe…

Consensus forecasts point to a cooling print: headline CPI is expected around +0.2% to +0.3% month-over-month (versus +0.6% in September), with core also near +0.2%.

Year-over-year figures may be limited by prior data gaps, but models such as the Cleveland Fed’s nowcast project roughly 3.7% headline and low 2.5% core. Energy moderation and softer goods prices are cited as drivers.

A print in line with or below these expectations would likely be viewed as dovish, supporting expectations of easier policy or delayed further tightening. That environment typically lifts Bitcoin (and risk assets more broadly) by reducing the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding assets and improving liquidity conditions.

Bitcoin has shown heightened CPI sensitivity since the 2022 hiking cycle; cooler-than-expected data has often produced positive short-term moves, while hotter prints have triggered quick sell-offs.

Treasury stocks, whose market values are heavily tied to Bitcoin holdings, amplify those swings. A hotter-than-expected number could reverse the dynamic, pressuring Bitcoin and the equities that hold it.

#5543. Staera launches with $4.6M to develop an optical interconnect for chiplets

Staera Semiconductor Inc., a startup that develops technology for linking together chiplets, launched today with $4.6 million in pre-seed funding.

Singaporean fund Openspace Capital led the investment. It was joined by SGInnovate, Black Kite Capital, 28 Holdings, In Group and financial software company Decimus Technologies.

High-end artificial intelligence accelerators comprise multiple chiplets, silicon dies that each perform a narrow set of tasks. They’re linked together by a kind of miniature network that also functions as the host accelerator’s base layer.

That miniature network takes the form of an interposer, an advanced device that sometimes includes computing circuits, or a bridge. A bridge is essentially a small interposer that costs less to make.

Interposers and bridges both use tiny copper wires to move data between the chiplets they connect. San Francisco-based Staera hopes to replace those copper wires with optical links. According to the company, optical technology is faster and uses less power. It can also transmit data over longer distances without slowing down, which enables chipmakers to build bigger accelerators.

“Copper performance plummets over the millimeter-to-meter distances that matter most in AI accelerators, and bolt-on optics add power and complexity.” said Chief Executive Officer Andrew Kim. “We build the light into the chip, the entire optical link inside a chip, so the connection gets smaller, cooler and faster with each generation.”

Staera’s first product is called Lightwire. It transmits data over optical links, or waveguides, made of a transparent material known as silicon nitride. Light beams can only travel through a transparent material if their wavelengths fall within a specific range. Silicon nitride supports a larger range of wavelengths than many alternatives and causes less light loss, which boosts connection speeds.

The light beams into which Lightwire encodes data traffic are produced by miniature LEDs. Those devices are made of gallium nitride, a compound that is widely used in optical systems because it has a direct bandgap.

The electrons that orbit an atomic nucleus have different energy levels known as bands. Light is produced when an electron jumps from one band to one another and then collides with a quasiparticle called an electron hole.

Usually, the process also involves a second quasiparticle known as a phonon. Direct bandgap materials such as gallium nitride don’t require a phonon, which makes the light generation process more efficient.

Staera says Lightwire transmits data between an AI accelerator’s chiplets at a rate of up to 8 gigabits per second. The technology can provide more than 600 optical links per square millimeter. In practice, that means a Lightwire-powered HBM4 memory stack can move up to 24 terabits of data per second instead of the 2.8 terabits supported by current technologies.

Staera’s funding round will advance its commercialization efforts. It will enhance Lightwire, grow its U.S. team and build out a manufacturing supply chain. The company hopes to begin commercial shipments in 2030.

#5542. What the World Series can teach real estate agents about focus

ST PETERSBURG, FLORIDA – OCT. 28: William Contreras, No. 24 of the Milwaukee Brewers, poses with the Willie Mays World Series Most Valuable Player award after defeating the Tampa Bay Rays in the 2026 World Series at Tropicana Field on Oct. 28, 2026, in St. Petersburg, Florida.

Mindfulness for real estate isn’t about calm. It’s about hearing clients under pressure. See what baseball teaches brokers about training attention.

The Milwaukee Brewers just won the World Series, and while I love baseball, I’ve been watching with a question that has very little to do with it: What happens to your attention when the outcome matters more than you can afford to think about?

Nobody at the plate can win a championship with the swing they wish they’d taken last inning. The players can only deal with the pitch (or batter) in front of them.

That sounds obvious until you notice how often we walk into a seller conversation still arguing with the deal that fell apart yesterday.

What’s interesting to me is that baseball has stopped treating this as a personality trait. Both the Rays and the Brewers have extensive mental performance training programs (as do all Major League ball clubs), but most brokerages treat mental health as a wellness issue, not a performance one.

Whatever name your office gives this kind of work, baseball has made it somebody’s job.

What makes this baseball tale useful to brokers and team leaders, though, is how much resistance the work still meets in a sport that has every reason to embrace it.

Andy McCullough’s recent reporting in The Athletic examines meditation in Major League Baseball, and I found the takeaways instructive.

For over two decades, most teams have invested in behavioral science and expanded their mental-performance staffs. It’s a sport that measures everything, with tens of millions of dollars on every roster, and it has decided the mental side is worth paying for.

What I find fascinating is that even as the evidence piles up, many players remain skeptical. Some call it “woo-woo.” One of the game’s best pitchers says he doesn’t need it. Coaches avoid the word “meditation” altogether because, as one put it, it intimidates people, and if you push it, they’ll tune you out.

My favorite part of the Athletic piece was this: The San Francisco Giants brought in a consultant, titled “Breathing Specialist,” and the players made jokes about it. The next season, the same man did the same work but with a new title: “Human Performance Coach,” and the resistance started to fall away.

By the time he left, about 15 players regularly attended his sessions (complete with Tibetan singing bowls). He concluded that the stigma had more to do with the title than the practice.

I don’t call it meditation when I train real estate teams either. But that doesn’t mean you can’t intentionally sharpen the skills involved.

When the market tightens, brokerages usually prescribe more activity: more calls, more door knocks, more open houses. We can count activity, so we reach for it. Ballplayers do the same thing when they skip the mental work and take extra swings.

The trouble is that pressure narrows attention, and narrowed attention is as poor a state for a batter with two on, two outs, behind two, in the bottom of the ninth as it is for a seasoned agent on a listing appointment, a price-reduction conversation or a buyer about to walk.

Don’t get confused. This kind of performance coaching is not about caring less about the result; it’s about letting go of the need to make it happen. A hitter can care enormously about winning the World Series and still recognize that thinking about winning doesn’t help him see the next pitch.

The same is true when a seller is deciding whether to take your advice. You need the listing, but needing it more isn’t any more effective than gripping and swinging the bat harder.

The goal isn’t calm, either. Mental-performance people who work with ballplayers talk about finding a usable level of activation for the task, since too much overwhelms you and too little leaves you flat. I’m not trying to produce agents who feel peaceful about losing business. I’m trying to help them notice when fear has taken over the conversation so that they can let it go and hear the client again.

There’s sports research worth knowing here. One study of Division I basketball players found that higher measured mindfulness predicted better free-throw percentages in games, a 5.75-point delta, to be exact. A separate training study found something more useful: under high stress, the gap between athletes who trained their attention and those who didn’t was larger than under low stress.

I won’t tell you a practice will add a specific number to your agents’ closing rates. Nobody can honestly promise that, and even baseball struggles to quantify the benefit. What I will tell you is that the moments that make or break an agent’s year are high-pressure, and training for them is a performance issue, not a wellness perk.

In each World Series game, every player must let the last pitch go before the next one arrives. Your agents face the same job on a smaller stage every week.

You don’t need agents who identify as meditators. You need agents who can hear what a client is saying while a deal they “need” is coming apart. That capacity deserves practice before the conversation, not a reminder to calm down halfway through it.

Aaron Hendon is the Managing Broker for Christine & Company with eXp and a mindfulness teacher. Connect with Aaron on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5541. Home prices rise in 78% of metros while weekly demand sinks to a low

Prices climbed in 78 percent of metros in the third quarter, according to NAR, as Redfin data shows pending sales at the lowest level in its records.

Home prices rose in 78 percent of U.S. metro areas during the third quarter, while pending sales in the four weeks ending Oct. 25 fell to the lowest level in Redfin’s records.

The national median single-family existing-home price rose 1.7 percent year over year to $432,900, matching the second quarter’s revised annual growth rate, the National Association of Realtors reported Thursday. Prices rose in 78 percent of the some 235 metros NAR tracks, down from 80 percent in the second quarter, and fell in 21 percent, up from 20 percent. Four percent of metros posted double-digit gains, down from 5 percent.

“Even with affordability challenges causing the housing market to stagnate, home prices continue to set record highs in most parts of the country,” NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said in a statement. “Homeowners are the beneficiaries of the price gains. Over the past seven years, the average house has appreciated by $146,000.”

Redfin’s data for the four weeks ending Oct. 25 shows prices dipping. The median U.S. home-sale price fell 0.1 percent year over year to $389,601, according to Redfin, following a 0.2 percent decline the prior week. The two drops are the first in more than three years.

NAR and Redfin measure different things. NAR tracks quarterly sales of existing single-family homes, while Redfin’s figures cover homes listed or sold across more than 900 metros on a rolling four-week basis.

The Northeast posted the largest annual gain, and the West was the only region where prices fell, according to NAR.

Prices declined in many Florida markets over the past year, Yun said.

“This quarter, however, homes in nearly all Florida markets are showing price gains,” he said. “In a similar vein, price declines in other markets may also be brief if the local job market and economy are solid.”

Gulfport-Biloxi-Pascagoula, Mississippi, led large markets with an 11 percent price increase, followed by Rochester, New York (10.9 percent) and Jackson, Mississippi (10.1 percent). Grand Rapids-Wyoming, Michigan; Cleveland-Elyria, Ohio; and Fort Wayne, Indiana, were among the Midwest markets in the top 10.

“Many markets in the Midwest offer exceptional value with more affordable homes, making homeownership more attainable,” Yun said. “Meanwhile, the artificial intelligence technology boom continues to push Bay Area home prices higher, keeping the region the most expensive in the country.”

San Jose-Sunnyvale-Santa Clara, California, remained the most expensive market at a median of $1.92 million, up 0.3 percent. Anaheim-Santa Ana-Irvine, California ($1.47 million) and San Francisco-Oakland-Hayward, California ($1.35 million) followed. Nine of the 10 most expensive markets are in California or Hawaii.

The monthly mortgage payment on a typical existing single-family home with a 20 percent down payment was $2,251 in the third quarter, up $48 from the second quarter and $69 from a year earlier, according to NAR. Typical families spent an average of 24.1 percent of income on mortgage payments, up from 23.9 percent last quarter and down from 24.5 percent a year ago.

First-time buyers faced a monthly payment of $2,208 on a typical $368,000 starter home with 10 percent down. That payment took up 36.3 percent of income, up from 36 percent last quarter and down from 37 percent a year earlier.

Pending sales fell 1.8 percent from a week earlier and 15.9 percent year over year, declining in all 50 of the most populous U.S. metros for the third straight week, according to Redfin. Seattle (down 31.6 percent) and Atlanta (down 25.9 percent) posted the steepest annual drops.

Redfin’s median monthly mortgage payment, calculated at a 7.32 percent rate, reached $2,786, up 10.7 percent year over year and the second-highest level in its records. The weekly average rate is down from 7.4 percent a week earlier and near a three-year high.

New listings fell 0.6 percent from a week earlier to their lowest level since January. Total inventory rose 0.3 percent because pending sales fell faster than new listings, Redfin reported. The share of listings with price drops rose to 21.5 percent from 20.9 percent a year earlier.

Redfin reported hundreds of thousands more sellers than buyers nationwide, giving buyers more negotiating power than they have had in more than a decade.

A First American analysis found that since 1991, rising mortgage rates have coincided with falling national home prices in some cases. In eight periods of sustained mortgage-rate increases since 1993, national home prices generally continued to appreciate, though the pace varied, First American Chief Economist Mark Fleming found.

During the rate run-up from December 2021 through October 2023, national prices rose an estimated 14 percent, according to the analysis. Affordability worsened at a steeper rate than prices, Fleming found. First American’s Real House Price Index, which adjusts prices for changes in income and mortgage rates, rose more than 70 percent over the same period.

Limited inventory can offset weaker demand when rates rise, Fleming wrote. Homeowners with mortgages below current rates may hold off on selling, and some sellers pull homes from the market rather than accept lower prices.

“Higher mortgage rates can put pressure on home prices, but the economy, household incomes and the number of homes for sale all play a role in what happens next,” Fleming wrote.

#5540. ‘It’s Like Facebook Again’: How AI IPOs Could Further Upend the Real Estate Market

A robotic hand presents a house icon with a percentage symbol, symbolizing growth and investment in a modern office space, merging technology with real estate. Synapse

(TNS)– The deluge of wealth the artificial intelligence boom has brought into San Francisco has already pushed luxury home prices to record heights. Now, with Anthropic’s initial public offering poised to bring even more money into the city, could things get even worse?

Real estate professionals say yes—but that a lot of the growth is already baked in.

Let’s take stock of what’s already happened. San Francisco’s home prices have risen most sharply in neighborhoods that were already exclusive, such as Pacific Heights or the Marina. The median home price for luxury homes in the San Francisco metropolitan area—properties sold in San Francisco and San Mateo counties at or above the 95th percentile price—was nearly $7.5 million from July to September 2026, Redfin data shows. That was up a whopping 23% from the same period in 2025, and up more than 60% from 2019.

Now, some experts suggest that AI IPOs could cause demand to spill even further, raising prices for the few home types—or communities—in the Bay Area where middle-income families might still afford a property.

Already, some data indicates that even non-luxury homes in the city have seen strong appreciation over the past year.

“Typical” San Francisco area homes—those in the 35th-to-65th percentile sale price range — saw a record median sale price of $1.6 million in September 2026, an increase of 6.5% from 2025. While that’s a much lower jump compared to the San Francisco area’s luxury market, it still diverges sharply from that of the rest of the United States, where high mortgage rates and economic woes have caused prices to dip.

Redfin economist Daryl Fairweather believes the heat in San Francisco will spread to other parts of the region. In some ways, it already has; the city’s surging rents have caused many tenants to seek refuge in relatively more affordable cities like Oakland, pushing up prices there.

“This has been the story for at least … 15 years: San Francisco prices and rents going up and people being displaced,” Fairweather said.

Demand for fancy homes will likely keep surging

Some real estate agents say that the AI workers and investors fighting bidding wars in San Francisco often don’t want to give up on their dream house, even as prices rise. That’s part of the reason demand has flowed into other expensive cities in Marin County or the Peninsula, where there are more fancy homes for the buying. Phil Chen, a real estate broker at Christie’s International Real Estate Sereno, said that demand for Hillsborough has soared, with buyers citing a desire for strong schools — and security.

“It’s my first time hearing, ‘Is the glass bulletproof and are there panic rooms?’” Chen said.

Zillow data indicates that home values in Hillsborough, Menlo Park and Piedmont have risen faster over the past year than any other Bay Area city with at least 10,000 people except San Francisco, suggesting that some wealthy buyers are expanding their search radius. In some cities, such as in Piedmont, starter home values—those in the 5th to 35th percentile—have actually climbed more than top-tier values. Still, a “starter home” in Piedmont still costs more than a mid-tier property in San Francisco.

It’s unclear how much demand could rise for homes that aren’t luxury properties or in expensive neighborhoods. One 2019 study found that IPOs increase demand for high-priced homes near the company’s headquarters, but not for low-priced properties. The study’s results also indicated IPOs increased the probability low-income residents moved to lower-income neighborhoods.

But Fairweather said that junior tech workers with smaller windfalls than their senior peers could start to make offers in parts of the Bay Area where their money will go further. Vanessa Hatvany Kitchen, a real estate agent with Compass’ Team Hatvany Kitchen, said her team has seen more people buying condos and smaller single-family homes in San Francisco, fearing they won’t be able to get a foothold after companies like Anthropic go public.

But much of the demand increase is baked in

If there’s any silver lining for buyers, though, it’s that a lot of those companies’ impact on the Bay Area real estate market is already here. Arrian Binnings, a San Francisco real estate agent at Christie’s International Real Estate Sereno, said many AI workers have been able to get cash by borrowing against their stocks or selling their shares via company-approved tender offers, while investors have benefitted from the strength of the public equity market. That’s consistent with some research showing that merely filing for IPOs can raise home prices near a company’s headquarters.

“I don’t see the IPO as the starting gun of a new race. I see it as … we’re probably already at the 50-yard line,” Binnings said. “But I do still see plenty of room to run.”

IPOs don’t always result in an explosion of wealth. In the months after Uber went public in 2019, the company’s stock price plummeted, erasing billions of dollars in value. A similar fate for a public Anthropic or OpenAI would send a chill through the real estate market, some real estate agents say.

But many buyers are optimistic. Chen said some of his clients plan to sell their newly purchased homes in five years, expecting to increase their budgets from $10 million to $25 million. after the IPO. Those buyers, he added, are relatively junior-level employees.

“It’s like Facebook again, but 10x,” Chen said.

#5539. Ring Drone Cam Becomes a Reality for Homeowners Eager To Level Up With Smart Home Security

If you remember Rosie from “The Jetsons,” congratulations—the future is here.

Amazon’s Ring announced the launch of two new products on Tuesday, offering homeowners room-to-room surveillance and smart home functionality in brand-new ways.

First, there’s an indoor security drone. The Ring Drone Cam is a security camera that takes flight in your home, including upstairs, to monitor your house activity, day and night.

At a demonstration in New York on Monday, Ring CEO Jamie Siminoff showed how the drone could be used as a home monitoring tool and as a crime “deterrent.”

“If someone is going around your house at night, and your motion detector goes off on your Ring doorbell, imagine if you see spotlights and something flying across the window,” Siminoff said, according to CNBC. “You’re probably not going to go into that house.”

Secondly, there is the Ring Rover Cam. Seen by most as an upgrade to Amazon’s 2021 Astro home robot, this free-roaming bot is being pushed more for companies to patrol offices, warehouses, and other workspaces.

But it is a clear indication of where the technology for your home may head next.

The Ring Drone is being touted as a product meeting the moment of consumers eager to keep their most powerful asset protected at every level.

“For years, customers told us they wanted eyes in the places a fixed camera couldn’t reach, and peace of mind in the spots they’d never want one,” said Siminoff in the company’s press release.

“The honest answer wasn’t more cameras; it meant reimagining what a security device could be. That kind of invention is hard, and it takes time. But we kept at it until we got it right—and that's Ring Robotics. It’s not just a new category of security; it’s the beginning of a future where proactive, autonomous protection is something every home and every business can have.”

Priced at $250, the Ring Drone flying indoor security camera is a first-of-its-kind Ring camera, “built from the ground up with AI at its core,” according to the company.

Spec and key features include the following:

Custom flight routes: Homeowners can set routes and a schedule, and Ring Drone flies them automatically. You can also deploy it on demand, as the promo video shows.

Automatic incident response: When a Ring camera, sensor, or alarm is triggered, Ring Drone automatically flies to previously set patrol points to investigate.

Wall-to-wall coverage: With a 148-degree field of view and the ability to rotate 360 degrees, Ring Drone provides a whole-room view in 2K video.

Captures video day or night: Two built-in LED lights activate automatically in low-light environments, so you always get clear, crisp video.

Seamless Ring integration: Works with Ring cameras, doorbells, sensors, and alarms out of the box, and can be controlled from the newly updated Alexa Home Map.

The Ring Drone was announced as part of the launch of Ring Robotics, which takes everything “customers already love and trust about Ring and puts it in motion,” according to the company announcement.

While the Ring Drone is presented as a home product, the company’s debut of Ring Rover is designed for business.

An autonomous security robot, the $1,000 device is designed to give a roving security to offices, warehouses, and other larger footprint facilities.

Admittedly, the company created the Ring Rover after receiving feedback from Amazon Astro customers who said the feature they loved seeing is security on the move.

“As leaders in home and business security, the Ring team took that feedback, leveraged the best of Astro, and built something new—not a home robot that also does security, but a purpose-built security robot,” reads the press release.

Key features and capabilities of Ring Rover include the following:

Full-spectrum scanning: The Ring Rover can travel to any saved checkpoint or room with one tap. It can then execute a complete 360-degree scan to ensure total coverage.

Customizable patrol schedules: Set automated monitoring routes that fit your business schedule, allowing Ring Rover to patrol off-hours when a workspace is empty.

Automated event investigation: Triggers from connected Ring devices prompt Ring Rover to autonomously navigate to designated patrol points to assess the situation.

Height-adjustable periscope camera: An extendable mast allows the camera to see above shelving, counters, and obstacles. Height settings can be customized and saved for specific stops.

Visible and audible deterrents: Equipped with an integrated siren, light tower, and two-way audio, Ring Rover signals an active security presence and enables direct real-time communication.

Continuous 4K video recording: Streams and records up to 4K video during motion and patrols, capturing footage along the entire route for later review.*

The Ring Drone Cam ships in the U.S. on Jan. 27, pending approval from the Federal Communications Commission, while the Ring Rover Cam will begin shipping to users on Dec. 16, the company said.

Dina Sartore-Bodo is the senior editor at Realtor.com covering real estate news, personal finance trends, and interior design. #5538. How Kyle Whissel built eXp’s top real estate team

The San Diego-based CEO recruits up to 15 agents a month, has a dress code and gives his trainer authority to cut newcomers.

Kyle Whissel has a standing instruction for his “60-day” bootcamp trainers: they should be willing to cut people.

His team brings in 10 to 15 new agents a month, puts them through approximately 60 hours of training over two weeks, and gives the trainer a goal of removing two people from each class.

It’s a striking approach from the leader of eXp Realty’s highest-volume U.S. team in San Diego, California. Whissel is CEO of the Whissel Beer Group, formed in 2025 when his Whissel Realty Group merged with Daniel Beer’s Beer Home Team.

According to Whissel, the team made $875 million in sales volume across 1,042 transaction sides last year (it was the first team in San Diego to break 1,000). The median price in San Diego — which is where he likes to focus his attention  (“we love that median price,” he said) — is around $1 million, he told Inman.

They’ve done that by hiring — and retaining — the right people. “We’ll give people an opportunity to prove themselves … but we’ve grown far more by cutting people than simply by hiring more people,” Whissel told Inman‘s Taylor Anderson during an interview at eXpcon in Salt Lake City earlier this month.

The company’s saying: “Expectations without enforcement are simply suggestions.”

Whissel’s recruiting process starts with a conventional, short interview, but he views the company’s two-week training period as a far better measure of whether someone belongs on the team.

Spending 60 hours in training gives leadership a chance to observe how that person behaves, learns and responds to expectations. Role-playing and scripting exercises also reveal whether new agents have the communication skills needed to work with clients.

The process continues after training, too. New agents are assigned mentors, and Whissel said those mentors are empowered to recommend removing someone who fails to meet team standards.

“If you’re going to be disrespectful to our team, I’ll be damned if I’m going to give you a client because you’re probably going to be disrespectful to them too,” he said.

Whissel also has activity and production expectations for agents already on the team. They include participating in role-playing sessions and attending meetings, along with meeting production targets.

Whissel’s hiring philosophy reaches back to his own first job, scooping popcorn at a movie theater, where he would compete with others to see who could serve the most customers. He looks for that same competitiveness in prospective agents, even if their previous accomplishments have little to do with real estate.

An applicant who participated in a college sorority, for example, might be asked whether they held a leadership position. Whissel said he wants to understand whether someone has a history of taking initiative.

In August 2025, Inman reported the merger of Whissel Realty Group and Beer Home Team, two of eXp’s highest-producing organizations. The combined company launched with approximately 160 agents and more than 60 staff members across five offices.

He said the first six months involved understanding the two organizations’ systems and getting them aligned. Whissel now believes it could take 18 months to fully integrate the companies.

“We’re going to be almost flat year-over-year,” he said, referring to the team’s expected 2026 performance, “but we’re setting up for a really, really big 2027,” he said. “You’ve gotta take a step back to take two steps forward.”

He remains optimistic about 2027, when he expects the operational investments to begin contributing to stronger growth.

Agents need to understand assumable mortgages, he said. “If you are working with a seller … and you’re not asking questions to figure out ‘does this seller have an assumable mortgage?’ (If it’s FHA, VA or USDA, those are assumable), I’m gonna beat you, because I am asking those questions.”

To find out whether a mortgage is assumable, agents simply need to get the closing disclosure from the seller. “It’s simple,” he said.

#5537. The next chapter for Red Hat: AI agents rewrite the cloud-native playbook

Red Hat LLC has spent years making Kubernetes manageable for enterprises that would rather run applications than tend clusters. As AI agents move into production, the company is extending that experience to a new generation of workloads. AI agents don’t just consume infrastructure. They execute commands, call external tools, access enterprise systems and take actions that can affect the business. The next phase of AI agent infrastructure requires enforceable security boundaries alongside efficient resource management.

Red Hat arrives at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America in Salt Lake City this week with a growing portfolio of technologies addressing those requirements. OpenShift provides the Kubernetes foundation; its work with Nvidia Corp. on OpenShell addresses agent execution and security; and the llm-d project has reached version 1.0 with capabilities for serving the context-heavy workloads agents create. Together, these developments position Red Hat to help enterprises manage agentic AI through open, Kubernetes-based infrastructure.

Unlike conventional applications, autonomous agents can generate commands, invoke tools and delegate work across multiple systems. That flexibility creates opportunities for automation while increasing the importance of consistent access controls and oversight.

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exploration of how cloud-native infrastructure is evolving to support enterprise AI, with Red Hat and the broader Kubernetes ecosystem addressing the security, operational efficiency and scalability requirements of autonomous agents. (* Disclosure below.)

The rapid adoption of OpenClaw has brought renewed attention to agent security. An agent that can read files, run shell commands and make network calls needs clearly defined permissions and isolation to operate safely within enterprise environments.

Red Hat’s response centers on its collaboration with Nvidia around OpenShell, a runtime that places agents inside isolated execution environments and applies policy to their access. Nvidia developed OpenShell; Red Hat is working with Nvidia and the wider community to integrate the technology into Red Hat AI and its open hybrid cloud platform. Red Hat’s announcement describes the work as part of a broader effort to bring security-focused agentic AI capabilities to enterprise infrastructure.

OpenShell uses sandboxing, process-aware policy and controls over network access and credentials. Red Hat has also described how OpenShell can work with OpenShift’s sandboxed containers, adding application-level restrictions inside a virtual-machine boundary. These complementary layers govern agent behavior and isolate the environments in which agents operate, as Red Hat explains in its technical overview of layered sandboxing.

The distinction matters because sandboxing does not make an agent trustworthy. It limits the damage an agent can cause when its instructions, generated code or external inputs lead it somewhere they should not.

In a recent interview with theCUBE, Pete Cheslock, principal AI community architect at Red Hat, described how OpenShell builds on Kubernetes infrastructure: “The agent sandbox is one of them, so that you can deploy these agents in a secure way using Kubernetes native APIs.” His comments get to the central issue: enterprises cannot delegate authority to agents without defining and enforcing its limits.

Red Hat Chief Technology Officer Chris Wright also emphasized the importance of agent isolation in a May interview with theCUBE. Agents that can take real actions in a business need sandboxing and least-privilege protections, he explained.

“You’ve got to give it the right sandboxing. You’ve got to put protections around the agent, give it least privileges so it doesn’t think about read versus read-write — very big difference,” Wright said in SiliconANGLE’s coverage of Red Hat Summit.

Beyond sandboxing, enterprises must manage agent identities, data permissions, tool access and authorization. That distinction is reinforced by Paul Nashawaty, practice lead and principal analyst for application development, modernization and cloud native at theCUBE Research, whose September analysis of AI agent governance examines the difference between observing what agents do and proving what they were authorized to do. The research identifies runtime enforcement, delegated authority and verifiable audit evidence as requirements that become more important as autonomous systems move into production.

“This creates an opportunity for platforms that can unify application development, infrastructure orchestration, security and observability rather than adding another layer of disconnected tooling,” Nashawaty said.

Beyond security, agents create new requirements for inference infrastructure. An agent may call a model, retrieve information, invoke a tool and return to the model with additional context. Each interaction consumes compute, memory and network capacity, while the system must preserve enough context to continue efficiently.

Red Hat’s llm-d project addresses part of that problem. Founded by Red Hat, IBM Corp., Google Cloud, CoreWeave Inc. and Nvidia, and now governed by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, llm-d uses Kubernetes-native components to distribute inference across accelerators and manage traffic between them.

The project reached version 1.0 on Oct. 20, adding session-aware routing, turn-priority scheduling, multi-tenant quality-of-service controls and high-availability operations. Those features aim to keep multi-turn requests close to cached context, prioritize latency-sensitive work and reduce disruption during maintenance. The Red Hat release announcement and Google Cloud’s technical overview describe the release.

The architecture provides operators with additional options for coordinating inference workloads and managing accelerator resources within Kubernetes.

Red Hat Senior Vice President and AI Chief Technology Officer Brian Stevens described one of llm-d’s central architectural decisions in SiliconANGLE’s report on Kubernetes inference: “We can independently scale the processing of the input from the production of the tokens.”

Other infrastructure providers are addressing complementary requirements. ScaleOps Labs Ltd. focuses on GPU utilization and resource optimization across Kubernetes workloads. Vultr Holdings LLC offers GPU infrastructure and Kubernetes-based model deployment, while Broadcom Inc. positions VMware Cloud Foundation as a private-cloud platform for Kubernetes and AI workloads. Together, these offerings reflect expanding enterprise choices for resource optimization, accelerator capacity and private-cloud operations.

The operational gap appears in theCUBE Research’s “Day 0 Build, Test Survey Research Report.” Based on a survey of 375 IT, development, operations and platform engineering professionals, the research found that cloud-native adoption is widespread but maturity remains uneven. Inconsistent automated testing, fragmented developer tools and gaps in rollback capabilities continue to complicate production deployment.

“Ninety-two percent of organizations are integrating AI into at least one stage of the software development lifecycle, while 79% expect full-scale AI agent adoption within the next three years,” Nashawaty said, adding that approximately 30% still face operational readiness challenges.

The broader industry is also moving toward production-scale infrastructure. The CNCF’s 2026 annual cloud-native survey found that 82% of container users run Kubernetes in production and that 66% of organizations hosting generative AI workloads use Kubernetes for some or all inference. Those figures reinforce Kubernetes’ expanding role as enterprises adopt AI workloads.

The open-source ecosystem is expanding alongside agentic AI adoption. On Nov. 5, Google announced the donation of Agent Substrate, gVisor and OpenRL to the CNCF following their acceptance into its Sandbox program in October. The projects address agent execution, isolation and reinforcement-learning workflows. Agent Substrate separates agent sessions and identities from active compute, allowing idle environments to pause and resume; gVisor provides an additional isolation boundary for untrusted code; and OpenRL supports reinforcement-learning post-training on Kubernetes. Google’s announcement describes the projects and their transition into CNCF governance.

These contributions complement broader efforts across the Kubernetes community. Red Hat is a co-founder of llm-d and is integrating Nvidia’s OpenShell into its enterprise AI platform, while Google is contributing technologies related to runtime and training requirements. The common emphasis on open infrastructure creates opportunities for interoperability as enterprise AI systems mature.

Broadcom added another development on Nov. 9, announcing that its VM API project had been accepted into the CNCF Sandbox. The project aims to let organizations manage virtual machines through Kubernetes application programming interfaces across different infrastructure providers. This extends the Kubernetes conversation to managing virtual machines alongside containerized workloads.

Project Lightwell adds another dimension to Red Hat’s enterprise strategy. Announced with IBM in May, the $5 billion initiative aims to use AI-assisted vulnerability identification and validated fixes to strengthen open-source software supply chains. The initiative extends security efforts to the software dependencies supporting production workloads.

Sam Weston, industry analyst for enterprise applications, development and modernization at theCUBE Research, points to the infrastructure mix enterprises already operate.

“With our data showing 61.8% of enterprises run hybrid deployments and an additional 10% operate across multi-cloud environments, Red Hat’s hybrid-first platform strategy aligns closely with where enterprise infrastructure lives today,” Weston said.

Red Hat’s established OpenShift footprint provides a foundation for connecting these developments. As enterprises deploy more autonomous workloads, the company is positioned to combine Kubernetes orchestration, agent isolation and distributed inference within its broader hybrid cloud strategy.

The opportunity extends beyond any individual project. OpenShift, llm-d and OpenShell illustrate how Red Hat is contributing to an open infrastructure model that accommodates both conventional applications and emerging AI agents.

For enterprises, the objective is to make AI workloads secure, efficient and manageable without losing control over how autonomous systems operate. Red Hat’s work across the Kubernetes ecosystem reflects how that foundation is taking shape.
