#5492. /C O R R E C T I O N - Supermetrics/

In the news release, Supermetrics Launches Campaign Manager, Bringing AI-Powered Insights and Campaign Execution Together, issued 10-Nov-2026 by Supermetrics over PR Newswire, we are advised by the company that changes have been made. The complete, corrected release follows, with additional details at the end:

New AI-powered capabilities help marketers move from answers to action across advertising platforms, with trusted data, human oversight and control over campaign decisions

HELSINKI, Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Supermetrics, the marketing intelligence platform powering more than 200,000 businesses, today announced the launch of Campaign Management, a new solution designed to help marketers bridge the gap between understanding campaign performance and taking action with AI. By bringing cross-platform performance marketing data and campaign actions into AI chats, Supermetrics is helping businesses turn AI marketing recommendations into optimization actions with a simple in-chat approval.

For years, marketers have relied on increasingly sophisticated tools to understand campaign performance, yet acting on those insights often remains a fragmented, manual process. Teams must navigate multiple advertising platforms, reconcile disconnected data and translate recommendations into campaign changes, losing time and slowing their ability to respond to campaign issues and changing performance marketing priorities.

Campaign Management addresses this challenge by connecting marketing intelligence directly to campaign execution. Built on Supermetrics' established data infrastructure, the solution combines trusted, connected marketing data with AI-powered workflows, so marketers can identify opportunities, evaluate recommended changes and take action across advertising channels from whichever AI solution they currently use.

"There's pressure on every marketing team to put AI to work, but not everyone is starting from the same place," said Anssi Rusi, CEO of Supermetrics. "Some are still getting their data connected. Others are already using tools like Claude to analyze performance and work out what to do next. For those teams, the question is, 'Why do I have to leave this conversation to make the change?' That's who we're building Campaign Management for. They want to act on the recommendations where they're already working, while staying in control of what happens to their campaigns."

From Marketing Intelligence to Intelligent Action

Campaign Management represents the next step in Supermetrics' evolution from marketing data integration to AI-powered marketing intelligence and execution.

Rather than relying on isolated, platform-specific recommendations, Campaign Management is designed to help marketers make decisions informed by a broader view of their marketing performance and business priorities.

The solution introduces capabilities designed to help marketing teams:

Premier Cru Solutions, a six-person digital marketing agency serving premium and luxury wineries, is already saving around 30% of its time using Supermetrics Campaign Management and Supermetrics for Claude. The team builds, restructures and optimizes Google Ads and Meta campaigns from one chat, directing the saved time toward deeper client analysis. In one Google Search rebuild, the agency completed a campaign build estimated at 14 hours in two hours, before final fine-tuning.

"Getting our data into Claude with Supermetrics changed how we analyze," said Matthew Thompson, Founder and Head of Growth at Premier Cru Solutions. "Campaign Management is changing how we work. We find the problem and make the fix across Google and Meta from the same chat, and every change gets checked before it goes live. A Search build we estimated at 14 hours, took two. We aren't using that time to take on more clients. We're using the time and richer data to give our clients answers they may have never had before."

Building a More Connected Advertising Ecosystem

As advertising becomes increasingly complex, marketers need solutions that bring together data, intelligence and execution across the platforms where their campaigns operate.

Supermetrics' Campaign Management can manage campaigns across Google, Meta, LinkedIn, Microsoft Advertising,TikTok, Snapchat and ChatGPT Ads, reflecting the growing importance of trusted data connectivity and more actionable marketing intelligence.

"Snapchat is dedicated to helping businesses of all sizes reach new customers and drive growth. Our partnership with Supermetrics helps advertisers turn insights into action with the AI tools they already use, simplifying campaign management and making it easier to drive better results." â Alfie Villanueva Brandt, Senior Manager, Ad Product Partnerships, Snapchat

"At Microsoft Advertising, we believe AI has the ability to make marketing simpler, more connected and more actionable. Together with partners like Supermetrics, we're helping marketers turn trusted, connected data into better decisions and faster action, while keeping them in control" said Jason McKay, VP Partnerships, Microsoft Advertising.

"Agentic AI is transforming marketing and it requires an interconnected ecosystem for marketers to realize its full potential. The TikTok MCP Server enables developers and platforms to build AI solutions that connect seamlessly with TikTok, helping reduce complexity, move faster, and drive real business outcomes" said David Kaufman, Global Head of Monetization Product Partnerships, TikTok

The introduction of Campaign Management builds on Supermetrics' broader investment in making marketing data more accessible, actionable and AI-ready.

As AI becomes more deeply embedded in marketing workflows, the challenge for organizations is shifting from simply accessing information to ensuring AI-driven recommendations are grounded in reliable data, relevant business context and appropriate human oversight.

With Campaign Management, Supermetrics is extending its role beyond helping marketers understand performance to helping them act on that understanding.

The launch also builds on Supermetrics' recent advancements in AI-powered marketing workflows, including its integration with Claude, reinforcing the company's vision of a more connected marketing ecosystem in which AI can support the full journey from data analysis to informed action.

"AI will only be as valuable as the data and context behind it," added Rusi. "The future of marketing isn't about handing every decision over to AI. It's about giving marketers the intelligence, confidence and control to act at the speed their businesses demand. Campaign Management is an important step toward making that future a reality."

About SupermetricsSupermetrics is the Marketing Intelligence Platform that helps marketers bring together data from unlimited marketing and sales sources, get answers they can trust, and act on them directly from their preferred AI chat tool. More than 200,000 businesses worldwide use Supermetrics, including TBWA, Dentsu, Dyson, Heineken, AirFrance, Levi's and Deloitte. Founded in 2013 and headquartered in Helsinki, Finland, Supermetrics has 350 employees across Europe, Asia and North America.

#5491. From chaos to close: Holly Mabery says agents need to quell confusion

eXp Realty chief brokerage officer Holly Mabery told NAR NXT attendees to separate headlines from actionable local impacts. She said clearer, story-driven communication and stronger CRM follow-up can help agents win share even if 2027 sales fall below 4 million.  AI Summary

In Holly Mabery’s view, 2026 has been a year filled with chaos. The year started off full of optimism and promise and much like many new year’s resolutions quickly turned. But, Mabery, who serves as eXp Realty’s chief brokerage officer, believes agents can turn the chaos into closed transactions.

“You see a bunch of headlines and does anybody feel like they just want to go back to bed? And then it is like how do I stay ahead? What does that look like? What do I say to people, consumers, team members?” Mabery said during a session at the National Association of Realtors 2026 NXT conference over the weekend.

For agents, brokers and team leaders feeling overwhelmed by it all, Mabery said it’s first important to remember that they are not going through this alone and that other agents and brokers are asking themselves the same questions. From there, the key to navigating the chaos, according to Mabery is figuring out what the most important things are and making them relevant to the person sitting in front of them.

“I can’t teach advanced geometry to a six-year-old. But I can show them the difference  between a square and a triangle,” Mabery, a HousingWire Woman of Influence, Insider and Vanguard award winner, said. “The more you and I make things relevant and connect the dots for people, it becomes easier. But also I find that in connecting the dots, that trust layer opens up and everybody exhales.”

In markets and environments currently experienced by real estate professionals, Mabery said it is easy to allow the chaos to turn in confusion.

“When we have confusion, then there is no action as we lose opportunities. The more people are confused, the more they are afraid to move. It is like being stuck in really deep, thick mud,” she said.

To prevent this from happening with their agents and clients, Mabery said brokers and agents need to recognize what has happened and explain it using no jargon terms and then translate it to their specific market or situation by employing a noise versus action filter. This will allow them to understand what a national headline means for them and what actions they may need to take as a result.

Mabery used an example of the Federal Reserve’s rate hike in September, noting that most people feel this is a buyer problem and would have a conversation with their buy-side clients about how this impacts them and how they may need to change their offer strategy. But, Mabery said in her view it is actually a seller problem.

“This is a seller problem because now, when less buyers feel like they can take action, it falls to the seller to take action,” Mabery said. “What are you willing to do in this market to actually make a difference to get people into your home and writing an offer?”

When you provide consumers or even agents with information like this, Mabery says it enables them to feel empowered and hopeful.

“As you look at 2027, I’m not scared for 3.8 million transactions, I’m just hunting for my piece of it,” Mabery said.

With agents and brokers seriously contending with the possibility of a sub-4 million home sales environment in 2027, Mabery said it is important that agents and brokers find news and data sources they can trust, that they get back in touch with past-clients in their CRM and that they work on their story-telling skills.

For Mabery, keeping client-facing messages short, personal and story-driven will enable agents to better connect with consumers and build trust.

“The relationships you and I have are making all the difference in the world,” Mabery said. “The more confidence you build the more you inspire people to take action. When people are confused they stop taking action and we don’t sell anything and that is what we saw in 2026.”

Despite this, Mabery noted that people still move and buy homes due to life events, inviting real estate professionals into their inner circles during some of the most exciting and trying times, but in order to be invited into these moments agents need to build trust in advance.

“Take away the chaos and talk about what is next,” she said. “I want you to calm the fears as we go forward. The more you share your knowledge, your value goes up. And if I don’t take action, is anybody hurt? No. But if I do, I get to help them.”

#5490. AI-driven managed security startup Daylight raises $80M on 40-fold revenue growth

Managed detection and response startup Daylight Security Inc. today revealed that it has raised $80 million in new funding after what it says was more than 40-fold revenue growth over the past year.

Daylight provides managed security operations in which artificial intelligence agents carry most of the routine load. Each customer gets a set of agents built by Daylight’s own security engineers and tailored to its systems and workflows. Decisions that need human judgment stay with those engineers.

Judging when to trust AI has itself become a bigger part of security work. In a survey of 856 cybersecurity professionals who use the technology, published by ISC2 Inc. in July, 65% said they spend more time on that call than they did a year earlier. Checking AI output takes longer for 63% of them.

Daylight lets customers hand over security operations entirely or run them jointly with an internal team. A third option puts forward-deployed Daylight engineers alongside the customer’s own staff. Customers also get access to Daylight’s Aura platform, which security teams can use to investigate their environment in natural language or to search a centralized data lake that the company began offering as a managed service in June.

According to Daylight, its service detects a threat within seconds and has it contained within minutes. Traditional managed security providers take up to 10 times as long, the company claims. Daylight’s coverage also reaches the AI systems that enterprises deploy internally, so an alert about prompt injection or a risky Model Context Protocol integration is investigated alongside identity, endpoint and cloud activity.

Visual collaboration company Miro is already using that capability. Other customers include AI app builder Lovable Labs Inc., password manager LastPass US LP, financial research startup Rogo Technologies Inc. and emerging-markets payments company dLocal Ltd.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Hagai Shapira said the measure of a security operation is shifting from headcount toward “how effectively AI agents can take on increasingly complex security work.” Under his model, human engineers still implement and govern the agents as they grow more capable.

Daylight’s founders met while serving in Israel’s Unit 8200 intelligence unit. Both later worked at security automation company Torq Technologies Ltd., co-founder Eldad Rudich as its first employee and eventual vice president of research and development. Shapira was an early product leader there and worked closely with enterprise security teams.

Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives led the Series B round. Existing backers Bain Capital Ventures, Craft Ventures Management, Vintage Investment Partners and Maple Capital also participated. Craft Ventures led Daylight’s $33 million Series A round a year ago, three months after a $7 million seed round.

Irit Kahan, managing director and global head of cybersecurity investing within Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives, said pairing human expertise with agentic technology could let Daylight’s customers respond “at machine speed.”

Daylight will use the funds to expand in the U.S. and enter markets across Europe, the Middle East, Africa and Asia-Pacific. The company also plans to grow its security engineering and technology teams and keep developing Aura. Investors have now put $120 million into the company.

#5489. Coinbase Bank Gets Full OCC Approval as Ripple Leads Crypto Banking Push

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Coinbase has moved closer to the center of the US financial system after securing full approval for its national trust bank charter. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) recorded the charter as effective on November 6. The development gives Coinbase a federally supervised framework for expanding its institutional custody and digital asset services.

The approval completes a process that began with Coinbase’s application in October 2025. The OCC granted conditional approval on April 2, 2026, before recording the charter as consummated. Coinbase can now operate through its national trust company under federal supervision.

Coinbase follows Ripple’s final OCC approval on October 26. Two major crypto companies have now secured national trust bank charters within weeks. Their progress shows how digital asset firms are increasingly seeking access to regulated financial infrastructure rather than operating outside traditional banking frameworks.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Coinbase’s approval follows a similar regulatory path taken by Ripple. The company received conditional approval for Ripple National Trust Bank in December 2025. Its final approval arrived on October 26, completing the process ahead of Coinbase.

Ripple’s charter has specific implications for its stablecoin business. Ripple National Trust Bank can manage the segregated reserves backing RLUSD. It can also act as collateral trustee and provide fiduciary digital asset custody services.

RLUSD will continue to be issued by Standard Custody & Trust Company, Ripple’s New York-regulated trust company. The new federal charter adds another layer of supervision around its reserve management and institutional services.

Coinbase Bank has a different commercial opportunity. Its national trust company can provide federally supervised custody and fiduciary services to institutional clients. Coinbase previously said the charter would support its Prime custody business and other regulated services.

The growing number of crypto trust bank approvals has not gone unchallenged. The Independent Community Bankers of America (ICBA) filed a lawsuit against the OCC on October 2. The group argues that the regulator exceeded its authority by expanding access to national trust charters.

The banking association claims crypto companies receive federal banking credibility without meeting several requirements imposed on traditional banks. These include FDIC insurance, certain capital and liquidity standards, and Community Reinvestment Act obligations.

🚨 BIG: ICBA Sues OCC Over Crypto Trust Bank ChartersThe Independent Community Bankers of America (ICBA) has sued the OCC, arguing that its rules allowing crypto firms to obtain national trust bank charters exceed the agency’s legal authority and do not impose the same… pic.twitter.com/kJ8fVcXPoj

The lawsuit challenges the OCC’s March 2026 rule and related guidance. It argues that the regulator has stretched the national trust charter beyond its original statutory purpose.

The dispute could have consequences beyond Coinbase and Ripple. A successful challenge could complicate the regulatory pathway for other digital asset companies pursuing similar charters.

However, the OCC’s approach reflects a wider shift in US financial regulation. The agency has increasingly opened the door to crypto custody, payments, and stablecoin-related activities under federal supervision. This shift also creates opportunities for emerging blockchain infrastructure projects.

Coinbase Bank’s approval represents more than another regulatory milestone. It shows that crypto companies are competing for a larger role in the financial infrastructure institutions will use.

#5487. Nearly Half of the Stolen Binance Basket Had a Freeze Button

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Tether, Circle and Ripple could freeze their tokens within hours of the Binance theft, and they did.

There is no one to call for the stolen bitcoin, ether and TRX, which makes up most of the money Binance is unlikely to get back.

In most hacks, the stolen total is the headline. In the Binance breach, the more useful number is how much of the stolen money could be stopped.

On-chain trackers estimate the stolen basket at more than $5.6 billion. Binance itself has put the estimated impact at $6.3 billion and says nearly $3 billion is frozen. That freeze was possible only because of how the stolen money was made up.

Almost half of it was in tokens whose issuers can freeze them. The rest was in assets that no company, foundation or council can stop on their main blockchains.

That second half explains why recovery stalled at about $3 billion despite a fast industry response. It is also the part Binance will most likely have to pay for itself.

The per-asset breakdown from on-chain trackers is:

Sorting by whether the issuer can freeze the token gives a near-even split:

That one division shaped everything that happened after the theft.

The response on the freezable side was unusually fast:

The pattern is the same in every case. A company that issues a token on a public blockchain usually keeps a way to block specific addresses from moving it. Critics see that power as a central point of control, but in this theft it worked. Within hours, the largest dollar-value block of the stolen money could not be moved.

There was one notable intervention outside the token issuers. On Arbitrum, the Arbitrum Security Council took emergency action and moved 74,559,805 ARB and 8,425 ETH, about $30.5 million, out of an address connected to the exploit.

It shows that some layer-2 networks keep emergency powers their base layers lack. The amount was small next to the size of the theft.

The other half is a different story. Bitcoin has no issuer. Ether on Ethereum's main network has no admin key. TRX is Tron's native coin, and no token issuer sits between the holder and the blockchain. Once these assets reached the attacker's wallets, stopping them depended on exchanges refusing deposits and investigators tracking the funds, not on any freeze function.

Together, the $1.45 billion in BTC, $875 million in ETH and $234 million in TRX make about $2.56 billion. That is close to Binance's own numbers: about $3 billion frozen out of a $6.3 billion estimated impact leaves roughly $3.3 billion still in play, and most of it is in assets nobody can freeze.

The bitcoin figure is the most contested part of the basket. Some BTC moving out of Binance-linked wallets during the incident may have been Binance moving its own reserves to safety rather than attacker withdrawals. So the true unfreezable total could be lower than $2.56 billion, but the split between the two groups is unlikely to change much.

The attacker appeared to understand this difference and acted on it right away.

On-chain records show the main sweep on Ethereum used an EIP-7702 delegation. This feature lets a regular wallet hand control to a smart contract. Within minutes, the drained hot wallet's contents, including more than 1.6 billion USDT, had moved to attacker-controlled addresses.

The clearest example of the next step is on Aave. According to Aave's governance forum update from risk manager LlamaRisk, one wallet in the exploiter's cluster acted between 20:58 and 21:01 UTC:

That trade left freezable USDT locked inside Aave as collateral and gave the attacker wrapped ether, which no issuer can freeze. The position stays over-collateralized, and LlamaRisk said it "does not put Aave suppliers at risk." The ETH, however, was already gone.

Aave responded on a large scale. Between 21:42 and 23:04 UTC, its guardian multisigs froze:

The freezes blocked new deposits and borrowing. Reports also describe stablecoins being swapped for ETH on Uniswap.

The race was easy to see in the timeline. Each hour before an issuer froze its token was another hour to swap that token for ether. Tether and Circle reacted within the first hour, so most of the stablecoin stash was frozen before it could be converted.

A freeze stops the attacker, but it does not put money back in Binance's accounts. Frozen tokens stay locked at the attacker's addresses until the issuer decides what to do with them. In past cases, issuers have destroyed frozen tokens and reissued the same amount to the rightful owner, usually after legal or law-enforcement checks. That process takes time, and each issuer has its own procedure.

Binance has said that its initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop. According to the company, that laptop let the attacker reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Binance said it found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked, and that it has revoked the affected address authorization and is working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms.

Deposits and withdrawals were suspended while security checks continue. Binance has not yet given a date for reopening them.

Binance has said it will cover all losses using its SAFU fund and its own money. Grouping the stolen basket by freezability gives a rough picture of what that bill could be.

The roughly $3 billion that is frozen should eventually be recovered, depending on how and when each issuer releases or reissues the tokens. The bitcoin, ether and TRX are another matter. Unless exchanges block deposits and investigators recover funds as they are laundered, that part is effectively gone. It accounts for most of the money Binance will have to cover from its own reserves.

The theft also raises a question for the whole industry. The assets that limited the damage were the issuer-controlled tokens that crypto purists often criticize. The assets that caused the real loss were the ones built so that no one can stop them. Exchanges have long decided hot-wallet sizes by liquidity needs. After this theft, they may also consider which assets in those wallets can still be stopped once they leave.

#5486. RealPlus brings HouseCanary Google Listings to NYC clients

RealPlus is partnering with My State MLS to offer HouseCanary’s Google Listings Program to NYC residential brokerages. Active listings can appear in Google mobile search with photos, pricing, and click-to-contact links to the listing agent.   AI Summary

RealPlus is partnering with My State MLS to make HouseCanary’s Google Listings Program available to its New York City residential brokerage clients, giving brokers and agents a new channel to surface listings directly in Google mobile search results.

The integration allows active listings to appear in mobile search with property photos, pricing and agent contact information, according to the company announcement. The placements appear above traditional sponsored real estate ads and include a click-to-contact feature that connects prospective buyers directly with the listing agent.

For brokerages, the offering effectively functions as an additional digital listing distribution channel, alongside portals and IDX, but inside Google’s search environment where most buyers begin home searches. In a tight lead-conversion market with rising online advertising costs, direct search visibility and agent-connected lead flows can help firms diversify away from solely portal-driven leads.

“We are always looking for ways to expand the value and capabilities we bring to our clients,” Jennifer Boucher, the chief product officer at RealPlus and a HousingWire Insider, said in a statement. “This partnership is a great addition to our offerings, giving brokers and agents another way to put their listings in front of prospective buyers and generate direct connections.”

The HouseCanary Google Listings Program will be available to RealPlus clients later in November and will be offered at no cost to participating listing brokers and agents, the company said.

RealPlus said the move aligns with its broader strategy of building listing and data infrastructure tailored to New York City residential brokerages at a time when firms are reassessing tech stacks, lead sources and marketing spend. For listing agents, a no-cost path to higher placement in search results could support listing presentations and seller expectations around online exposure.

The Google Listings Program is powered by HouseCanary, which negotiates agreements with multiple listing services to send their brokerage members’ listings to Google. Participating MLSs include  Arizona Regional MLS, Bright MLS, California Regional MLS, IRES MLS, Permian Basin Board of Realtors, REcolorado and San Diego MLS.

HouseCanary said it also works directly with brokerages, like the three announced Wednesday, to ensure their listings flow into the program via a participating MLS. Brokerages that want their listings included need either to belong to an MLS that is in the program or to encourage their local MLS to opt in.

Over the past few weeks, HouseCanary has announced that real estate brokerages REMAX Advantage, Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices Florida Properties Group, ENRG Realty, Side and The Keyes Company and Illustrated Properties, all RealTrends Verified firms, have signed on to the program, sharing its listings with HouseCanary via My State MLS.

These announcements also comes as HouseCanary continues to work through its Chapter 11 restructuring. Under the firm’s proposed plan, which remains subject to court approval, HouseCanary is targeting emergence from bankruptcy before year-end, with full recovery for all approved creditors. Management has positioned initiatives such as the Google Listings Program and the AI platform as core to its go-forward strategy while it continues to serve existing customers.

Launched in early 2026 and slated to expand to all eligible U.S. markets this fall, the program is one of several industry experiments that put MLS and brokerage listings in front of consumers in new contexts, potentially changing how buyers first encounter a property and which party — portal, brokerage or platform — captures the initial inquiry.

#5485. Strategy Buys $82M in Bitcoin as STRC Tokenized Stock Adds New Twist to Saylor’s BTC

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Strategy Bitcoin holdings climbed to 850,364 BTC after Michael Saylor’s company purchased another 1,036 Bitcoin for $81.9 million. The latest acquisition came as Bitcoin traded below the company’s average purchase price, putting its enormous treasury under renewed market pressure.

According to a November 9 SEC filing, Strategy bought the Bitcoin between November 2 and 8 at an average price of $79,012 per coin. Its total acquisition cost now stands at $64.16 billion, with an average purchase price of $75,456.

Strategy has acquired 1,036 $BTC and repurchased $188M of $STRC. As of 11/8/26, we hold 850,364 BTC and $4.9B of USD Assets. $MSTR https://t.co/Pxqso5aVRU

The latest purchase also coincided with a $188.3 million repurchase of Strategy’s STRC preferred shares. The company funded both transactions through its common-stock offering program, highlighting how Michael Saylor continues using capital markets to finance its Bitcoin accumulation.

Strategy sold 2,051,348 shares of its Class A common stock through its at-the-market offering program during the reporting period. The sales generated $283.8 million in net proceeds. The company allocated then $81.9 million toward Bitcoin purchases, while $188.3 million went toward repurchasing 1,887,464 STRC preferred shares. Another $13.6 million was allocated to its general USD cash balance.

The latest transactions show how Strategy accumulation involves more than simply issuing shares and purchasing Bitcoin. The company is also actively managing its preferred securities and liquidity.

Strategy maintained approximately $4.77 billion in its USD Reserve and another $146.2 million in general USD Cash. This reserve supports preferred-stock dividends and interest payments on outstanding debt.

Meanwhile, Bitcoin’s decline below Strategy’s average acquisition price has put its treasury underwater on paper. At $74,000 per BTC, the company’s holdings would carry an unrealized loss exceeding $1 billion. But the latest purchase shows that Saylor has not backed away from accumulation despite the weaker market environment.

The $188.3 million repurchase also puts Strategy’s preferred securities back into the spotlight. STRC, known as Stretch, is a variable-rate perpetual preferred stock designed to trade around its $100 stated amount. It pays cash dividends, with its rate adjusted periodically to encourage price stability.

The instrument has also entered the tokenized securities market through Ondo Finance’s STRCon. Launched in April 2026, STRCon provides blockchain-based economic exposure to Strategy’s Stretch preferred stock. The token is available across Ethereum, Solana, and BNB Chain, subject to geographic and investor restrictions.

Tokenholders receive economic exposure and dividend-related benefits, but do not obtain conventional shareholder voting rights. This gives Strategy’s digital credit securities another distribution channel. Investors outside traditional brokerage platforms can access tokenized exposure through supported blockchain infrastructure.

However, tokenized trading does not generate fresh capital for Strategy automatically. Secondary-market transactions change ownership between investors and do not directly fund additional Bitcoin purchases. Still, this fits into Strategy’s longer-term ambition to build digital credit products for an increasingly tokenized financial system.

Strategy’s latest purchase arrived during a difficult period for institutional Bitcoin demand. US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $1.3 billion in net outflows last week. Last Friday alone accounted for $411.9 million in withdrawals.

BlackRock’s IBIT led Friday’s outflows with approximately $403 million in redemptions. Fidelity’s FBTC recorded $42.8 million in inflows, offering only a partial offset.

Bitcoin also fell toward $74,000 this morning, reaching its weakest level since August. The decline followed broader crypto selling pressure and growing concerns surrounding regulatory uncertainty as AI stocks slide.

The contrast between ETF withdrawals and Strategy’s continued accumulation highlights two different approaches to Bitcoin exposure. ETF investors can reduce exposure through daily redemptions, while Strategy continues using equity financing and its preferred-stock structure to expand its treasury.

The latest Bitcoin acquisition from Strategy reinforces the company’s long-term commitment. Strategy Bitcoin holdings now exceed 850,000 BTC, leaving the company with more than 4% of Bitcoin’s maximum supply.

Whether that commitment pays off will depend heavily on Bitcoin’s next market cycle, alongside Strategy’s ability to maintain access to capital markets.

#5483. Third spaces perform a star turn in this new Florida master plan

Wyld Oaks, a 215-acre mixed-use project in Apopka near Orlando, is underway with 325 apartments starting. The plan totals 6,000 multifamily units, 300,000 SF retail, and major nonresidential uses after a nearly 2-year delay tied to financing constraints.  AI Summary

In a crowded, competitive and bumpy market, residential developers and builders do their best to stand out in a sea of sameness. Some bet that they’ll seize a competitive edge by leaning into walkable communities with “third spaces,” ones where residents can easily connect with one another and feel a sense of belonging.

Wyld Oaks, an upcoming mixed-use community near Orlando, Florida, where construction is now underway, will put that thesis to the test. In October, Hathaway Development became the first developer to begin horizontal construction at Wyld Oaks, where it is building 325 apartment units.

That’s for starters. Once fully built out, the community is expected to have 6,000 multifamily units and a small adjoining single-family portion with fewer than 100 homes.

Residential, mind you, is only part of the plan. Wyld Oaks is designed around a walkable main street anchored by a large park and 300,000 square feet of retail space. Elsewhere in the community, the master plan calls for two hotels, a medical campus, 1.5 million square feet of industrial and distribution space, multiple other parks, an outdoor concert venue and a gas station.

For Wyld Oaks master developer Joseph Beninati, the goal is to create a walkable, mixed-use community that functions like a complete neighborhood, with daily needs all within walking or biking distance.

“Could you take your car? Of course you can,” Beninati said in an interview with HousingWire TBD. “But the option to walk is going to be there.”

With walkability at its core, Wyld Oaks stands apart from the overwhelming majority of new suburban development in the region, which is largely car-centric.

Getting the project off the ground has been difficult, however. The original multifamily development, which only just broke ground, was slated to begin in late 2024 or early 2025. The delay resulted from a challenging local multifamily capital environment that has plagued many other Sun Belt markets.

The 215-acre Wyld Oaks community is located in Apopka, a high-growth suburb of Orlando that saw its population grow by roughly 20% between 2020 and 2025. Despite this growth, and the rapid growth of adjacent communities, there remain relatively few walkable, mixed-use neighborhoods for residents and visitors alike.

This need in the market was among the top considerations for Wyld Oaks, which was designed with walkability, livability and community in mind.

“It all starts with density, and trail systems and parks, and having everything closer to one another as opposed to further apart. We have multifamily, and we’re working on retail, food and beverage, coffee stores and grocery stores, all within walking distance,” Beninati said. “Run the list. [Residents] need fitness. They need healthcare. They need a convenience store and daily conveniences, dry cleaning, hair salons and barber shops.”

All of the commercial uses designed within easy walking distances in the community will work together to keep residents in the neighborhood, bring in employees to work at the industrial park and various businesses and draw in visitors to enjoy the local shops, restaurants and parks. Once fully built out, Beninati expects, or at least hopes, that Wyld Oaks will become a top-tier regional destination.

“Economic activity begets economic activity. If you’re bringing your kids to the dentist, that allows you to also maybe do a little grocery shopping. Or if you’re going to work out and you’re with some friends, maybe you’re going to go out and have a drink or supper together. When everything is in one place, it allows that to happen,” Beninati explained.

Beninati envisions a neighborhood where residents can get outdoors and meet one another, whether at local parks, restaurants, the community’s future farmers market or other events. For visitors, he wants a community that is memorable and draws people back in.

“For me, some of the softer things would be, are prom pictures getting taken and wedding pictures getting taken there? Or is it a meaningful place that the community rallies around? Is there a Christmas tree, and is there going to be a Halloween event for the kids? Things like that are what make a community something that is memorable,” he said.

Although Wyld Oaks is primarily multifamily and non-residential, homebuilders could potentially learn lessons from it. The community’s emphasis on third spaces – places that bridge work, home and school – where residents can connect and feel a sense of belonging, could apply just as well to many single-family neighborhoods.

Central Florida, like many other high-growth Sun Belt markets, experienced a post-COVID multifamily building boom. A surge in new construction following the pandemic led to a coinciding surge in new deliveries.

In 2021 and 2022, developers delivered about 8,500 to 8,800 new multifamily units in the Orlando MSA, according to data from Cushman & Wakefield. In 2023 and 2024, the number of deliveries rose to about 12,500 and 13,000, while 2025 saw about 11,000 new units completed.

Like many other Sun Belt markets, this surge in completions oversupplied the market and pressured rents to soften. As a result, financing new multifamily projects in Central Florida became quite challenging by 2024, the reason the first multifamily community at Wyld Oaks was delayed by nearly two years.

According to Beninati, the biggest challenge in the multifamily financing environment in the Orlando market over the past couple of years hasn’t been securing construction loans so much as finding equity investors to fund projects. Investors have grown more discriminating, directing available capital toward established developers with strong track records and projects in desirable locations.

In Wyld Oaks’ case, the developer’s reputation and the project’s location and desirable master plan helped it secure an equity partner, despite the challenging environment.

However, Beninati believes local financing conditions may be starting to improve. A slowdown in new multifamily development over the past couple of years means that the market has become more balanced, and rent power has begun to stabilize. That dynamic could help other multifamily projects become more financially viable.

For Beninati, breaking ground on the community’s first phase was a major milestone, especially after a delay of nearly two years. But it is only a small piece of a much larger vision, and bringing the full community to life will take years, with market conditions shifting along the way. Weathering those changes, Beninati said, comes down to one thing.

“I think it’s just patience. This is a business where you need to be incredibly, incredibly patient,” he said. “It doesn’t just happen overnight. That’s the nature of the real estate business.”

#5482. CoreWeave arrests stock slide after posting a strong earnings beat and raising its full-year guidance

Neocloud infrastructure darling CoreWeave Inc. delivered an impressive revenue beat and raised its full-year guidance today as it demonstrated that demand for artificial intelligence computing remains strong, pushing its stock higher in late trading.

The report comes at a prickly moment for the AI industry as investors increasingly sour on heavily indebted cloud infrastructure startups, while the broader market continues to get to grips with the spy scandal surrounding Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Jensen Huang.

The company reported a third-quarter loss before certain costs such as stock compensation of $1.27 per share, trailing Wall Street’s target of a $1.16 per share loss. But the 168% growth in revenue meant sales came to $3.66 billion, topping expectations of $3.55 billion. All told, CoreWeave reported a net loss in the quarter of $709 million, rising from a $110 million net loss in the same period one year earlier.

Investors may be pleased with CoreWeave’s guidance, though. Company executives said they’re now looking for between $1.275 billion and $1.375 billion in adjusted operating income and $13 billion to $13.3 billion in revenue for the full year. Wall Street analysts are looking for just $1.07 billion in adjusted operating income and $12.86 billion in total sales. CoreWeave’s forecast is notably much higher than the $960 million to $1.15 billion in adjusted operating income and $12.4 billion to $13.2 billion in revenue it had forecast three months earlier.

The report was well-received by investors, as CoreWeave’s stock climbed more than 5% in late trading, helping put the brakes on a slide that has seen the company lose more than 40% of its value over the last month. Many investors have sought to abandon stocks that are closely tied to the AI infrastructure buildout amid fears that rising interest rates have made capital much more difficult to come by. Recently, some CoreWeave bond yields have topped 16%.

CoreWeave Chief Executive Michael Intrator (pictured) told analysts on a conference call that most of the company’s capital requirements in fiscal 2027 will be sourced from clients via pre-payments on infrastructure services and from hardware partners such as Nvidia. He added that the company will also seek to raise a “limited amount” in outside funding.

When pressed on this, CoreWeave’s finance chief Nitin Agrawal said the company plans to raise new debt that will be tied to a set of contracts. “At current yields we do not intend to issue additional parent-level unsecured debt through 2027,” he told analysts. “By contrast, the asset-level secured debt market has remained stable, with our loans continuing to trade around par value.”

CoreWeave, along with other neoclouds like Nebius Group N.V., which is set to report its own earnings results on Thursday, has become increasingly reliant on its hardware partner Nvidia as a major benefactor. Nvidia provides CoreWeave with not only the graphics processing units needed to populate its data centers, but also much of the capital it needs to procure those chips.

Eessentially it’s recycling the money it earns throughout the AI economy in order to keep everything ticking over. But investors have become concerned about the long-term viability of what looks like an increasingly circular economy, and Nvidia’s stock has struggled to maintain momentum this year.

With this week’s revelations that Nvidia boss Jensen Huang had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, the chipmaker’s stock has lost almost 10% of its value to start the week. Nvidia’s board of directors has responded by launching an internal investigation, hiring the services of the high-profile legal firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to look into Huang’s personal life and determine if any company or national security secrets were compromised.

The fallout from that probe will likely have a strong bearing on CoreWeave’s fortunes going forward, as will next week’s widely anticipated initial public offering from AI leader Anthropic PBC. In an update to its IPO prospectus earlier today, the model maker said it’s hoping to achieve a $1.4 trillion valuation through its share sale.

In the meantime, CoreWeave continues to forge ahead with its buildout. During the quarter it said it’s planning to build its first data centers in Asia. It also announced a new cloud-based service called Forge for running and evaluating AI models.

The company said it hopes to have 1.85 gigawatts of active compute power in service by the end of the year, and anticipates its capital expenditure will reach between $37 billion and $39 billion. That’s more or less in line with the Street’s forecast of $37.69 billion in capex this year.

At the end of the quarter, CoreWeave’s total debt was approaching $47 billion. Like its much larger peers in the cloud computing industry, such as Amazon Web Services Inc., Microsoft Corp. and Oracle Corp., CoreWeave is racing to add more compute capacity to serve its clients.

But there are signs it may struggle to do this in the U.S. Last week, American voters either backed restrictions on data center construction or rejected pro-data center development measures in 40 of 41 states.

Intrator addressed those concerns in the conference call, insisting that he wasn’t overly concerned. “If data center construction across the sector were to slow, installed compute becomes scarcer and the knock-on effect is that GPU pricing may stay higher for longer,” he said.

In the meantime, CoreWeave continues to see demand for cloud compute escalate, and is now sitting on a massive $132.5 billion revenue backlog, Intrator said. That’s up from just $104 billion three months earlier.

(the "Issuer" or the "Company"), an affiliate of Nielsen Holdings Limited ("Nielsen"), announced today that it has priced an offering of $1,400,000,000 aggregate principal amount of 10.500% Senior Secured Notes due 2033 (the "Notes"). #5480. Mamdani gives nonprofits first dibs on buying apartment buildings

Mayor Zohran Mamdani signed COPA, requiring owners to notify the city and qualified nonprofits before selling covered buildings. The law takes effect in 1 year, as a 38 building portfolio with 850 mostly rent stabilized units heads to foreclosure auctions.  AI Summary

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani signed legislation Tuesday giving vetted nonprofits a first shot at buying troubled city apartment buildings.

The new measure arrived too late to spare hundreds of rent-stabilized units from foreclosure, a second loss in Mamdani’s bid to protect such units.

Mamdani ran for office and won on creating and protecting affordable housing. National attention has since focused on his efforts to build more housing and cut red tape. His political inspiration and influence have spread to other parts of the country.

Nithya Raman is a prime example. Under a similar affordability theme, the Los Angeles City Council member, also a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, ousted an incumbent to become L.A. mayor.

The Community Opportunity to Purchase Act, known as COPA, requires owners of covered buildings to notify the city and qualified nonprofits before selling. Those groups then get time to make an offer and a right to match a later one. The law takes effect one year after enactment, after the Department of Housing Preservation and Development writes rules.

“This law will give New Yorkers a tool to keep their homes out of the hands of predatory investors seeking to make a quick and easy buck,” Mamdani said at a signing event Tuesday.

He also won in court last week. A Brooklyn appellate panel ruled Nov. 4 that the administration can resume collecting its pied-à-terre tax on high-end second homes, reversing a Staten Island judge who found the rollout flawed. Mamdani says the tax could raise $500 million a year. Other legal challenges remain.

But his administration could not stop the sale of a 38-building portfolio with 850 mostly rent-stabilized apartments. Spatial Equity, an affordable housing developer with City Hall’s backing, failed to close a deal to buy the portfolio before an East Harlem auction began Tuesday afternoon.

Had COPA been in effect, a deal like Spatial Equity’s might have followed a defined timeline. Once notified of a sale, qualified groups have 20 days to tell the owner and the Department of Housing Preservation and Development they intend to buy. They then have 70 days to submit a competitive offer.The clock favors the owner if no one steps forward. A property can go to the open market if no group signals interest in the first 20 days. The same goes if the owner rejects every offer by the end of the 70-day window.

Eligible buildings have four or more units and meet at least one test: a year in a city housing enforcement program, an average of three or more hazardous violations per unit, or affordability restrictions under agreements with HPD.

“Those buildings are not just any buildings, Mamdani said. “They are multifamily buildings that have long been victim to pernicious cycles of speculation.”

The 38 buildings belonged to bankrupt Emerald Equities Group. Banks and other institutions that control about $250 million in mortgage loans will foreclose on each building over three auction days.

Lenders rejected Spatial Equity’s initial $68 million bid, according to a City Limits report. They also turned down a $110 million offer last month, tenant leader Cara Polte told Gothamist.

Polte said tenants will keep pushing for a buyer committed to fixing the buildings. Tenants had hoped to turn her building and four others on the block into a community land trust.

A trust managed by several banks and by Sabal Investment Holdings controls the loans. Freddie Mac partially insured them. Sabal has yet to respond to media requests.

Cea Weaver, director of the Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants, said the sale does not end the city’s effort to force owners to improve conditions.

This setback follows Mamdani’s first loss on this front. On Jan. 1, he stood in a Pinnacle-owned building and vowed to take on bad landlords. He then sought a 30-day delay of the bankruptcy auction of Pinnacle’s rent-regulated portfolio, hoping to find a buyer other than Summit Properties USA.

A judge allowed the sale to proceed. Summit won about 5,100 mostly rent-stabilized units from Pinnacle, which had filed for Chapter 11 after Flagstar Bank foreclosed.

Emerald bought the 38 buildings for $350 million in 2016 and began raising rents on stabilized apartments. It took out another $180 million loan in December 2018, six months before state lawmakers passed tenant protections that outlawed many of those tactics.

Lenders foreclosed in 2024. Emerald filed for bankruptcy a year later.

A state investigation found Emerald had illegally removed 21 apartments from rent stabilization. The buildings had more than 2,300 housing code violations in April. A retaining wall behind buildings on East 103rd Street collapsed earlier this year, days before Mamdani and Weaver visited in March.

About 1,600 rent-stabilized buildings face financial distress, according to Rent Guidelines Board data. Landlord groups blame rent restrictions, including the board’s two-year rent freeze. Tenant advocates say owners like Emerald borrowed heavily expecting rent increases that later law barred.

In June, Mamdani won a rent freeze through the Rent Guidelines Board for the city’s roughly 1 million stabilized apartments.

Landlords sued to reverse the freeze. The case began in Staten Island, but Justice Ralph Porzio moved it to Manhattan in August, handing Mamdani a partial win. In September, the judge ordered City Hall to turn over communications with the board and signaled he would likely not rule by Oct. 1.

Oct. 1 came and went without a ruling, and the freeze took effect for new and renewing leases.

Meanwhile, a federal lawsuit remains pending over a 2019 state law that limits rents on stabilized units. Small property owners sued in November 2025, arguing the law unconstitutionally keeps stabilized apartments vacant.

COPA’s path was uneven until Mamdani took office. The City Council passed an earlier version in December 2025, but then-Mayor Eric Adams vetoed it, and the Council did not override him. A revised, narrower version passed Oct. 22.

“Progress … is something that we celebrate, and also, we know that it is not inevitable,” Mamdani said. “It has to be won.”

#5478. Higharc, ECI launch MarkSystems integration for big builders

Higharc and ECI Software Solutions launched a MarkSystems integration that syncs 3D home design, options and pricing with ERP workflows, aiming to cut manual data entry, errors and rework for production homebuilders.  AI Summary

Higharc and ECI Software Solutions have released a generally available integration that connects Higharc’s 3D home design and configuration platform with ECI’s MarkSystems ERP for production homebuilders, aiming to cut manual data entry and tighten the link between what is sold and what is built.

The companies announced the launch Nov. 10, saying the jointly developed connection is now available to MarkSystems builders and is already in use at New Home Inc., a Carolinas-based builder that has deployed the integration across its sales and construction operations, according to the announcement.

For many production builders, moving a home from sales to construction requires rekeying pricing, plan configurations and buyer selections across multiple systems and departments. That creates opportunities for discrepancies between sales contracts, purchase orders and what gets built in the field, which can show up as margin erosion, delays and rework.

MarkSystems functions as the system of record for housing production, scheduling and accounting for many small and mid-sized builders. Higharc positions itself as the source of truth for plans, options and the buyer-facing design experience. The integration is designed to let data flow between the two instead of relying on manual handoffs.

“The biggest difference we’re seeing is speed and confidence,” said Matt Riley, owner of New Home Inc., in the announcement. “Our sales team can now sit down with a buyer, configure their home with accurate, up-to-date pricing, and send those selections straight into MarkSystems to write the contract. We’re no longer relying on people to keep information updated in multiple places, where mistakes inevitably happen and we end up absorbing the cost.”

The Higharc–MarkSystems connection is built to close gaps between marketing, sales and operations in a typical production homebuilding workflow. Key capabilities, according to the companies, include:

For builders, this type of connection is aimed at tightening margins and shortening cycle times by eliminating redundant work between sales offices, options studios, purchasing teams and field superintendents. Aligning pricing and configurations across systems can also help reduce surprise variance purchase orders and options that are sold but not built—or built but not paid for.

Production builders have accelerated their adoption of connected ERP, sales and design tools over the past decade, but many still run option pricing, elevations and structural changes through spreadsheets or local databases that do not fully sync with ERP. As build costs and cycle times remain under pressure, misaligned data between sales contracts and job budgets can quickly erode gross margin on a per-lot basis.

By placing Higharc’s 3D, rules-based design engine upstream of MarkSystems and tying the two together, the new integration is trying to turn the plan and option configuration itself into structured data that can feed estimating, purchasing and scheduling. That is a shift from traditional workflows where sales and marketing produce static collateral and construction teams translate that material back into quantities and tasks.

For entry-level and move-up builders running high volumes of similar plans across multiple communities, even small reductions in change orders, option mistakes and rework can compound across hundreds or thousands of closings a year.

Homebuilders can learn more about the integration during ECI Connect, ECI’s customer conference that begins Nov. 16. Representatives from Higharc and ECI plan to be available at the event to discuss how the connection links home design, buyer selections, pricing and construction operations, according to the announcement.

Builders not attending the event can schedule personalized demonstrations with either company.

Higharc describes itself as an AI-driven homebuilding platform for design through construction. The company uses 3D spatial data to generate plans, estimates and construction documents, replacing static plan sets with “live” models that respond to design changes with updated drawings, lot-specific estimates and buyer-facing experiences.

ECI Software Solutions, based in Westlake, Texas, provides cloud-based business software for small and mid-sized businesses in manufacturing, building and construction, field service and distribution. Its portfolio includes ERP, CRM, business intelligence, e-commerce and payment tools, and it serves more than 30,000 customers in over 90 countries, according to the company.

Company leverages in-house precision sensors and plasma modules to target hospitals, schools, and welfare facilities in B2G and B2B markets

SEOUL, South Korea, Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- NIDS Co., Ltd. is expanding its air quality management business for high-traffic public facilities with Airvom, its in-house air purification and sterilization brand. The company plans to broaden its public- and private-sector supply network, targeting hospitals, nursing homes, schools, welfare facilities, and subway stations.

According to NIDS, Airvom is an air care product that combines a precision sensor that detects indoor air conditions with a plasma module. The company explained that the system links purification and sterilization functions to the air quality data measured by the sensor, applying its environmental measurement component technology to air quality management in real spaces.

The core of what NIDS is presenting to the high-traffic facility market is the link between measurement and operation. Built on a structure that identifies air conditions in real time and reflects them in how the product operates, the company aims to address air quality management needs within facilities. The company said it applied plasma technology targeting airborne viruses and harmful bacteria in addition to its purification function.

Airvom uses dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) low-temperature plasma technology. NIDS said the product combines its independently developed plasma radical technology with its sensing technology. The company cites owning both the sensor and the sterilization module as proprietary technology as a key competitive strength in product development and operation.

This structure of directly handling core components also ties into how the company develops finished products. NIDS explained that it can control sensor sensitivity and tune operating algorithms to suit the system. It plans to use this tuning capability when linking the sensor and plasma module, developing products in a direction that improves performance and quality stability.

The product line is organized by usage space, ranging from vehicle and personal models to residential and office units and models for hospitals and high-traffic facilities. Among these, the company identified hospitals, nursing homes, schools, welfare facilities, and subway stations as targets for future supply expansion. NIDS plans to establish Airvom in the market through B2G and B2B business aimed at facilities.

Airvom's business offering also includes S+Link, an Internet of Things (IoT) platform for real-time air quality management. NIDS presents a solution that connects sensors, finished products, and the platform to monitor and manage air conditions. The company aims to extend its business scope beyond supplying individual devices to the management domain that makes use of air quality data.

The foundation of the Airvom business is NIDS's experience in environmental sensor manufacturing and plasma module development. Founded in 2000, NIDS has designed and mass-produced particulate matter sensors, optical gas sensors, and composite environmental sensor modules in-house. The company has also been developing and supplying plasma ionizers for odor removal in domestic automotive air conditioners since 2000, a technology that was developed to eliminate bacteria and viruses. By applying its experience developing core air-measurement components to finished air purification and sterilization products, the company is pursuing its own-brand business.

This represents a move to secure customer touchpoints distinct from its sensor component supply. While the component business primarily targets home appliance, automotive, and HVAC companies, Airvom seeks supply opportunities with public institutions and facility operators that run actual spaces. The company plans to operate the sensor supply business and the Airvom business as two pillars and expand its presence in the finished-product market.

NIDS is also exploring the potential for supplying its air quality management solutions overseas. It plans to contact buyers and identify local partnership opportunities through its existing overseas branch network in the United States, Japan, and China. Alongside expanding supply to domestic high-traffic facilities, the company intends to pursue overseas sales channels in parallel.

Going forward, NIDS will promote the product competitiveness of its combined sensor and plasma technologies and continue supply discussions with public and private facilities. Its goal is to extend its in-house component technology into a finished air care product business and secure a market foundation for Airvom.

The company is also preparing to build a business foundation for its entry into the U.S. market through exchanges with Yale University and Johns Hopkins University.

"Airvom will expand its supply network centered on high-traffic facilities such as hospitals, nursing homes, schools, welfare facilities, and subway stations (B2G/B2B)," a NIDS representative said.

#5476. Reverse mortgage leaders on alleviating sales and referral pain points

Presenters at NRMLA’s Annual Convention discussed practical tactics for a rate-sensitive reverse mortgage market, from LESA reduction and insurance shopping to borrower communication. They also stressed using partner introductions, explaining line-of-credit growth and leveraging CRMP training.  AI Summary

The National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA) kicked off its Annual Convention & Expo on Tuesday in San Antonio with some practical advice for originators who are looking to close more deals in a rate-sensitive environment.

Reverse mortgage production has shifted in 2026 as the majority of borrowers are now using proprietary products rather than federally insured Home Equity Conversion Mortgages (HECMs). But regardless of the product being used, experts stressed creative problem-solving, proactive communication, financial planner relationships and next-level education as ways for loan officers to distinguish themselves in a difficult market.

Dan Hultquist, co-founder of REVERSE plus and director of reverse mortgage communications at Movement Mortgage, focused his presentation on transactions that are short to close — when the proceeds don’t cover the required payoffs and closing costs.

Common reasons why a borrower needs to bring more money to the table include lower principal limit factors tied to higher mortgage rates, borrowers who have refinanced repeatedly and the required life expectancy set-aside (LESA) for HECMs. He advised loan officers to consider different solutions for the level of severity.

When borrowers are short to close by a small amount like a few thousand dollars, a potential solution is to schedule their closing within six months of the borrower’s next birthday, so they “age up” and qualify for additional proceeds and/or a smaller LESA.

For borrowers who are short to close by a larger amount, shifting from a HECM to a proprietary loan or a second-lien product can make more sense as it eliminates the need for an upfront mortgage insurance premium. Additionally, the LO might look to persuade the borrower to dip into their retirement savings or obtain gift funds from a relative, since the elimination of the monthly mortgage payment may help them recover that sum over time.

Hultquist said he’s seen deals that are short to close by more than $100,000 saved in this fashion.

When a borrower is short to close specifically because of the LESA, property tax exemptions may provide a way forward. With HECM transactions, Hultquist noted that the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) does not have a flat discount on taxable assets. While 15% is the default discount, the client’s actual tax rate can be used, potentially saving money.

Shopping for a new homeowners insurance policy with a lower deductible should also be looked at. “Your insurance company, they know that seniors don’t shop. Guess what happens to their insurance premiums every year? They keep going up until they shop,” Hultquist remarked.

John Luddy, senior vice president at Supreme Lending, has spent 25-plus years exclusively originating reverse mortgages. Over the course of thousands of conversations, he’s identified some key questions to ask of borrowers, spouses and lead sources at the start of the transaction.

The first question Luddy asks every client is, “How did you get my name?” The answer can tell him whether paid advertising campaigns are working.

“Advertising is the empty well that will take as many buckets of your money as you want to put into it,” he said. “You might feel good seeing your name on the marquee somewhere, but if it’s not drawing results, you’re wasting money.”

The same question also helps him identify who to call if a borrower stalls. Many clients, Luddy said, hesitate before closing as they look for an alternative. But lead sources like attorneys, financial planners or accountants “can be a little bolder” in their interactions than an originator, so they may be able to nudge the client across the finish line.

With lead sources, Luddy’s key question is, “What can I do to earn your business?” Real estate agents, for example, want their phone calls to be returned and for the LO to demonstrate deep product knowledge, while financial planners want any loan to fit into their existing strategy with a client.

Banks that don’t offer reverse mortgages can be a rich source of leads due to customers who are denied for other types of credit. And Luddy said bank branch managers will send repeat referral business if there’s no surprises in the reverse mortgage process.

He also urged the audience to consider borrower disabilities, such as hearing loss, as a potential hurdle.

“If they were a veteran, if they worked in manufacturing, if they worked in construction, or if they’re over 62, they may be suffering from hearing loss,” he said. “They’re not going to feel comfortable moving forward if they only understand every third word.”

Ryan Ponsford of Equity Wealth Academy, who’s well known to the NRMLA audience, argued that psychology matters more than math in reverse mortgage sales, even when dealing with financial advisers to capture more business.

Originators should discuss voluntary payments and the lack of a prepayment penalty for reverse mortgages. This gives borrowers a better sense of control over their financial responsibilities.

When speaking with business partners, don’t ask for referrals, which Ponsford called “transactional.” Instead, ask for introductions.

“An introduction is different than a referral because an introduction done right is a transfer of trust. Somebody that is trusted is transferring their trust to you,” he explained.

Financial advisers, he said, should leave conversations with an understanding that reverse mortgages apply to more people than they realize and that homeowners should consider them earlier in life.

Ponsford recommended three questions to ask advisers when attempting to forge a referral relationship.

And while psychology means a lot, it doesn’t mean everything. For example, the compounding growth feature of a reverse mortgage line of credit is essential for LOs to comprehend before they approach advisers. “If you can’t explain how line-of-credit growth works, you’re a nonstarter in the financial solutions industry,” Ponsford said.

Scott Harmes, national manager of reverse at C2 Financial — and his daughter Christina Harmes of Barrett Financial — are on the short list of Certified Reverse Mortgage Professionals (CRMPs), a designation earned through industry experience, a letter of recommendation and passing a complex exam.

He originated his first reverse mortgage about 16 years ago for the parents of a previous client, a deal that “changed their lives, and it changed mine,” he said. He stopped doing traditional forward mortgages about eight years ago to focus solely on reverse,

Harmes said he passed the CRMP exam on his first try and later built a detailed study guide for his colleagues to use that resulted in a “virtually 100%” pass rate. The designation, he said, has helped him to solidify more referral partnerships, to the point where he said he rarely loses deals except for when retail shops offer pricing he can’t match.

At C2 Financial, Harmes has constructed a mentorship model in which an experienced LO and a novice LO work together on three reverse mortgage files, with the trainee gaining additional responsibilities with each file. After that, they’ve typically gained enough knowledge to do the work on their own.

When it comes to borrower education, Harmes stressed that the process works best when information is offered in bite-sized chunks, rather than loan proposals accompanied by dozens of pages. Counseling is a key part of that process and there are pitfalls to be aware of.

“My policy is, I never tell them to look for a free session or a session paid for by a grant, because honestly, I think that’s too much work. We’re (sometimes) giving them three pages of counselors. I don’t want them dialing for dollars for four hours,” Harmes said.

“I originate in California, and there’s a state law that you can’t order the appraisal or any services that would cost the borrower until the eighth day after counseling. So we want to get that counseling session as soon as possible.”

#5475. Dreeze launches with $33M to recover entire cloud applications, not just their data

Israeli cloud application recovery startup Dreeze Inc. formally launched today with $33 million in new funding to bring what it calls Application Revival to enterprises running workloads in the public cloud.

Dreeze provides software aimed at what happens after a backup has done its job. Cloud-native applications depend on infrastructure, identities and secrets as well as data, and all of it has to come back in the right order before an application will run.

The company calls the manual work that follows a “recovery scramble.” Searching for credentials and rebuilding connections by hand can keep an application down for days or weeks after its data is restored.

Preparation starts well before an outage, when Dreeze’s software traces each cloud resource and dependency back to the application that relies on it. Its recovery plan comes from what is actually running, and changes to the environment update it automatically.

Configuration files, keys and application data go into an immutable, air-gapped vault, which customers can replicate across regions. When an outage hits, Dreeze rebuilds those pieces, plus the infrastructure and identities around them, in dependency order. Teams can also rehearse the full plan ahead of time as an automated test that ends with a working copy of the application, and production is left alone while it runs.

Getting the data back “doesn’t mean the business is back,” co-founder and Chief Executive Ziv Kedem said. With cyberattacks increasing, he said, enterprises need to plan on the basis that a critical application will go down at some point.

Jeremy Miller, founder and chief executive of Denver-based technology consulting firm Coravant LLC, said his firm wanted to work with Dreeze “from the start.” Most of its customers can back up public cloud data without much trouble, he said. Their worry is restarting a whole application with every dependency in sequence.

Dreeze is the third recovery company from Kedem and his brother Oded Kedem, its chief technology officer. The pair sold Kashya Inc. to EMC Corp. in 2006. Zerto Ltd., the disaster recovery software company they started in 2009, went to Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. for $374 million in 2021. Avi Raichel, Dreeze’s third co-founder, became Zerto’s chief operating officer that year, shortly before the sale.

Norwest Venture Partners and Bessemer Venture Partners led the seed round. Claltech also participated. Dreeze employs 70 people across Israel and the U.S. and plans to put the money into product development and a larger sales and marketing team.

Few teams understand the recovery problem “as deeply as this one,” Norwest General Partner Dror Nahumi said. In a blog post, Bessemer said Dreeze uses artificial intelligence to work out how thousands of cloud resources connect to the applications they serve. That picture shifts with every change, including ones made by AI agents.

Dreeze’s software is generally available now for Amazon Web Services Inc. customers. A version for Microsoft Corp.’s Azure is in early access, with general availability planned for early next year.
