#5453. TIER IV unveils end-to-end autonomous driving adaptable to map information and sensor configurations

Multiple open-source AI models are available with Autoware

TOKYO, Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- TIER IV, the pioneering force behind Autoware, open-source software for autonomous driving, today announced the development and open-source release of multiple end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving AI models that support different system requirements, including map information and sensor configurations. The models offer flexible options ranging from camera-only configurations to those incorporating LiDAR, radar and high-definition (HD) maps, enabling developers to select AI models suited to their performance requirements. Through Autoware, TIER IV provides a development environment for optimizing these models and integrating them into vehicle systems, helping automakers and technology partners develop and deploy their own autonomous driving stack.

Overview of the Autoware 2.0 Architecture

TIER IV is leading the development of Autoware 2.0, the next-generation architecture of Autoware. Autoware 2.0 is a scalable and adaptable architecture that flexibly combines AI models with conventional rule-based technologies. By supporting different AI models and sensor configurations, it enables autonomous driving systems to be built for a range of applications and system requirements. The E2E autonomous driving AI models announced today are concrete technological outcomes designed to leverage this architecture.

As part of its collaboration with NVIDIA announced in March 2026 , TIER IV has been evaluating the performance of NVIDIA Alpamayo, a vision-language-action (VLA) foundation model, and integrating it with Autoware. The latest model, Alpamayo 2 Edge, is an E2E autonomous driving AI model that takes only camera images as input and uses reasoning to generate driving trajectories. With 2 billion parameters, compared with 34 billion in Alpamayo 2 Super, it is substantially smaller and offers promise for practical deployment in vehicles. TIER IV is currently optimizing the model and adapting it to real vehicles, while having completed its integration with Autoware.

AutoE2E, whose development is led by the Autoware Foundation (AWF) and TIER IV, is an E2E autonomous driving AI model capable of running on computing platforms beyond NVIDIA hardware. It adopts a FastâSlow architecture combining a Reactive Model for real-time driving decisions, a World Model for predicting future changes in the surrounding environment, and a Reasoning Model that supports driving decisions. It can accommodate configurations ranging from cameras alone to those incorporating LiDAR and radar sensor data. With 79.9 million parameters, it is lighter than Alpamayo 2 Edge. The Reactive Model has been released, while development of the World Model and Reasoning Model continues, alongside consideration of commercialization for robotaxi applications. Integration of the Reactive Model with Autoware has been achieved.

Developed independently by TIER IV, METEOR is a lightweight, multitask E2E autonomous driving AI model primarily intended for privately owned passenger vehicles. Built on a convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture, it uses a bird's-eye-view (BEV) representation to perform everything from perception of the surrounding environment to driving trajectory generation within a single neural network, without relying on high-definition maps. It supports configurations using images from one to eight cameras and can also incorporate LiDAR and radar sensor data. With 16 million parameters, it is even lighter than AutoE2E and supports operation across different semiconductor platforms, including NVIDIA and Renesas. TIER IV also uses CoMET, the automated labeling platform within Co-MLOps, together with agentic AI to automate data labeling and model training, evaluation, and improvement, eliminating the need for manual coding and labeling. Automakers and component suppliers can optimize the open-source model to meet their own vehicle specifications and performance requirements.

OnePlanner is an E2E autonomous driving AI model that integrates perception of the surrounding environment with motion planning. It currently uses BEVFusion, which generates a BEV representation from LiDAR point-cloud data, with a planned transition to PTv3. Its flexible architecture allows the perception model to be replaced while directly using features extracted during perception for motion planning. Conventional autonomous driving systems convert perception results into information such as object positions and velocities before passing them to the planner. OnePlanner reduces these intermediate conversions, enabling richer use of information about the surrounding environment. It also incorporates HD maps, route information, traffic-signal states, and vehicle motion states to generate driving trajectories for the next six seconds. Integration with Autoware has been achieved.

LatentDrive is an E2E autonomous driving AI model that uses a world model to integrate predictions of the surrounding environment with motion planning. Using V-JEPA, a self-supervised learning approach, it represents features of the surrounding environment extracted from camera video in a latent space and uses these features to generate vehicle trajectories. Its distinguishing feature is that it directly leverages information from video for motion planning without intermediate processes such as object detection and tracking. It does not require HD maps and generates trajectories for the next four seconds using camera video, route information, and vehicle motion states. It supports configurations with either one or three cameras, and work is underway on integration with Autoware and validation in an in-vehicle environment.

"Advances in E2E autonomous driving are fundamentally changing how autonomous driving systems are developed." said Shinpei Kato, founder and CEO of TIER IV. "For automakers and component suppliers to incorporate AI technology into their own products, however, it is essential that they be able to internalize technologies according to their applications and performance requirements, without depending on a particular AI model or semiconductor platform. By releasing multiple AI models developed under the leadership of TIER IV and the Autoware Foundation, alongside the results of our collaboration with NVIDIA, we have significantly expanded those choices. We will continue to advance the open-source ecosystem centered on Autoware and work with partners around the world to democratize autonomous driving."

"Advancing autonomous driving requires AI that can reason through complex situations and run efficiently in the car." said Ali Kani, vice president of automotive at NVIDIA. "TIER IV's integration of NVIDIA Alpamayo 2 Edge with Autoware gives developers an open foundation to bring that intelligence from research into their own vehicles."

"The advancement of autonomous driving technology depends on an ecosystem in which diverse AI models can be developed and evaluated openly, then applied according to their respective use cases." said Muhammad Zain Khawaja, President of the Autoware Foundation. "The AI models released today are an important demonstration of how Autoware is evolving into a flexible development platform that is not tied to any particular technology or hardware. We welcome TIER IV's continued technology development and its collaboration with partners including NVIDIA. The Autoware Foundation will continue working with the global open-source community to make advanced autonomous driving technology accessible to everyone."

TIER IV will continue improving the performance of the AI models released today and optimizing them for in-vehicle environments, while promoting the development and commercialization of E2E autonomous driving technology by automakers and partners through Autoware. TIER IV will also strengthen collaboration with the global open-source community and work to expand the adoption of autonomous driving systems across diverse vehicle types and applications.

TIER IV stands at the forefront of deep tech innovation, pioneering Autoware, open-source software for autonomous driving. With a comprehensive suite of platforms and services built around Autoware, TIER IV provides everything from software development and vehicle procurement to operational support. Through the Autoware ecosystem, TIER IV works with partners worldwide to shape the future of intelligent vehicles with open-source software, aiming to create mobility that is safer, more sustainable, and accessible to all.

#5452. First X-BAT fighter jet prototype unveiled as Shield AI preps Seattle area factory for 2027 launch

by John Cook on Nov 4, 2026 at 8:26 amNovember 4, 2026 at 8:41 am

Defense technology startup Shield AI has completed its first full-scale prototype of the X-BAT autonomous fighter jet as the company prepares its manufacturing and engineering hub south of Seattle.

Constructed in 12 months at a facility in Frisco, Texas, the prototype is currently en route to the company’s flight-test center at Newton City-County Airport in Kansas.

The milestone keeps Shield AI on track for its major manufacturing push in the Seattle area, one that it says could employ 4,000 workers in the region by the early 2030s.

In late September, the company announced a 420,000-square-foot facility dubbed “X-Forge 3” at the Des Moines Creek Business Park, which is scheduled to open in spring 2027. The company has already posted dozens of Seattle-area job openings across avionics, mechanical design, software engineering and aircraft manufacturing.

The unveiling of the X-BAT prototype keeps the company on schedule for its planned regional buildout in Des Moines, a spokesperson tells GeekWire.

“This milestone represents a year of sustained effort and discipline from a team that committed to an ambitious design and build schedule and delivered,” Armor Harris, senior vice president of aircraft engineering at Shield AI, said in a blog post. “That is no small feat.”

San Diego-based Shield AI expects the first X-BAT aircraft to roll off the line in Des Moines in 2028, with full production ramping up to about 150 aircraft per year by the early 2030s, Harris told GeekWire in an interview in September.

It’s an extremely ambitious timeline, but one the company says is necessary given the changing dynamics of warfare.

“The team is laser focused on keeping pace because we know a capability is only useful if it arrives in time to matter,” Harris said. “We cannot take decades to develop an aircraft when the need is already here. That urgency has shaped how we approach the engineering work, and how we work with partners in the U.S. government.”

Unveiled last year, the X-BAT is an AI-piloted strike fighter that takes off and lands vertically, carries up to 2,000-pound class weapons in internal bays, and is designed for a 1,000-nautical-mile combat radius — which, when it takes flight, would top the estimated 590 nautical mile combat radius of the Lockheed Martin F-35A.

One of its key tactical advantages is the ability to take off and land without concrete runways — hence the tagline for the X-BAT: “Earth is our Runway.”

The X-BAT launches from and returns to a mobile, trailer-mounted Launch and Recovery Vehicle, which allows the AI-piloted jet to deploy from cargo ships, naval destroyers or remote areas where it’s too costly or dangerous to build traditional runways.

“Our adversaries have invested in long range missiles that put our aircraft at risk when they’re on the ground. Aircraft are hard to shoot down in the air, but easy to destroy when they’re on the ground,” Harris notes in the blog post. “X-BAT is the answer to this threat because it forces the adversary to take all those assets that are overhead looking down at our airbases and makes them try to go and find where the X-BATs are hiding.”

Last month, the U.S. Navy awarded Shield AI a $150 million contract modification through the Pentagon’s Defense Exportability Features program, matched dollar-for-dollar by $150 million in private Shield AI funds. Alongside a prior $100 million joint Navy and Defense Innovation Unit award in August, total program backing stands at approximately $400 million.

Co-founded by former Navy SEAL Brandon Tseng, Shield AI raised a $2 billion venture capital round at a $12.7 billion valuation earlier this year.

With the prototype built, Shield AI’s engineering team is focusing on proving out its vertical-takeoff-and-landing mechanics in Kansas ahead of initial flight trials later this year.

Harris detailed a multi-phase testing campaign ahead:

“We’ve built the first aircraft,” Harris wrote. “Now it’s time to go prove what it can do.”

#5451. Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

As of ZecStats' latest update on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Users need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

The September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

That has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

The useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

#5449. Washington voters keep millionaires tax, splitting tech leaders over the state’s competitive edge

by Todd Bishop, Lisa Stiffler & Kurt Schlosser on Nov 4, 2026 at 10:10 amNovember 4, 2026 at 10:18 am

Washington voters appear to have upheld the state’s new tax on high earners, putting the state on track to lose its place among the nine states without an income tax — a status that tech leaders have long touted as an edge in recruiting companies and talent.

Initiative 645, which would repeal the 9.9% tax on household income above $1 million, was trailing 58% to 42% in election-night returns. King County voters rejected the repeal by an even wider margin, with 66.5% voting no. The repeal would need about 62% of the remaining ballots to pass, according to a Seattle Times estimate.

The tax has divided the Seattle tech community since lawmakers unveiled the proposal in February. Some founders and investors warned it would drive talent and capital out of the state, while others called those fears overblown.

Madrona, the Seattle venture capital firm, gave $250,000 to the repeal campaign, making it one of the biggest donors.

“The outcome on the income tax should be disappointing for all Washingtonians as having no income tax was a major source of competitive advantage for the state,” said Matt McIlwain, a Madrona managing director, responding to questions from GeekWire.

McIlwain, who urged voters to repeal the tax in a GeekWire op-ed in October, said the state saw record economic growth and job creation after voters rejected an income tax in 2010. “I am concerned for the future ability of Washington state to be competitive,” he wrote.

Ben Golden, an attorney and advisor to Pacific Northwest startups and investors, countered that the election outcome demonstrates “that Washingtonians are ready to invest in ourselves.”

“There’s lots of hard work to follow to ensure that revenue is spent wisely, but at least (Washington) will be ready for the wave of Medicaid cuts and AI job disruption on the horizon,” added Golden, who in February penned an op-ed in support of the tax.

And while some residents will leave for tax havens, Golden said, “the opportunity remains ripe for the investor community and startups to build and grow in this healthy and talent-packed region.”

Brian Fioca, a Seattle-based serial entrepreneur and investor, hopes the additional tax dollars will improve the quality of life in the state overall.

“Washington is a wonderful place to live and build a company, full of extraordinary people and talent,” said Fioca, who also offered an earlier op-ed on the issue. “If someone decides not to start a business here, or chooses to leave because of this tax, that’s not someone I’d be particularly excited to work with or invest in anyway.”

Asked whether the outcome changes how Madrona thinks about investing in Washington, McIlwain didn’t address the state specifically. “Our goal remains to find and partner with amazing founders and their teams to build enduring companies that create innovative products, jobs and economic returns,” he said.

State Sen. Jamie Pedersen, D-Seattle, was an original architect of the tax and the prime sponsor of the bill that created it. As Senate majority leader, he kept reworking the measure to win votes until the final days of this year’s legislative session. Pedersen, who has been in the Legislature since 2007, is also executive vice president and general counsel at Seattle construction and engineering firm McKinstry.

At the No on 645 campaign’s election-night event in Seattle on Tuesday, Pedersen celebrated the outcome.

“We have been saddled with an anchor around our neck, with a tax system that is bad for working people, that’s bad for small businesses, that’s bad for just about everybody except for the one percent,” he said, as seen in a video posted on Instagram.

The No on 645 campaign touted a coalition of working families, labor unions, teachers, small business owners and others — and attracted endorsements from state celebrities like Rick Steves, the Edmonds-based travel writer, and “Jeopardy!” host Ken Jennings.

The tax applies only to income above the $1 million threshold, so a household earning $1.5 million would owe $49,500. It takes effect on 2028 income, with the first payments due in April 2029.

Jeff Bezos, Howard Schultz and Rich Barton have all moved out of state in recent years, though each described the move in personal terms.

McIlwain, who moved with his family from Georgia to Seattle 26 years ago, became a Georgia resident again two years ago. That was before lawmakers unveiled the millionaires tax in February.

In 2010, Steve Ballmer and Microsoft helped fund the campaign that defeated a statewide income tax, but the region’s biggest tech companies stayed out of this fight. The state projects the tax will raise $3 billion to $4 billion a year from roughly 25,000 households. Gov. Bob Ferguson signed it into law in March, along with tax breaks for small businesses and lower-income families.

A lawsuit filed in April by former Attorney General Rob McKenna and former state Supreme Court Justice Phil Talmadge argues the tax is unconstitutional, citing a 1933 ruling that classified income as property, which the state constitution says must be taxed at a uniform rate.

The case will likely go to the state Supreme Court, where Democrat-backed candidates led four of five races on Tuesday’s ballot as of election-night returns, according to the Washington State Standard.

#5448. A rare second exit: AI startup Suplari acquired by Docusign nearly 3 years after Microsoft spinout

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 12:43 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 12:44 pm

Some startups dream of getting acquired by a big tech company. Suplari has now done it twice.

Docusign on Tuesday announced its acquisition of the AI-powered spending analysis company, five years after Microsoft bought the Seattle-based startup and nearly three years after the Redmond tech giant spun the company back out to its founders.

Financial terms of the latest deal weren’t disclosed. Docusign said it plans to fold Suplari’s technology into its contract management platform, pairing the startup’s analysis of corporate spending and supplier data with Docusign’s Iris AI engine.

The idea is to find savings, track what suppliers agreed to deliver, and flag purchases that fall outside contract terms.

“Joining Docusign allows us to connect that intelligence more closely to the agreements that shape a company’s spending,” Suplari CEO Jeff Gerber said in a statement.

It’s a remarkable double-dip in startup M&A for a company that was applying AI to corporate spending years before the current agentic boom.

Suplari was co-founded in 2016 by Nikesh “Niki” Parekh, a Seattle tech veteran who previously held leadership roles at Trulia and Market Leader, along with Gerber, a longtime engineering leader, and product leader Brian White. Gerber and White had worked together at iConclude, an earlier startup that Gerber co-founded.

The startup, in its first incarnation, pulled together procurement and spending data scattered across corporate systems such as SAP, Workday and Oracle, and used machine learning to flag savings opportunities, supplier risks and other inefficiencies. The pitch was an alternative to having teams of analysts comb through the data in Excel or Tableau.

Gerber has traced the idea to his time at Apptio, the IT cost management company, where he helped lead machine learning work. That opened his eyes to the ways that connecting financial data with IT activity could turn up problems such as auto-renewing contracts and services still running for employees who had left.

By 2021, Suplari had raised about $18 million from investors including Madrona, Amplify Partners, Shasta Ventures, Two Sigma Ventures and Workday Ventures.

Microsoft acquired Suplari in July 2021, saying it would pair the technology with its Dynamics 365 business software. The startup had about 40 employees at the time.

Then ChatGPT arrived in November 2022. Microsoft redirected all of its new-product investment to Copilot, Parekh recalled in a blog post earlier this year.

Succeeding inside Microsoft would have meant rebuilding Suplari from scratch to deploy across 400 to 500 data centers, “exactly the kind of investment Microsoft was now reserving for Copilot,” he wrote. By then, Suplari had become core to the finance and procurement operations of 40 to 50 of Microsoft’s most strategic customers.

“Microsoft concluded, and we agreed, that customers would be better served if Suplari operated as an independent company again,” Parekh wrote.

Suplari’s founding team bought the company back in late 2023, with Microsoft retaining a minority stake. Gerber, Suplari’s original CTO, led the spinout and became CEO. He had been chief AI strategy officer for Microsoft’s Dynamics finance and operations products after the acquisition.

Parekh stayed at Microsoft, working on Copilot Studio and the Power Platform, before leaving in June 2025 to start the AI recruiting startup Provn.

Since the spinout, Suplari has added an AI agent that helps procurement teams act on what its software finds, Gerber said on an Art of Procurement podcast in June. Its customers include BT Group, Nordstrom and MediaNews Group, according to Docusign. The company has about two dozen employees, according to LinkedIn.

Gerber declined an interview with GeekWire after the acquisition announcement, citing a quiet period. In a statement, Docusign CEO Allan Thygesen said Suplari’s “technology and talent” will help Docusign connect what companies’ supplier agreements say with their actual spending.

Parekh has remained a Suplari shareholder and advisor. Asked about the deal, he said via email that generative AI is “enabling a renaissance in many ‘traditional’ systems of record” like enterprise resource planning and contract lifecycle management.

Connecting contracts with their outcomes, he said, “will be the future.”

As for Suplari’s own outcome, Parekh said he’s “ecstatic” about the startup’s second exit.

#5447. A year in, Smartsheet CEO Raj Singh bets on a new vision beyond the company’s flagship product

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 3:31 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 5:53 pm

Smartsheet’s biggest new product in years doesn’t require Smartsheet.

The Bellevue, Wash.-based company on Wednesday unveiled vsActual, as in “plan versus actual,” an AI product that reads a company’s strategy and budgets, tracks the work across tools such as Jira, Workday and Slack, and flags when projects drift off course.

It’s the first standalone product under CEO Raj Singh, the Concur co-founder who took over Smartsheet a year ago, and it’s aimed at CEOs, CFOs and COOs rather than the project managers who have long been Smartsheet’s core users.

At the company’s Engage conference in Seattle, Singh showed a slide from a year ago labeling Smartsheet “a product company,” with the company and its software in a single box.

“Smartsheet, the company, and Smartsheet, the product, were exactly the same thing — same box, same ceiling — an attractive ceiling, but still a ceiling,” he said. Now, he explained, Smartsheet is a multi-product company, with vsActual as a key milestone.

Singh was relaxed and at home on the stage, engaging warmly with the crowd and his fellow presenters like someone who’d been running Smartsheet for years. He went off script often enough that he paused at one point to reassure the teleprompter operator everything was OK, and his talk ultimately ran so long that it threw off the morning’s schedule.

In an interview with GeekWire after the keynote, Singh said the company has more room to grow by working with the software that customers already use than by trying to move everything into its flagship product.

“Most of the competition is saying, ‘Well, if you move all your stuff onto my platform, you’ll be totally in control,’” he said. “I think every CIO is thinking, I’m never going to do that.”

Founded two decades ago, Smartsheet is best known for spreadsheet-style software that teams use to plan projects, track tasks and automate routine work.

It went public in 2018 and was taken private in January 2025 by Vista Equity Partners and Blackstone in an $8.4 billion deal, when it had more than $1 billion in annual revenue. Its rivals include Microsoft, Google and Salesforce, as well as Asana, Monday.com, Airtable and ClickUp.

Singh described vsActual as part of a broader product lineup that also includes Smartsheet’s flagship software and Brandfolder, the digital asset management service the company acquired in 2020.

All three draw on the same underlying data, built from 20 years of tracking how work gets planned, approved and done in Smartsheet, which the company calls its Execution Graph. Future products will be built the same way, Singh said.

“The Execution Graph is the long-term differentiated value of our company,” he said.

A change in pricing: Smartsheet is also moving away from charging by the user. Under a new consumption-based model, customers pay a base fee plus credits that are drawn down as people use the software, including its AI features, automations and API connections. Seat-based plans remain available.

Singh said customers balked at paying full price for people who use Smartsheet only occasionally. As an example, he said creating a dashboard might cost 50 cents, rather than a license that runs hundreds of dollars. Customers who switch won’t be charged for going over their credits, though he didn’t say for how long.

He said the net effect on revenue should be “nothing but positive,” describing the shift as a way to unlock demand from customers who held back under per-seat pricing.

“Agents are clearly going to be users moving forward,” he added.

Competition and risks: The new product enters a crowded field. Microsoft, ServiceNow, Workday and others are adding AI agents that plan and track work inside their own products, and AI-native startups are going after the same status-report busywork.

The software also depends on data from systems run by other companies, including rivals such as Asana. Singh said Smartsheet connects to them through APIs and the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard for linking AI models to outside software, depending on how deep the integration goes.

The approach carries some risk: if companies can track their work through vsActual without moving it into Smartsheet, they have less reason to expand their use of the core software, the company’s main business.

Asked about that, Singh pointed to new AI features in Smartsheet itself, including its Smart Assist agent and an MCP server that lets customers use Smartsheet from AI assistants such as Claude and Copilot. “The core keeps growing,” he said.

Keith Kirkpatrick, a Futurum Group analyst, wrote Wednesday that vsActual is “the company’s clearest move yet from managing tasks to governing strategy,” but said the strategy requires Smartsheet to sell to a different kind of buyer.

“Its sellers are also not used to finance-led deals with long evaluation cycles,” he wrote, adding that many executives still see Smartsheet as a “glorified Excel” project management tool.

Singh said Smartsheet’s sales force already knows how to sell to large enterprises, but acknowledged that the company will need people who understand corporate planning. It will build a team of vsActual specialists, as it has for Brandfolder.

Kirkpatrick also noted that vsActual requires a company to work from one official plan, unlike Smartsheet’s more flexible core software, and said the company will need to show that its Execution Graph offers the same depth for customers whose work lives mostly in other systems.

“Decoupling widens the market but strains the main differentiator,” he wrote.

Smartsheet hasn’t said when vsActual will be generally available or how it will be priced. It’s building the product with 12 enterprise design partners, including some of the world’s largest food service, financial services and health systems, Singh said.

From Concur to Smartsheet: Singh started Concur in the early 1990s with his brother, Steve Singh, and Mike Hilton, and the company grew into a top provider of corporate travel and expense software before SAP acquired it for $8.3 billion in 2014.

Raj Singh later led health benefits company Accolade through its IPO and sale, and took over as Smartsheet CEO in October 2025, after longtime CEO Mark Mader retired and Apptio co-founder Sunny Gupta served as acting CEO.

Smartsheet cut jobs that month and again in February. Singh has since rebuilt the leadership team, including several executives he worked with at Concur and Accolade.

Singh said the leadership team is now fully assembled and the company is hiring, though AI means headcount won’t grow the way it once did.

He didn’t disclose revenue but said the business is growing, especially internationally and with government customers, and that retention remains strong despite fears that AI would lead companies to abandon traditional software. More than 100 customers now pay Smartsheet at least $1 million a year, a record, he said.

He credited Smartsheet’s founders and past leaders with building a successful tool for project managers, calling former CEO Mark Mader and co-founder Brent Frei friends.

Singh said the bigger opportunity is to help businesses run better, and he sees no reason Smartsheet can’t become one of the most important software companies in the world.

“I’m 58 years old,” he said. “I’m not doing this because I need to make an extra buck. I’m doing this because I think there’s a very important company in here, and we just have to unearth it, and then we have to get to customers and make them see that new vision.”

#5446. Claude can now join video calls as an active, visible teammate in Anthropic’s latest push to reinvent white collar jobs beyond coding

Anthropic ‘s Claude Code reinvented the field of software engineering, turning AI into a must-have tool for programmers. Now the company is seeking to do the same across the corporate workplace with a new suite of office productivity tools launched on Tuesday.

The new products are an important part of Anthropic’s effort to broaden its base of paying customers and boost its revenue as it moves closer to a widely-anticipated initial public stock offering. The IPO, which could value Anthropic at roughly $1.4 trillion, is scheduled for as soon as next week, the company revealed separately on Tuesday.

To help create momentum around the product launch, Anthropic held a buzzy launch event in San Francisco Tuesday with hundreds of guests. Anthropic’s Chief Product Officer Ami Vora spoke on stage about how Claude has changed computer coding over the past year. Engineers can now delegate entire tasks to AI, but at the same time the work for most other teams has largely stayed the same, save for perhaps an email getting written faster, or a meeting being summarized.

The new products aim to bring the same AI benefits programmers have enjoyed “for over a year,” Vora said, to knowledge workers across corporations. Anthropic’s renewed push to attract corporate knowledge workers could put the company in closer competition with other software vendors such as Microsoft, whose shares were down more than 2% after the news was announced.

Anthropic’s vision is to turn Claude into an active member a team, rather than an optimization tool for individuals. For example, with Claude Meetings, professionals can add Claude to video calls as a “visible participant,” Anthropic said. The AI listens to the conversation and can “start on the work while people are still talking.” It lays out the proposed plan and timeline, answers questions in the call chat, and handles tasks such as pulling up last year’s numbers, using “the work apps people have connected,” Anthropic said. The results surface in claude.ai after the call.

Claude Meetings is in beta for Team and Enterprise plans, and starting with Google Meet, with plans to expand to other video platforms.

With Claude Whiteboards, humans can brainstorm ideas and collaborate with Claude. “A team talks through a messy plan out loud, and Claude turns it into a board with a timeline, owners and dates,” Anthropic said. Same goes for Claude Sheets, which are spreadsheets teams can build and edit alongside Claude, and can export to Excel or CSV files. Both these products are also in beta.

If these products can automate a meaningful portion of non-coding roles, they could encourage more businesses to sign up for Claude subscription plans. However, they could also create mayhem or burn tokens on AI-generated materials that never get used.

Anthropic is also seeking ways to deeply embed Claude in critical business functions. Another product called Claude Data, formerly Claude Dashboards, connects the AI to systems where companies keep their most important numbers, such as a data warehouse or CRM. Claude Data became available for paid plans today.

Similarly, new Claude Connectors “link Claude to the apps a company already uses, so Claude can pull information from them and take actions in them,” Anthropic said. Over 9,000 apps are available as Claude Connectors, such as Salesforce and Workday. “Teams already do much of their work in apps like these,” Anthropic said. “Now they can open the full app beside the conversation and ask Claude to work in it with them.” That means “no more switching tabs,” said Nicholas Lin, who leads product for knowledge work at Anthropic, on stage at today’s event.

Tuesday’s launch event came on the same day as Anthropic kicked off its pre-IPO roadshow with investors.

The idea of Claude revolutionizing non-coding roles in the same way it’s done for coding could energize the IPO and drive up the share price. Several sources we spoke to think Anthropic’s $70-$78 target share price is intentionally low, a tactic to set expectations and leave room to shatter them.

“Anthropic is moving forward with its IPO at a steeper discount than market initially anticipated,” said Lior Prosor, managing partner of Deep33, a deep-tech venture fund. “We think that is a smart pricing strategy. It gives nervous ‘AI-trade’ investors meaningful potential upside while securing the capital Anthropic needs to take full control of its destiny and fund its compute commitments.”

Also this week, Anthropic debuted new frontier models, Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, at a lower price with allegedly stronger performance than OpenAI’s latest frontier model, GPT-6 Astra. This also got investors’ attention.

“Anthropic has shown incredible advances recently and their announcement about Fable 5.2 yesterday suggests they could have a bigger impact in hardware domains like robotics than people might have given them credit for previously,” said Bastiaan Janmaat, General Partner at Lithos Capital.

#5445. Zillow CEO’s reality check on AI agents: ‘Finding a home isn’t a chore to hand off to a robot’

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 5:41 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 5:54 pm

People will let AI agents cancel subscriptions and book appointments, but most won’t want one to do their house hunting, predicts Zillow Group CEO Jeremy Wacksman.

Wacksman made the case Wednesday afternoon in prepared remarks on Zillow’s quarterly earnings call, addressing a big issue for the online real estate company: whether AI agents will shop on people’s behalf, bypassing sites such as Zillow.

“No one wants an AI agent to watch a movie or play a game for them, because the enjoyment is the point,” he said. “Dreaming and searching for a home is similar. It’s the fun part of the moving process that people want to do.”

Few decisions are as high-stakes as choosing a home, he said. “Finding a home isn’t a chore to hand off to a robot; it’s a milestone people want to live themselves.”

It’s a key issue for Zillow, which makes most of its money from the home-buying process, including fees from partner real estate agents and its mortgage lending business.

That depends on people browsing Zillow’s listings and connecting with those (human) agents and loan officers. An AI agent that does the searching could change those dynamics and potentially cut Zillow out of the process.

The issue has become more pressing with the rise of personal AI agents such as Meta’s Muse, which launched in September and can book travel and make purchases on people’s behalf, among other everyday tasks.

Amazon blocked Muse from shopping on its site less than two weeks after launch, saying it never agreed to let Muse shop there and that the agent doesn’t identify itself. Amazon is also suing Perplexity over the shopping agent in its Comet browser. A federal appeals court in August overturned an injunction Amazon had won in that case.

So far, Wacksman said, Zillow isn’t seeing meaningful traffic from AI platforms. The company has integrated with OpenAI and Google’s Gemini, and is now working with Anthropic. About 80% of its traffic comes directly to Zillow.

For the third quarter, Zillow’s revenue rose 7% to $724 million, short of its own forecast of $745 million to $760 million, as a sharp rise in mortgage rates slowed home sales.

The company posted a $158 million net loss for the quarter, mostly from agreeing to settle a shareholder lawsuit over Zillow Offers, its defunct home-flipping business.

#5444. One mom tallied 23 hours a week of household work. Then she built a company to turn ‘invisible labor’ into a paid profession

Kelly Hubbell worked full-time in tech sales and raised two children when the overwhelm set in. She didn’t need a nanny—both kids were in daycare—but the household work kept piling up, and she was desperate for support.

So she made a list of everything she did to keep the house running. It added up to 23 hours a week. Most of that time, Hubbell realized, wasn’t the chores themselves. It was the mental work of planning them.

“I just thought, wouldn’t it be awesome if I could clone myself?” Hubbell said.

Instead, she went looking for what she called a “house manager,” someone who could take over the logistics and errands she had been cramming into her evenings and weekends. She found one.

“It completely changed my life,” Hubbell said. “Overnight, I felt like I could be a present parent, and I had relief from the mental load, because I was able to fully hand off tasks.”

That relief became a business. In 2023, during her third maternity leave, Hubbell founded Sage Haus, a white-glove service that helps parents hire a house manager and set up the “home-management systems” that make handing off work possible. Its pitch arrives as women hold more U.S. payroll jobs than men for only the third time in the country’s history, while still shouldering most of the planning that keeps a household running.

Sage Haus isn’t alone. “House manager” now turns up in job listings on Indeed and Care.com, and other agencies have emerged to place house managers with busy parents.

The difference between a house manager and a babysitter is ownership. A babysitter who noticed your child had outgrown their shoes, took your credit card, and bought a new pair without asking would be overstepping. For a house manager, that is the job.

That kind of help doesn’t come cheap. Sage Haus families typically pay a house manager $25 to $45 an hour for 15 to 20 hours a week, according to the company, or roughly $20,000 to $47,000 a year. Full-time house managers generally earn $50,000 to $120,000, depending on location and scope, and Sage Haus charges families a flat placement fee rather than a percentage of salary.

Those rates run well above the broader market. House manager job postings on Indeed average about $23 an hour.

The services are marketed to dual-income families who simply don’t have enough hours in the day. Hubbell said many of the women she has worked with told her that before they hired help, they feared they would have to leave careers they loved to take care of their homes.

That fear has data behind it. KPMG research found that mothers of young children cut hours or left work at higher rates than fathers, pushed by return-to-office mandates and scarce, expensive childcare.

In the U.S., mothers handle 71% of household mental-load tasks, the cognitive work of planning meals, arranging activities, and keeping family life on schedule, according to a 2024 study by researchers at the University of Bath and the University of Melbourne. Fathers report handling 45%; the shares overlap because some tasks are shared.

In a world where someone from an app will deliver your dinner or build your IKEA furniture, Sage Haus wants to break the taboo around hiring help at home.

“We are putting a value on what has historically been invisible labor on the backs of mostly women, and that makes a lot of people uncomfortable,” Hubbell said. “Part of our mission is to normalize this, to take out the shame and the guilt around getting the kind of support that we need.”

In 2024, Hubbell quit her job to run Sage Haus full time. The company now has more than 60 employees and works with about 100 families a month across the U.S. and Canada, she said.

Sage Haus also draws on a network of more than 7,000 house managers and sells a $99 House Manager Certification course, which teaches them to anticipate needs, practice discretion, and become an integral part of a household.

Hubbell sees the role as a career path in both directions. She thinks house managers could move into corporate administrative work, and she has watched executive assistants switch into house management.

“I do believe that it takes high executive functioning to be in this role,” Hubbell said.

The work being handed off was never small. In 2020, Oxfam estimated that the unpaid care work done by women and girls worldwide is worth at least $10.8 trillion a year. In the U.S. alone, unpaid household labor is worth up to $6 trillion a year, about a fifth of GDP, and none of it appears in official growth figures.

Perhaps paying someone to make your grocery list is a late-stage-capitalist offering for families that have it all. But while hiring help has long been considered a luxury, companies like Sage Haus are asking why work traditionally done by women was ever free in the first place.

#5443. Amazon teams up with Uber on restaurant delivery, years after shutting down its own service

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 3:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 1:39 pm

Amazon is bringing Uber Eats inside its own app, letting U.S. Prime members order restaurant delivery without a separate Uber account and skip the delivery fee on orders of $25 or more.

The deal replaces a Prime perk with Grubhub, which Amazon made an ongoing benefit in 2024 after a one-year trial. Amazon said in a statement to GeekWire that it has ended that agreement after identifying “an opportunity to deliver an even better restaurant delivery experience.”

The new Prime benefit covers hundreds of thousands of restaurants in nearly 10,000 U.S. cities and towns, from major metros to rural communities. Orders are placed with existing Amazon logins and payment methods, on Amazon.com or in the Amazon Shopping app.

Amazon says Prime members could save more than $175 a year through the delivery fee waiver and Prime-only promotions, which it notes is more than the $139 annual cost of Prime. Service fees still apply, the company confirmed. New users get $20 off their first two orders of $25 or more within 14 days, and Prime Visa cardholders earn 5% back on Uber Eats orders through Dec. 5.

Members who already pay for Uber One, which includes $0 delivery fees, keep those benefits. But Amazon said the two memberships operate independently, and the Prime perk applies only to Uber Eats orders placed through Amazon.

The deal marks Amazon’s latest approach to restaurant delivery. The company shut down its own Amazon Restaurants service in 2019, four years after launching it in Seattle and expanding to more than 20 U.S. cities. Uber had listed Amazon as an Uber Eats competitor in its IPO filing earlier that year.

The service let Prime members order meals through its website or the Prime Now app. Amazon cut jobs on the team in early 2018, closed the London service later that year, and also shut down Daily Dish, a workplace lunch delivery service it launched in 2016.

The Uber deal is part of Amazon’s broader push to add value to Prime. In February, the company made its Alexa+ AI assistant free for U.S. Prime members. Last year it ended a program that let members share free shipping with someone outside their household.

“We’re excited to connect our restaurant community with new Prime fans, while giving Prime members a seamless way to enjoy great food from restaurants through Uber Eats,” Andrew Macdonald, Uber’s president and COO, said in a statement.

Members can share the Uber Eats benefit with one adult in their household through Amazon Family.

The reaction would likely be sharpest in the first 30–60 minutes after the release, followed by a digestion period. Sustained upside would depend on whether yields continue to ease and whether equity markets also respond positively.

A “Goldilocks” outcome, soft enough to calm inflation fears but not so weak that it raises recession concerns, would be the most constructive scenario for digital assets. Of course, risks remain.

If core inflation prints at 0.3% or higher, or if energy and shelter components stay sticky, the opposite reaction is probable: a quick drop in Bitcoin toward the low $70,000s and further pressure on Ethereum.

Positioning is already fragile after recent outflows, so any hawkish surprise could amplify selling. Overall, the balance of probabilities points to a modest cooling that gives the crypto market temporary breathing room.

While one data point will not reverse the broader macro narrative, a softer CPI could provide the spark needed for a short-term relief rally and remind participants that the inflation path is not a one-way street higher.

#5441. Longtime investor Martin Tobias says no to 99% of startups — his new AI tool helps them find a yes

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 7:01 amNovember 5, 2026 at 7:01 am

Martin Tobias was pitched by about 4,500 startups last year. He wrote 10 checks.

Now the pre-seed investor is offering the rest of them a consolation prize: an AI tool that tells founders which investors are most likely to say yes.

Tobias, a longtime figure in the Seattle tech scene, is now based in Spokane, Wash. He founded Loudeye, a digital media company that went public during the dot-com boom and later sold to Nokia, and went on to lead biofuel maker Imperium Renewables and group-buying startup Tippr.

He was a venture partner at Ignition Partners, an early backer of DocuSign, before starting Incisive Ventures in 2020. The firm closed a $10.5 million fund last year to back early-stage B2B software companies.

Investor Match started as an internal tool to help Incisive’s portfolio companies find seed and Series A investors. Tobias said he has 17,000 contacts but can only keep about 150 of them in his head, a limit known as Dunbar’s number.

To use the tool, founders upload a pitch deck, and Investor Match returns 20 investors ranked by fit, based on stage, check size, geography and what each firm has actually backed. It also drafts outreach emails, but it doesn’t send them.

Most founders send those emails cold, or pass the list to their existing investors and ask for warm introductions, Tobias said. Investors who have accounts on the platform can also respond to founders directly.

A free preview shows all 20 matches with fit scores, with the top three fully expanded. The full list costs $20, which Tobias said roughly covers the API costs of running it, about $1,000 a month.

Every founder Tobias turns down now gets pointed to the tool.

“Just because I wasn’t the right investor for that company doesn’t mean that the right investor wasn’t out there,” he told GeekWire.

Incisive appears on the platform like any other investor. Some founders who were matched with the firm asked whether Tobias had tilted the algorithm toward himself. He said he hadn’t, and that he only wants pitches that actually fit.

“Just because I wasn’t the right investor for that company doesn’t mean that the right investor wasn’t out there.”

Other companies offer investor matching as part of broader fundraising platforms, including Metal and OpenVC, which Tobias said charge founders monthly subscriptions. He said OpenVC relies on simple keyword matching, while Investor Match uses AI to read each investor’s website, portfolio and blog posts, which takes “millions and millions of tokens.”

Some of those companies are trying to build venture-scale businesses off founders’ fundraising, Tobias said.

“I think that’s just f—ing evil,” he said. “I don’t think you should try to make money off people who quit their job and are putting everything into trying to raise their first one to $2 million.”

Founders have told Tobias they’ve raised more than $100 million from investors they found through the platform since it launched about six months ago, though he acknowledged he can’t verify that because the money doesn’t flow through Investor Match.

Investor Match is also an extension of his investing thesis. He said his fund looks for B2B software companies like DocuSign that “reduce friction at scale” by taking a business process and doing it better in software.

“That’s exactly what Investor Match is,” he said. “What’s the friction in the market that you’re dealing with? Investors finding founders, founders finding investors. OK, can software help with that? I think it can.”

#5440. Circle Begins CCTP V1 Wind-Down Amid Doc Mismatch

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still says Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

Most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It says: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

The schedule is fixed. Circle announced in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026."

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide says "message limits will tighten over time until no new burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the company wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible."

Funds already in transit are protected. The guide says "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations."

The migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1."

The main text above it says something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:

Circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

As of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle said "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small issue, but the timing makes this one more serious.

Many developers now ask AI assistants to write or update integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

The fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

For teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

For Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

For everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

#5439. Anthropic inks $3.4 billion deal for gas-powered data centers—the largest of its kind—to secure AI autonomy ahead of planned IPO

In late September, investment banking company Piper Sandler released a short memo saying it had served as a financial advisor for San Antonio-based equipment supplier OnePWR Solutions on its $3.4 billion sale of its power generation platform to a “frontier AI lab.”

Now, the AI lab in question has been revealed. Anthropic is committing $3.4 billion to secure gas-fired power generators for its expanding data center operations—the largest direct investment in power generation equipment by an AI company, according to the Financial Times.

The deal involves 1.7 gigawatts of heavy-duty natural gas generators from OnePWR Solutions, according to the FT. Anthropic agreed to the transaction, taking over generator commitments that OnePWR had previously made with Caterpillar. The arrangement also includes engineering and construction capabilities necessary to install the equipment. The generators are expected to become available in the next two years.

Meanwhile, Anthropic is preparing for its IPO, with the company filing its S-1 with the SEC in September. In the registration statement, Anthropic disclosed approximately $900.9 billion in aggregate committed spending on computing and infrastructure, which would include purchase commitments and lease agreements. Of that amount, about $451.6 billion is expected to be spent before 2030, with most of the remaining commitments extending through 2045. Another $70.7 billion is due within the 12 months following Sep. 30, according to the amended S-1 filed in November.

The company is seeking a $1.3 trillion valuation, selling 825 million shares at a range of $70 to $78 a piece.

The S-1 also outlined key concerns for Anthropic, of which gas-powered data centers were included. The company warned that the dependence on natural gas could put the data center buildout under threat of volatile prices.

“As data center operators increasingly rely on natural gas-fired generation, and because behind-the-meter and on-site arrangements are feasible only in some jurisdictions given the applicable regulatory frameworks, we expect increased competition among users for the same natural gas supply and pipeline capacity in those areas,” the filing read.

Anthropic and OnePWR Solutions did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fortune.

The commitments outlined in Anthropic’s S-1 reflect the company’s effort to secure its own computing capacity needed to develop and operate its AI models. Currently, Anthropic’s infrastructure strategy spans several technology suppliers including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, Nvidia, and AMD.

But the S-1 describes a strategy called “Anthropic Direct,” in which the company can lease chips directly and place them in dedicated data centers on its behalf. According to the filing, it allows Anthropic to separate its “commitments for data center capacity” from its “commitments for the compute infrastructure deployed inside them.”

“Because data centers require longer lead times but represent a smaller fraction of total compute costs,” the S-1 reads, “this approach enables us to secure data center capacity early while deferring larger accelerator investments until our specific compute needs are more certain.”

The filing also makes it clear electricity and power are becoming a major constraint on that expansion. Anthropic warned that transformers, turbines, generators, substations, and other electrical equipment can take years to procure, with manufacturers facing higher prices, tariffs and limited production capacity. Alongside those concerns, the company also acknowledged it may need to purchase long-lead-time power generation at prices above market rates.

Anthropic specifically disclosed that some planned data center facilities rely on dedicated natural gas-fired generation, exposing it to fluctuations in fuel lines, pipeline capacity constraints, and disruptions to natural gas supplies.

While Anthropic just agreed to the largest acquisition deal for power generation equipment as of yet, it’s not the only AI-forward company looking to secure its own power generation.

In December 2025, Alphabet—the parent company of Google—acquired energy developer Intersect Power for $4.75 billion. Intersect had been working with Google to colocate data centers with new electricity generation, and the deal gave Google greater control over how quickly it could bring new power generation online.

Elon Musk’s xAI also turned to natural gas turbines to power its Colossus data centers in Tennessee and Mississippi after the existing grid connections couldn’t provide sufficient power.

Meanwhile, Meta has pursued on-site natural gas generation for its Ohio data center campus, working with energy infrastructure company Williams on a project worth approximately $1.6 billion in energy generation equipment, according to the Milken Institute.

And Microsoft signed a 20-year agreement with Constellation Energy in September 2024 to purchase electricity from the Three Mile Island nuclear facility in Pennsylvania, a $16 billion agreement.

Amazon has also pursued data center energy capacity through an agreement with Talen Energy, a nuclear-powered data center campus adjacent to the Susquehanna nuclear power plant in Pennsylvania.

“We’re making the largest private sector investment in state history–$20 billion–to bring 1,250 high-skilled jobs and economic benefits to the state, while also collaborating with Talen Energy to help power our infrastructure with carbon-free energy,” AWS Vice President of Global Data Centers Kevin Miller, said in a Talen Energy press release at the time.

Joshua Hong is a News Fellow at Fortune covering data, AI, cybersecurity, energy, and retail.

#5438. Uncommon Thinkers: Curiosity led Mary Brunkow to an immune breakthrough — and a Nobel Prize

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 5, 2026 at 7:54 amNovember 5, 2026 at 9:03 am

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Mary Brunkow had considered becoming a veterinarian or doctor — she knew she wanted to do good in the world and help people. Then, as an undergraduate at the University of Washington, she stepped into a research lab for the first time.

Inside, a professor she admired and his team were using fruit flies to study genetics.

“You walked in this door and it was like entering this new world,” Brunkow said, recalling the collaborative, passionate environment. “I just loved it. There was the smell of ether in the air. There was this real love of the science.”

After graduating and going on to earn a doctorate, Brunkow built a career in research. She joined Seattle-area startup Darwin Molecular and oversaw a team studying mutant mice afflicted by severe autoimmune disease. The scientists painstakingly identified the responsible gene, which led to valuable insights into the immune system’s T cells.

Brunkow worked on other projects at Darwin, too. But after an acquisition and a merger, the company’s local R&D operation shut down. Brunkow moved on. She ultimately landed at the Institute for Systems Biology (ISB), her immune-system research well in the past.

Then, in October 2025, came an unexpected call: She would share the Nobel Prize in Medicine with former Darwin colleague Fred Ramsdell and Osaka University’s Shimon Sakaguchi for discoveries explaining how the immune system avoids attacking the body’s own tissues.

Now a distinguished investigator at ISB, Brunkow was stunned by the honor. But Jim Heath, president of the institute, sees it as well deserved.

“Mary brings an exceptional combination of scientific rigor, intellectual curiosity, and humility to her work,” he said. “She’s driven by fundamental questions about biology and isn’t afraid to challenge conventional thinking in pursuit of answers.”

Beyond her scientific prowess, Heath also praised Brunkow’s efforts to create a workplace as welcoming and vibrant as the one that captivated her as a college undergrad.

“She’s a generous colleague who values collaboration and helps create an environment where other scientists can do their best work. She’s deeply committed to creating opportunities for students who will become tomorrow’s scientists,” Heath said. “Those qualities are every bit as important as the discoveries themselves.”

When Brunkow joined Darwin in 1994, the biotech — whose backers included Microsoft co-founders Bill Gates and Paul Allen — was riding a wave of advances from the Human Genome Project, an effort to sequence humanity’s DNA playbook. Darwin scientists sought genes linked to disease that might point the way toward new treatments.

“It wasn’t a one-drug company. It wasn’t hyper-focused on something very specific. It was trying to figure out how we can affect change in patients,” Ramsdell said at Life Science Washington’s annual conference in April.

One project focused on “scurfy” mice, which carried an inherited mutation that caused devastating autoimmune disease. Researchers suspected the mutation disrupted a crucial regulator of the immune system. Darwin wasn’t set up for mouse research, so Brunkow commandeered a janitor’s closet and began carefully breeding the mice to narrow down the area containing the mutant gene.

The work was far more laborious and slow compared to today’s technology, but it was groundbreaking for that period. It delighted Brunkow.

“It was a really exciting time,” Brunkow said. “It took a lot of problem solving and troubleshooting to get to the answer.”

The scientists narrowed their search to 20 genes on the X chromosome and began painstakingly sequencing them. In the final gene, they found a tiny error — two extra DNA letters inserted into the sequence that rendered the protein useless.

Working with Ramsdell and other collaborators, the researchers identified the mouse gene and showed that mutations in its human counterpart, FOXP3, cause a rare autoimmune disorder called IPEX.

“It was nice to pull the story together. So we published a couple of nice papers. We filed patent inventions. We went to conferences and talked about it,” Brunkow said. “And then in 2004, the company closed down.”

Brunkow stayed friends with Ramsdell and followed developments in the field, but her own interests took her elsewhere. She was drawn less to one particular disease than to the challenge of finding a tiny genetic change that could have an enormous biological effect — and potentially point toward a treatment.

Meanwhile, other researchers were building on the discoveries.

Later research established the gene’s essential role in regulatory T cells, or Tregs — cells that restrain immune responses and protect the body from attacking itself.

“I didn’t actually understand the extent to which our publications kind of blew open a whole new area in immunology,” Brunkow said.

That work is now reaching patients. In June, the FDA approved Tregzi, a treatment incorporating regulatory T cells that helps prevent a serious complication of donor stem cell transplants in adults with blood cancers.

At ISB, Brunkow has embraced a broader view of biology. The organization takes a holistic approach to medical research, bringing together scientists in areas including cancer, infectious diseases and chronic illnesses.

For her, it is a natural progression from studying individual genes to investigating the complex networks in which they operate. The ultimate goal is personalized medicine: understanding what pushes someone from health toward disease, detecting those changes early and finding ways to intervene.

The Nobel recognition has given Brunkow a chance to broaden her impact beyond research — a platform to advocate for issues she cares about. That includes sustained research funding, support for women and other underrepresented groups in science, and stronger STEM education. She also wants to encourage scientists to support one another and work well together — the qualities she encountered in that UW fruit fly lab.

“You’ve got to figure out how to play well with others,” Brunkow said. “It makes science more fun. It makes science move faster.”
