#5437. Delaware’s federal court forced litigation funders into the open. Its most important court still lets them hide

Sonnenfeld is one of the nation’s most recognized experts on corporate governance. Sonnenfeld and Tian  have co-authored Trump’s Ten Commandments (Worth/Simon & Schuster)

We warned in the pages of Fortune last week that the corporate flight from Delaware would only accelerate on the heels of Delaware Chancery Court Vice Chancellor Travis Laster’s controversial and widely criticized decision in the highly watched Cloudflare case. Since then, Virtu Financial has announced its own relocation from Delaware to Texas on Nov. 4, following the recent exits of at least 30 companies over the last two years. Virtu’s move comes as it too is embroiled in pending litigation in Laster’s court, after Laster denied Virtu’s motion to dismiss.

As we’ve written previously, the boards of companies moving out of Delaware most often cite the same concern: they can no longer predict how the state’s Chancery Court, once prized for its consistency and predictability, will treat them, amidst a series of decisions widely construed as judicial overreach. The legislature has tried to correct this problem through SB21, but certain Chancery judges continue to seemingly defy the will of the legislature, and the Delaware Supreme Court has inadvertently undermined their own efforts to overturn erroneous decisions by remanding cases back to the same judges.

But a second blind spot gets far less attention, and it may matter just as much. A Delaware company can be hauled into the Court of Chancery today with no way of knowing who is paying for the lawsuit against it, whether that backer controls settlement, or whether it is a competitor or a foreign state amidst a surge in litigation backed by litigation finance firms.

The legal philosopher Jeremy Bentham wrote that “publicity is the very soul of justice.” One of the quiet strengths of the American legal system is how much of that ideal it has honored. Our courts function in the open, with public proceedings, published rules, and disclosure requirements designed to ensure that judges, litigants, and the public can understand who is driving a case—and why. Those features are not procedural niceties; they are cornerstones of trust in the judiciary itself. Delaware’s century-old promise to corporate America rested on the same idea: boards and litigants could see the rules and the players before they acted. Undisclosed third-party litigation funding cuts against that promise in the one court that matters most to American business.

A growing, mostly invisible market of litigation finance which has become perverted away from original noble intention

The global litigation finance market was estimated at $20.6 billion in 2025, with forecasts that it will more than double over the next decade, and U.S. commercial funders alone managed roughly $16 billion in assets at the end of 2024. This is a market which has already grown exponentially, as it barely existed merely two decades ago. At its best, litigation funding expands access to justice for plaintiffs who could not otherwise afford to be heard, a noble founding intent as it was envisioned by the widely admired founders of the field. But as litigation finance firms have proliferated exponentially over recent years, the actual practice of litigation finance has frequently become perverted from those noble founding aims, with key challenges including that too often, it is opaque, undisclosed, and strategically deployed. It obscures the real parties who have an interest in dragging out litigation and obfuscates what ulterior motives they may have, distorts the incentives that are supposed to drive a case toward resolution, and risks undermining the integrity of the courts themselves.

Unlike the contingency-fee arrangements familiar to American law, many third-party investments by litigation finance firms involve opaque layered structures of who gets paid, and complex ownership that remain invisible to judges and opposing parties. No federal statute or rule requires disclosure of even the existence of a litigation funder—let alone whether that litigation funder holds sway over litigation strategy or settlement decisions, as they sometimes do.

Real risks of undisclosed hidden litigation finance, including most alarmingly to national security

The potential harms are concrete from undisclosed litigation finance firms underwriting litigation. First, an outside litigation funder’s investment return thresholds can push it to resist settlement and prolong disputes, at real cost to litigants and to judicial resources. Second, a funder may not be motivated by financial profit at all. An undisclosed entity can underwrite suits to impose burdensome costs on a competitor for competitive harm, and when the money answers to a foreign state, the concern becomes one of national security. A December 2024 Government Accountability Office report found stakeholders pointing to funders from China, Saudi Arabia, and France, while conceding that the full extent of such funding is unknowable given how little is disclosed. The industry’s ties to foreign capital are not speculative, as one firm has announced a “strategic capital relationship” with a sovereign wealth fund, while another is now majority-owned by a consortium led by Mubadala, Abu Dhabi’s sovereign investor. Our courts are open by design, but openness should not mean naïveté.

This isn’t hypothetical. A Shenzhen-based firm led by the general counsel of Chinese electronics giant TCL was revealed to be financing patent suits against Samsung in U.S. courts , and Samsung later alleged that the funder had misused its confidential information to compete unfairly.

America’s famously broad civil discovery magnifies the danger. Justified by the principle that both sides should have access to the facts, discovery is estimated to account for 50% to 90% of the cost of litigating a case. That lets a funded plaintiff run up a defendant’s bill as an end in itself, or as a way to operationally hinder a competitor by requesting a document dump of sensitive strategic files of limited relevance to the actual litigation at hand, but of huge importance to sensitive industry and strategic competition. Indeed, when a lawsuit is secretly financed by an entity with strategic or geopolitical motives, discovery can become nothing more than a mechanism for extracting sensitive information under the protective cover of judicial process, with that sensitive information subsequently used by hostile foreign powers to undermine American companies unfairly.

Delaware’s federal court has already proved disclosure works

Patent litigation shows the pattern at scale. Patent cases absorbed 32% of new litigation-funding commitments in 2024, up from 19% a year earlier and the largest single category, and roughly 30% of patent suits are now estimated to be funded. Most of the large technology companies the GAO interviewed said that more than half the patent suits filed against them involve confirmed or suspected third-party funding. The suits increasingly come from non-practicing entities that make no products but acquire patents to monetize them in court: in 2025, NPEs filed 55% of all district-court patent cases and 90% of those in the high-tech sector.

Because the U.S. Supreme Court held in TC Heartland that a corporation “resides” for patent-venue purposes only in its state of incorporation, Delaware’s federal district court is a default venue for patent suits against Delaware corporations. In April 2022, Chief Judge Colm Connolly ordered parties before him to disclose any litigation funder and whether it controls litigation or settlement decisions. The results were revealing. Patent filings in the district fell 41% over the following two years, against a 15% national decline, and funded patent cases in his courtroom virtually disappeared. It was Connolly’s order that surfaced the profoundly disturbing Chinese TCL-linked funder behind the Samsung suits mentioned previously. Transparency, it turns out, discourages the litigation that least wants to be seen.

Delaware’s state courts have been slower to follow. To their credit, on Sept. 30, 2026, the Superior Court amended its rules to permit discovery into a funder’s existence, identity, and control rights while shielding the funding agreement itself absent a showing of good cause. But the Court of Chancery—the most important court in the nation for corporate disputes—has adopted no corresponding rule and proceeds case by case. Its judges have taken notice of the problem. In Burkhart v. Genworth, a putative class action decided in 2024, Vice Chancellor Nathan Cook ordered the plaintiffs to produce their funding agreement in full, warning that such cases are “especially ripe for a third-party funder to exercise improper control over the litigation.” That ruling shows the court understands the stakes, but a single order in a single case by one of the court’s seven judges, won only after a motion to compel, falls well short of a universal disclosure requirement.

The gap matters, because Chancery is where corporate America’s stockholder litigation lives, as the single most important court for American businesses in the entire country. When a court and defendants do not know who stands behind a complaint, it cannot fully assess conflicts of interest, police litigation conduct, or tell whether decisions are being driven by the named plaintiff or by an undisclosed backer with very different and ulterior objectives. None of this is a criticism of judges, who can only manage what is disclosed to them. The problem is structural – and easily fixable by the Delaware Chancery Court.

The case for reform is increasingly difficult to ignore. Members of Congress have pressed the judiciary to move faster. The chairman of the House Oversight Committee urged the Judicial Conference in 2024 to consider mandatory disclosure, citing foreign money in U.S. lawsuits; a bipartisan Senate bill introduced in 2023 would require any foreign funder to disclose its role and bar sovereign wealth funds from financing U.S. litigation; and four senators introduced legislation this February requiring disclosure in federal class actions and multidistrict litigation.

Regulators and states are moving too. The International Trade Commission proposed in April to require disclosure of funders in Section 337 proceedings, the arcane but consequential cases that determine whether foreign goods can be blocked from the U.S. market. Ohio enacted a law in July requiring funders to register and disclose their agreements, barring them from influencing how a lawsuit is handled or settled, and prohibiting foreign funders outright. North Carolina on June 22 became the first state to prohibit third-party litigation investment altogether. More than 20 states have now enacted laws regulating the practice, and New Jersey’s Assembly passed a disclosure bill in June.

Transparency is the remedy. Full, universal disclosure simply ensures that judges and litigants know who the real stakeholders are and what their motives may be —just as they already do when funders back class actions in the Northern District of California, when creditor groups organize in a bankruptcy, and when an investor accumulates more than 5% of a public company. Capital markets function on disclosure, not secrecy. Shareholders disclose ownership. Political donors disclose contributions. Judges disclose conflicts. The notion that litigation funders should be uniquely exempt makes no sense.

Boards leaving Delaware cite the increasing unpredictability of the Delaware Chancery Court and the cost of stockholder litigation, but undisclosed litigation funding feeds both. The fix is a Chancery rule modeled on Chief Judge Connolly’s order, requiring parties at the outset of a case to disclose whether a funder exists, who it is, and whether it controls strategy or settlement.

Justice Louis Brandeis observed that sunlight is said to be the best of disinfectants. Delaware built its reputation by letting everyone see the rules. It should let everyone see who is paying to litigate under them.

Disclosure: The authors presented their research on dual class shares to a special committee of Cloudflare’s board, a Delaware company currently in litigation in the Court of Chancery.

#5436. No sweat: High-tech T-shirt brand Neat survives ‘Shark Tank’ and lands $400K deal with Lori Greiner

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 9:45 amNovember 5, 2026 at 9:45 am

If Jim Huffman and Tyler Stelter were sweating during their pitch on ABC’s “Shark Tank,” their T-shirts didn’t show it. It probably helped them land a deal.

Huffman is CEO and Stelter is COO of Seattle-based Neat, which makes shirts designed to hide sweat. They survived a grilling from the Sharks on the popular reality TV series and secured an investment from Lori Greiner on Wednesday night’s episode.

Greiner agreed to invest $400,000 for a 15% stake in the company, plus 75 cents per order until she earns back her investment. Huffman said the deal is still being finalized.

“I love the product. I’m gonna be a huge customer,” Greiner, an inventor and longtime QVC personality, said on the show. “I already have 10,000 ideas of videos we’re gonna do.”

“It felt like a business knife fight,” Huffman told GeekWire on Thursday. The most intense part, he said, was negotiating with several Sharks at once while doing revenue-share math in his head.

Neat sells T-shirts and other tops lined with a patented “Sweat Maze,” a pattern of water-repelling and water-attracting zones that pulls moisture inward and spreads it across the inside of the shirt so it dries before it shows through.

The technology came out of research funded by the National Science Foundation and was originally developed for military personnel, firefighters and first responders.

“Shark Tank,” now in its 18th season on ABC, features entrepreneurs pitching their businesses to a panel of wealthy investors, known as Sharks, in hopes of landing an investment in exchange for a stake in their company. The show is based on “Dragons’ Den,” a Japanese format, and has won five Emmy Awards.

Joining Greiner on Neat’s panel were Kendra Scott, founder of the jewelry brand that bears her name; Kind snack bar founder Daniel Lubetzky; investor Kevin O’Leary; and Rashaun Williams, a venture capitalist and chief investment officer of Harbinger Sports Partners.

Huffman applied for the show on a whim, filling out an online form late one night. About 10,000 companies apply each season and roughly 70 make it on air, he said producers told him.

Huffman and Stelter filmed their pitch in June at Tyler Perry Studios in Atlanta. Taping there in the summer made it “the ultimate test” for the shirt, said Huffman, who added that he runs hot when presenting, even without studio lights.

Huffman and Stelter came into the tank asking for $400,000 for 5% of Neat, valuing the company at $8 million. O’Leary was so put off by the valuation that he said a lightning bolt should “come through the ceiling and fry you both.” He then dropped out.

O’Leary and Williams saw Neat as a niche product, Huffman said. But Scott and Lubetzky both made offers, and Lubetzky’s interest caught the Neat team off guard. “We weren’t ready for that!” Huffman said.

When O’Leary argued that the shirts only appealed to men, Scott countered that women sweat, too. “Have you heard of a hot flash, darling? Because it’s a real thing,” she said.

Scott offered $400,000 for 20%, saying the product “has got licensing power, but your valuation is nuts.” Lubetzky offered the same amount for 25% before pulling out. Greiner then came in at 15% plus the per-order royalty, and the Neat team took her deal.

“We’ve never built an eight- or nine-figure brand, and Lori has, so bringing in someone with that experience and knowledge is extremely exciting,” Huffman said.

Huffman and Stelter began working on the brand in 2024. Huffman also runs GrowthHit, a Seattle-based growth marketing agency he founded in 2016.

Huffman came across Neat through a GrowthHit client, a sports performance brand whose team had developed the technology. Having grown up in Oklahoma and lived in Texas and New York, Huffman said he knew the pain of hot days when you can “never wear heather gray.” When the client sent him a shirt, his reaction was, “Oh my gosh, this is amazing!”

GrowthHit had been looking for a brand of its own after earlier attempts to launch products didn’t pan out, Huffman said. The agency took over Neat, with the original team continuing to handle product development while GrowthHit ran branding and marketing.

Neat’s net sales grew more than 300% in 2025, to about $700,000, and the company is on track for $1.5 million to $2 million in sales this year, Huffman said.

Huffman credits the growth to basic growth-marketing moves. Neat positioned itself as something other than a regular cotton tee, pushed bundles over single shirts, upgraded its product photos and raised prices.

Neat’s newest shirt, the Sweat Defender Crew, sells for $59.99, with discounts for bundles. Huffman told the Sharks that each shirt costs about $11.70 to make.

The company scaled through Instagram and Facebook ads, going from about $20 a day in ad spend to roughly $2,000 a day.

Its best-known ad pops a water balloon inside a shirt to show the outside staying dry. “We need to be able to demonstrate the product in five seconds, or you’re toast,” Huffman said.

Neat is profitable and hasn’t raised venture funding, Huffman said. He said the company is on track for a 15% profit margin this year.

The company has four employees, two in Seattle and two in Portland. Its shirts are made in Vietnam and sold directly to consumers. They’re not on Amazon or in stores yet, but Huffman said “Shark Tank” could open new sales channels.

Traffic to Neat’s site jumped about 20-fold from the East Coast and Central time zones as soon as the segment aired, Huffman said. The company did more sales during the nine-minute segment than it does on a strong holiday, with a second wave when the show aired on the West Coast.

The most popular color since the show aired is the sage green Huffman and Stelter wore in the tank, which is also the color Neat has the least of in stock.

“Our main priorities right now are making sure the site doesn’t crash and that customer service can keep up,” Huffman said.

#5435. ‘It’s just about fairness’: United’s CEO doubles down on a wealth tax despite his $32 million pay

United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby took home about $32.3 million in total compensation last year, according to Fortune’s reporting on United’s proxy statement. He says people like him should be paying more, starting with a tax on the wealth they already hold.

In a wide-ranging interview with The New York Times in mid-October, Kirby said wealth inequality “has become a danger to our society” and called for a national wealth tax, plus inheritance taxes that “get close to 100% at some level.” “I would pay them,” he added.

The remarks drew swift pushback, much of it aimed at his paycheck. Fox Business asked United how Kirby squared his pay with his warnings about inequality; the company didn’t respond.

Kirby doubled down a few days later on CNBC’s Squawk Box, framing the idea as a matter of fairness.

“I think a wealth tax… is just about fairness…. If you’re wealthy enough, you can put money aside, and by the way, I think it would apply to me, put money aside, let it grow forever, never realize income on it, you can let it grow forever and it never gets taxed,” he said.

That is the gap Kirby wants to close. The federal system taxes income: in 2025, the top rate of 37% applied to single filers’ taxable income above $626,350, according to the IRS. Investments that rise in value but are never sold aren’t taxed.

Kirby’s view stands out because of who holds it. He runs a company on the 2026 Fortune 500 that brought in $59.1 billion in revenue last year.

He stressed that these were personal views and that he has no interest in politics or policymaking. If it were up to him, he said, he would prefer a system “where we had lower income taxes, and higher taxes, or some kind of taxes, on the gain in wealth.”

In practice, the idea draws pointed objections. Mariana Trujillo, managing director of government finance at the Reason Foundation, a libertarian-leaning think tank, tells Fortune it would undercut the very growth it’s meant to share.

“Taxing accumulated wealth discourages investment and entrepreneurship — the very forces that have made our lives better than those of our grandparents and great-grandparents. Economic progress, not the state, has driven improvements in our material condition. A wealth tax discourages the very thing it aims to promote,” she says.

Trujillo draws a sharp line between the two ideas Kirby floated. An inheritance tax hits wealth once, when it changes hands. An annual wealth tax hits it every year, and she argues that gives the wealthiest Americans, and their capital, a reason to leave.

“An annual wealth tax is entirely different from an inheritance tax…. People move out of states and countries for tax reasons. National wealth taxes failed in Europe, where countries including France, Sweden, and Germany abandoned them amid concerns about capital flight, administrative costs, and disappointing revenues.”

A few European countries have held on: Norway, Spain, and Switzerland still levy net wealth taxes, according to the Tax Foundation.

Trujillo also had a message for Kirby himself. “If Kirby believes his wealth could be better used to improve others’ lives, he is free to put it toward that purpose,” she said. “But I hope he recognizes that his compensation reflects the perceived value of his contributions to his company and, therefore, to society at large. Wealth does not need to be redistributed to be productive; it is already the result of creating value for others.”

Kirby has argued that a state-by-state approach is doomed. “We should have a national wealth tax—it won’t work by state because people will just move,” he told the Times, as Fortune reported.

California just tested a state version. In the Nov. 3 election, voters rejected Proposition 40, the so-called billionaire tax, which would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of state residents worth more than $1 billion. The Associated Press called the race on Nov. 9, with 52.8% of voters opposed, according to CalMatters.

The measure had high-profile backers, including six Nobel Prize–winning economists who argued it could kick-start similar efforts elsewhere. But opponents spent about $378 million against it, while the yes campaign raised $33.5 million, and Silicon Valley voters broke against it even as Los Angeles and San Francisco voted yes.

Trujillo sees the result as a verdict on the idea itself. “California’s wealth tax proposal failed at the ballot box for good reasons: first, because voters recognized it may reduce government revenue as people leave, and second, because they saw it as discouraging investment and innovation, which make our lives better.”

Kirby says the emails he received about his comments split about evenly for and against. If California is any guide, the rest of the country isn’t far off.

#5434. Shield AI to buy Bill Gates-backed radar maker Echodyne in $5.3B deal, doubling down on Seattle area

by Todd Bishop & John Cook on Nov 5, 2026 at 9:47 amNovember 5, 2026 at 10:41 am

Shield AI, the defense tech company planning to build its AI-piloted X-BAT fighter jet south of Seattle, agreed to acquire Kirkland, Wash.-based Echodyne, which makes compact radar systems that detect and track drones, in a transaction valued at up to $5.3 billion.

It’s a major exit for one of the Seattle region’s best-known deep-tech startups. Echodyne spun out of Intellectual Ventures, the Bellevue invention lab, in 2014 with a $15 million round led by Bill Gates and Madrona.

Echodyne, ranked No. 9 on the GeekWire 200, has raised about $200 million in total, and PitchBook put its valuation at $485 million after its last priced round in 2022.

The deal is believed to be the second-largest acquisition of a private venture-backed company in Washington state history, behind Okta’s $6.5 billion acquisition of Auth0 in 2021, Madrona’s Tim Porter wrote in a blog post. It’s among the top exits in the history of the Seattle-based venture firm, Porter said, noting that Echodyne is profitable.

To help pay for the acquisition, San Diego-based Shield said it’s raising $2.5 billion, including $1 billion in new funding at a $28.8 billion valuation. That’s more than double the $12.7 billion valuation it reached in March.

What Echodyne does: Echodyne’s radar is built into hundreds of counter-drone and security systems used in more than 40 countries, according to the companies. It’s used in remote weapon stations, high-energy lasers and microwave weapons, and it helps point interceptors at incoming drones.

Stadiums and airports use the same technology to spot drones that aren’t supposed to be there. Shield, best known for its Hivemind autonomy software and V-BAT drone, has served only government end users so far, CEO Gary Steele told Bloomberg.

Steele called Echodyne the company’s first step into hardware with civilian as well as military uses. “Think about public safety — whether it’s the Super Bowl or FIFA, just literally every single thing is going to need protection from drones,” he said.

Impact on jobs: Echodyne has about 400 employees, up from 260 when it opened a $40 million manufacturing facility in Woodinville, Wash., in July. No layoffs are planned, and Echodyne employees won’t be required to relocate, a Shield spokesperson said.

The combined company will have about 2,700 employees. Eben Frankenberg, Echodyne’s co-founder and CEO, will remain in that role, reporting directly to Steele, and will stay in charge of its products and manufacturing as well as its relationships with customers and partners.

Madrona invested $5.5 million in Echodyne’s initial $15 million round, at a $24 million pre-money valuation, and Porter joined the board. Madrona and other Echodyne investors will become significant Shield shareholders, according to the venture firm.

Echodyne makes all of its radar systems in the Seattle region, and Shield will continue to double down on that growth along with its investment in X-BAT manufacturing, Porter said via email.

“Seattle as a defense tech hub is real,” he said.

Shield said in September that it expects to employ about 4,000 people in the Seattle region by the early 2030s as X-BAT production ramps up at its site in Des Moines, Wash. The company projects the program will support about 8,000 jobs in the region in that time, including at suppliers.

The deal is Shield’s fifth acquisition and its largest. The others were Heron Systems and Martin UAV in 2021, Sentient Vision Systems in 2024 and Aechelon Technology in June.

The acquisition is expected to close in early 2027, pending regulatory approvals. Shield will pay $4.8 billion at closing, with up to $500 million more if Echodyne hits performance targets, and the $2.5 billion financing won’t go through if the deal falls apart, according to the companies.

Dartmouth and Onyx roots: Frankenberg has “a unique knack for getting brilliant people to believe in a vision, even when there’s plenty of skepticism around them,” said Brent Frei, the Smartsheet co-founder, who met Frankenberg as a freshman at Dartmouth and later roomed with him.

“We were a little bit like the Odd Couple; he was the consummate gentleman from North Carolina: well-mannered, organized, focused and very smart,” Frei said. “By contrast, I was the other character.”

Frei founded Onyx Software in 1994 and built it largely with a group of Dartmouth friends, including Frankenberg. Mark Mader, another of the group, later built Smartsheet with Frei, and Rob Eleveld went on to sell Ekata to Mastercard for more than $800 million.

“Our running joke is that we keep building 10-to-12-year overnight successes,” Frei said.

Matt McIlwain, a Madrona managing director who also goes back to Dartmouth with Frankenberg, called the Onyx “family tree” a “great example of how the innovation ecosystem and flywheel gets built over decades in a community like Seattle.”

#5433. Residents Make Big Decisions About Local Businesses Within 30 Days of Moving In. Here’s How One Campaign Used That Window to Fill a Slow Monday Night.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

On a rainy Monday, a Manhattan restaurant landed 50 diners by reaching people who lived just a few blocks away. The exec behind the campaign explains why new neighbors are ready to pick their go-to spots.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

A campaign targeting nearby residents brought 50 diners to a restaurant in Manhattan’s Meatpacking District on a rainy Monday night, says.

For Sam Bakhshandehpour, president of local merchants at Bilt, the evening illustrated an opportunity for restaurants facing rising costs and pressure to fill seats.

“No one’s traveling on a Monday night to go grab a meal,” he says.

Rather than trying to attract diners from across the city, Bilt targeted residents in nearby apartment buildings who wouldn’t have to travel far for dinner. The restaurant’s chef-founder was pleased with the results.

“We got 50 covers locally, came on a Monday night where it would’ve been a disaster of a night,” Bakhshandehpour recalls the founder saying.

The guests also spent more, on average, and joined the restaurant’s loyalty program, Bakhshandehpour says.

Bakhshandehpour spent six years helping lead José Andrés Group, most recently as CEO, before moving to Bilt. Years of running hospitality businesses had given him plenty of problems he wanted to solve.

“The costs are going higher, and our margins are getting squeezed every single day,” he says.

When Bilt founder Ankur Jain asked what restaurateurs needed help with, Bakhshandehpour answered, “How much time do you have?”

Bilt began by allowing residents to earn rewards on rent payments. That housing network created an opportunity to connect local businesses with the people moving into nearby homes. Bakhshandehpour says residents make important decisions within their first 30 days in a neighborhood.

“This is my dry cleaner. This is my pharmacy. This is my restaurant, my bar,” he says. “And they’re loyal to their local neighborhood.”

Restaurants once sought those introductions through flyers and menus slipped under apartment doors.

“That’s been digitized,” Bakhshandehpour says. “And that has been localized and personalized to you.”

On that rainy Monday, the campaign gave nearby residents a reason to try the restaurant. Their first visit gave the team a chance to earn the next one.

A restaurant sends something to a table as a complimentary gesture. Then the guest finds it on the bill.

“I didn’t order this, and now you charged me for it,” Bakhshandehpour says.

“Thanks for that level of hospitality,” he adds sarcastically.

The restaurant intended to do something thoughtful. A missed instruction turned it into an awkward conversation.

Bakhshandehpour knows how many details restaurant teams have to carry from one person to another. A reservation request arrives by text. Someone needs to respond, pass it along and make sure the team is ready when the guest walks in.

Technology should help those details reach the people responsible for them.

“You’re able to focus on what you do best, and that’s deliver hospitality to your guests, not worry about the reservation book,” he says.

But every new tool can create another responsibility. As Bilt developed its use of AI agents, Jain set an expectation that Bakhshandehpour remembers clearly.

An operator should be able to ask, “Who’s coming to my restaurant tonight?” in everyday language. Getting an answer shouldn’t require learning how the technology behind it works.

Bakhshandehpour sees that simplicity in a device his father already uses.

“My 84-year-old father sets up his iPhone in a matter of minutes,” he says. “It’s effortless.”

Restaurants also have existing systems they depend on. When I asked whether operators using Toast could connect to Bilt without replacing their point-of-sale platform, Bakhshandehpour said they could.

“We can integrate, you keep Toast,” he says.

To hear where the experience needs work, Bilt sends executives to different cities each quarter for gatherings called Close Friends. Members are invited to give candid feedback.

“They’re the ones who challenge us, they give us the straight talk,” Bakhshandehpour says.

For restaurant teams, the value comes through in the follow-through. The reservation is ready. The instructions reach the right employee. A dish sent as a gift arrives without a charge.

#5432. 2 scandals, 1 destination—Why Nvidia can’t shake China smuggling allegations

For more than a year, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has repeated the party line about covert smuggling of his highly coveted premium chips: There’s no evidence Nvidia AI chips are being diverted to China, Huang has asserted.

But now two bombshell scandals, both allegedly running through Southeast Asia, have blasted a data-center sized hole through Huang’s credibility. The first case, in which $2.5 billion in computer servers equipped with Nvidia chips are under scrutiny, involves Super Micro, a company led by a longtime friend of Jensen Huang’s and one of Nvidia’s closest partners. More recently, a separate string of reports has revealed that Nvidia’s largest Southeast Asian customer, Megaspeed, is under U.S. investigation for chip diversion.

There is no evidence so far that the two cases are directly connected, though some industry observers have pointed to potential areas of overlap. Whether the two cases are ultimately determined to be part of a larger scheme, or completely separate incidents, the dual scandals have left Nvidia, shareholders, and its famous CEO, reeling.

On Sunday, Huang told employees in an email he had betrayed his wife and family in an extramarital affair. His confession followed reports claiming that intelligence officials believe Huang’s affair partner, Alice Huang (no relation), was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to purportedly report on his doings to Beijing. Alice Huang is a former executive of Megaspeed International, a Singapore company that reportedly became Nvidia’s largest chip buyer in Southeast Asia.

Alongside Huang’s admission, Nvidia’s board announced it has opened an independent investigation into whether Nvidia co-founder Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence operation but noted that board members maintain “confidence” in Huang. The board said it has no reason to believe that “either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.” Nvidia board members have retained acting U.S. Attorney of the Southern District of New York Joon H. Kim and his firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to run point on the investigation, Nvidia announced Tuesday.

Nvidia’s GPU chips are critical components for training and running advanced AI models such as those made by OpenAI and Anthropic. The U.S. government considers the chips to be dual-use technology with potential military applications, and requires specific export licenses to sell them to countries such as China—which haven’t been granted to Nvidia’s most high-powered chips.

How things will shake out for Nvidia is evolving in real time, but it’s likely that a terse letter Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) sent to Nvidia in June will turn into a subpoena. That’s thanks to midterm election results that saw Democrats regain the Senate with Warren poised to chair the powerful Senate Banking Committee in January. Warren and Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.) called Monday for Nvidia to answer questions, and three House committee chairs have asked Huang to accede to a closed-door grilling before lawmakers November 18, the day after Nvidia is scheduled to report its third quarter financial results.

The June letter, which went to Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter and audit committee chair Brooke Seawell, sought answers from Nvidia regarding the state of its compliance program and noted that Nvidia continued to include Super Micro Computer (Supermicro) as a key partner in its network. The letter also cited Culper Research, a short seller who bet against Nvidia and published a report that alleges possible smuggling links between Supermicro, Nvidia, and Megaspeed, the company where Alice Huang was a top executive. U.S. authorities have investigated whether the billions in Nvidia hardware Megaspeed bought through Nvidia’s server partners went to Chinese firms barred from getting the chips. Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing.

Alice Huang is now the link between the CEO infidelity and coverup scandal facing Jensen Huang, the poster CEO for the AI buildout, and a question that has persistently dogged Nvidia, which is where its chips actually wind up after they’re purchased. And as far as export control compliance goes, an alleged honey trap espionage case carries a lot more public-interest tailwind than the at times byzantine regulations involved in obtaining and complying with export restrictions and licensing. Meaning, this latest revelation is unlikely to blow over as a single rogue actor or administrative export record issue.

One export-control veteran, who asked to speak anonymously because of his clients, said if he were an independent director or general counsel, he’d be looking at whether the company they oversee has a Huang honeytrap problem—and not just at the CEO level. Executives who are supposed to inspect data centers or conduct due diligence have been the targets of these types of seduction schemes going back decades.

He also nodded to the March Supermicro indictment that pointed out that a compliance auditor was “off-site enjoying entertainment paid for by” another company. It’s a fairly common tactic, he said.

Until recently, the most high-profile case of contraband Nvidia chips involved one of Nvidia’s closest partners, a company run by Huang’s longtime friend, Supermicro CEO Charles Liang. Neither Liang nor Supermicro was charged and Supermicro has said it is cooperating with authorities. Liang and Huang, who both founded their respective companies in 1993, often took the stage together at an event called Computex in Taiwan and joked back and forth during their joint keynotes.

“When we’re together, sometimes we speak Taiwanese, sometimes we speak Mandarin, and then when we disagree, we speak English,” Huang joked before an adoring crowd at Computex in 2024. (Huang was photographed with Alice Huang, his affair partner, at a Taipei cocktail bar during Computex that year.)

In March, federal prosecutors charged Supermicro co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw and two others with routing about $2.5 billion in servers laden with Nvidia H200 and B200 GPUs to China via a Southeast Asian front company. Supermicro was not charged and has said it was a victim of the scheme. Liaw has pleaded not guilty, although one of the three who were charged pleaded guilty last month. Liaw cofounded Supermicro with Liang and Liang’s wife, Sara Liu the same year Huang co-founded Nvidia. Neither Liang nor Liu were named in the indictment.

According to Liaw’s indictment, the elaborate scheme involved staging thousands of nonworking dummy servers in three warehouses to trick auditors. Contractors used hair dryers to soften the adhesive on serial-number labels and peel them off. That alleged scheme followed a similar playbook as one that had ensnared Supermicro in 2006, when the company pleaded guilty to illegally exporting computer equipment to Iran through a distributor in Dubai. Both routes involved selling to a neighboring country to keep the real buyer hidden.

The Liaw indictment does not accuse Nvidia of wrongdoing, but it lays out how the front company’s orders for Supermicro hardware fed into Nvidia’s chip allocation. In December 2024, Liaw allegedly asked the front company for monthly forecasts, writing that the forecasts were “the only way” to get Nvidia to promise B200 chip allocations, according to the indictment. Bloomberg later reported and Culper agreed that the front company in the alleged scheme is OBON, a Bangkok AI infrastructure firm. OBON has not been charged.

Supermicro has since disclosed that it received a grand jury subpoena from the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York, subpoenas and inquiries from foreign authorities, the Securities and Exchange Commission, and the Bureau of Industry and Security. In Liaw’s case, his lawyer told the judge the documents Supermicro would give the government could be material to his defense, and his trial was pushed back from November 2026 to March 2027.

As details of the Megaspeed scandal emerge, Nvidia’s chips are now at the center of a second major smuggling case—this time involving one of its own customers. Megaspeed reportedly bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips during the past two years, with nearly $2 billion of the chips installed in data centers in Malaysia and Indonesia that are alleged to serve Chinese customers remotely, according to New York Times reporting.

Nvidia, in what could become a grave misstep, repeatedly assured the public that Megaspeed was credible. In October 2025, a spokesperson said Nvidia had visited Megaspeed operations and found no evidence of chip diversion. Last month, as reports about suspected Chinese spying emerged, Nvidia said the diversion allegations against Megaspeed had been “thoroughly investigated and debunked.” Jensen Huang, in a statement that has depreciated faster than an older-generation GPU, told Bloomberg his interactions with Alice Huang were “completely normal and not unusual.”

In May, Culper Research, which has shorted Nvidia, argued there were connections between the Supermicro indictment, alleged Nvidia chip smuggling, and Megaspeed. Culper wrote that Megaspeed’s website once listed Supermicro as a partner alongside Nvidia, Intel, and Gigabyte. The web entry was removed, but it still sits in the site code, Culper found. In addition, the report called the reported Supermicro-OBON smuggling route one of many that Nvidia chips travel before they get to China.

Huang next faces analysts on Nov. 17, when Nvidia reports third quarter earnings. The following day, House lawmakers have asked for a closed-door briefing. And in January, Warren is expected to wield the subpoena power of the Banking Committee and get the answers she originally sought back in June.

Amanda Gerut is the west coast editor at Fortune, overseeing publicly traded businesses, executive compensation, Securities and Exchange Commission regulations, and investigations.

#5431. What a Billion-Dollar Shipwreck Can Teach You About Relentlessly Chasing Your Big Idea

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Bestselling author Julian Sancton dives into his new book, “Neptune’s Fortune,” the story of a legendary sunken treasure, the man who found it and what entrepreneurs can learn from his tireless quest.

Every entrepreneur knows what it means to chase something nobody else can see yet — there’s self-doubt, exhaustion, and long stretches where the only result you’re seeing is money going out the door. But still, you press on.

That pursuit is at the heart of Neptune’s Fortune: The Billion-Dollar Shipwreck and the Ghosts of the Spanish Empire, historian Julian Sancton’s account of one man’s relentless hunt for a legendary sunken Spanish galleon.

The book, named one of Barnes & Noble’s Best Books of 2026, tells the story of the San José, a Spanish galleon loaded with gold and silver that sank off the coast of Colombia in 1708 during a battle with a British squadron. Centuries later, Roger Dooley, a mostly self-taught underwater archaeologist born in New Jersey and raised in Cuba, dove deeply into Spanish archives, found maps that pointed where nobody else was looking, rounded up his own investors and, in 2015, located the wreck 2,000 feet below the surface. His reward? Getting left out of Colombia’s national celebration and an avalanche of lawsuits that have stalled efforts to raise the ship.

This incredible adventure story, Sancton’s follow-up to his New York Times bestselling book Madhouse at the End of the Earth, is a must-read for anyone who has chased a big idea and refused to take no for an answer. I spoke with the author about the book and the countless hours of work that went into writing it, which, as it turns out, has a lot in common with treasure hunting. Here are some highlights of our conversation, edited for length.

Writing a book like this takes years and untold hours of research. Where did it all start?After Madhouse at the End of the Earth, I was looking for my second book, and I didn’t want to be pigeonholed as a writer of harrowing nautical stories. But there was one story that would not let me go. I remembered this almost fairy-tale-like headline about a sunken galleon containing billions of dollars’ worth of gold and silver. But I really didn’t know the story yet. I had no expertise.

So I got it commissioned as an article with my former employer, Vanity Fair. I had another story I was working on at the same time, and I kind of A/B tested it. I’m speaking to Entrepreneur now, so that’s a close analogy to how you road test two products and realize which one is more viable. In writing that article, I discovered my main character, Roger Dooley, who I had really no idea about when I started reporting. People were trying to present him as the villain. And I realized that, no, he was far, far from the villain. He was the person without whom we would not be discussing the San José. I knew that the article just skimmed the surface, and went ahead with the book.

Dan Bova: You describe a scene where Dooley is looking for clues to the sunken ship’s location in an archive that has no discernible organization, and he stumbles onto a map with markings that tell him, “It’s here!” As a historian, do you have those moments? Julian Sancton: Absolutely. I spend a lot of time diving into archives without really knowing what I’m going to find in there — those archives are the equivalent of an ocean for me. And when you find something that can make the facts come alive, those are nuggets of gold. With Madhouse, one of the characters who dies early on is this Norwegian deckhand. While talking to archivists who talk to other archivists, his diary popped up. And it gave all kinds of details and poignant observations about life on that boat. Those finds are the equivalent of Roger Dooley chancing on this critical map, which led him to shift his search area to an area that nobody else was looking at.

Dooley pitched the search for the San José to financial backers and government officials, got yeses, then things fell apart, and he had to start over again. Multiple times. Did that teach you anything?Well, perseverance. Push, push, push. He is absolutely relentless, even now in his 80s. Since the book was published, he’s been giving me advice on how to promote it. He’s saying, “You need to get it in this store and that hand. I went to the Barnes & Noble the other day — it wasn’t even there. You gotta talk to them!” And by the way, I’m proud to inform you that Barnes & Noble selected the book as one of their best books of 2026, so maybe Roger’s sending good vibes out there.

While examining the sea floor, I loved the mindset about why it was good not to find anything. Can you explain that way of thinking?They broke Roger’s search area into sections that could be surveyed using a tried-and-true technique of all surveyors and treasure hunters, which is called “mowing the lawn.” It involves methodically going over an area strip by strip.

By the end of the spring, they hadn’t found anything, and the Colombian authorities were starting to get impatient. But one of his investors, who you would have expected would be upset by this news, was not upset at all. He said something cryptic like, “The remaining 50% is 100%.”

The idea is that when you’re surveying an area, not finding something is determining where it isn’t, and that is very helpful, because it reduces the amount to be searched. But that implies that your research is correct. Not finding something sometimes just also means not finding it.

At Entrepreneur, we talk a lot about imposter syndrome. Dooley seems like the polar opposite. This man was utterly convinced he was the man for the mission, despite not having “official” qualifications and training. What lessons did you learn from him?Dooley believes very much that he has a seat at the table. He never thinks that he’s an imposter, even though many people think that he is. He’s kind of a fake it till you make it guy. In Cuba, he invented the field of maritime archaeology. Did not wait to have a degree in it. He created his own course of study. Because nobody else was cataloging the wrecks around Cuba, he started doing it himself, and then he became the de facto authority.

As eccentric as he is, his drive and his motivation are infectious. He learned valuable lessons working in the film industry in Cuba, and he understood the value of showmanship and presentation and narrative. He created these amazing presentations. He understands the value of a colorful, exciting deck, and that is probably more effective than some exhaustively researched survey.

As you said before, Dooley has been villainized as a “treasure hunter,” which I never really thought of as a derogatory term.I think it’s easy to villainize treasure hunters. But I think their entrepreneurial spirit is actually quite admirable. Treasure hunters like Mel Fisher, Kip Wagner, or Bert Webber embody a kind of quintessential American entrepreneurship. It’s literal venture capitalism. You’re out there taking a massive risk. Frequently, you’re not the one putting down the money, but you’re convincing capitalists of the value of what you’re doing. They’re investing not just because they’re gonna get a huge return on investment if they find something, but because they wanna be involved in something grand. And I think if it weren’t for the adventurism of treasure hunters, a lot of these wouldn’t be found at all.

Legal battles continue over ownership of the shipwreck and its treasure. What do you think would be the fairest outcome?I am in the position of having no horse in the race and just observing this as a writer, as ultimately a romantic. But what I would like to see happen is some kind of international collaboration between the stakeholders in Spain, in Colombia, in the UK. I would love to see a rigorous academic excavation and some kind of museum that would involve Roger as a principal architect. He deserves that not only because of his past accomplishments, but because he knows more about the San José than anybody on earth.

And for the treasure, I mean not just the gold and silver and emeralds, but all the contents — this should be preserved and available for study and admiration for the public and academia. There is no other Spanish galleon from this era that has been rigorously and ethically excavated.

We both live in Westchester. Say you’re kayaking around the Long Island Sound and you tip over and you hit your head on a sunken treasure. Do you report it?Of course!… Well, how big is this treasure? [Laughs]

Every entrepreneur knows what it means to chase something nobody else can see yet — there’s self-doubt, exhaustion, and long stretches where the only result you’re seeing is money going out the door. But still, you press on.

That pursuit is at the heart of Neptune’s Fortune: The Billion-Dollar Shipwreck and the Ghosts of the Spanish Empire, historian Julian Sancton’s account of one man’s relentless hunt for a legendary sunken Spanish galleon.

The book, named one of Barnes & Noble’s Best Books of 2026, tells the story of the San José, a Spanish galleon loaded with gold and silver that sank off the coast of Colombia in 1708 during a battle with a British squadron. Centuries later, Roger Dooley, a mostly self-taught underwater archaeologist born in New Jersey and raised in Cuba, dove deeply into Spanish archives, found maps that pointed where nobody else was looking, rounded up his own investors and, in 2015, located the wreck 2,000 feet below the surface. His reward? Getting left out of Colombia’s national celebration and an avalanche of lawsuits that have stalled efforts to raise the ship.

#5430. Seattle startup OneCourt brings tactile tablets for blind and low-vision fans to NHL games

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 2:01 pmNovember 6, 2026 at 7:00 am

Seattle startup OneCourt is bringing its haptic devices for blind and low-vision sports fans to hockey, with the NHL and Ticketmaster making the tablets available free at the league’s marquee events this season and at all home games for four teams.

The device turns real-time game data into vibrations that users follow with their fingertips. For hockey, OneCourt draws on the NHL’s EDGE puck and player tracking data.

The tablets debuted at the Heritage Classic on Oct. 25, and the Washington Capitals, Colorado Avalanche, Chicago Blackhawks and Detroit Red Wings are the first clubs to offer them at every home game.

“Our community has been asking us for hockey since day one, and launching it with Ticketmaster and the NHL is a milestone for OneCourt,” CEO Jerred Mace said in a news release.

The hockey launch builds on OneCourt’s work in other leagues, starting with the NBA’s Portland Trail Blazers. Since 2025, Ticketmaster has offered the tablets at every home game for nine NBA teams, and it backed an NFL pilot during the 2025 season with four clubs, including the Seattle Seahawks, along with Super Bowl LX.

Mace started OneCourt as a University of Washington student studying industrial and product design. His co-founders are three fellow UW grads: COO Antyush Bollini, CTO Andrew Buckingham and CIO Nick Durand.

Time named OneCourt’s tablet to its Best Inventions of 2026 list last month, in the accessibility category. It was one of several Seattle-area innovations on the list.

#5429. Nvidia built itself around one man. A scandal is testing that bet

Few executives loom larger over a single company than Jensen Huang does at Nvidia. His 33-year reign as CEO, and the success he’s overseen during the AI boom, have made him a hugely powerful force at the $4.3 trillion company. Now, the linchpin of the AI industry will test the limits of its corporate governance and succession planning.

After Huang on Sunday acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife, Nvidia’s board announced an investigation into reports that he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. The admission followed reporting about his relationship with a woman whom U.S. authorities concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset, according to The New York Times. The board said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” but that its inquiry would examine “all available information.”

The trick for investigators, according to business and law experts, is that they are investigating, and will potentially consider ousting, perhaps the most critical executive to America’s AI success. And they will do so under a company power structure in which Huang reigns as an outsized decision-maker.

Huang is “synonymous with Nvidia, and Nvidia is synonymous with him, and he and Nvidia are synonymous with AI, so he’s bound up in the company’s identity much more than other cases,” Brian Burke, founder of Burke Law & Strategy and a corporate board advisor, told Fortune. Nvidia is “a paradigm out there that people look up to and they say, ‘Oh, I want to be like Nvidia.’ Other CEOs say, ‘I want to be like Jensen Huang.’ So, it’s really almost like a cult.”

Huang, 63, has set up a unique structure around him at Nvidia that has concentrated decision-making in his hands. He has been CEO for 33 years, astonishingly long for any company. Nvidia has no chief operating officer, and Huang has about 60 direct reports, creating uncertainty about who is next in line to lead.

Huang is known to play a central role in strategic and technical decisions, and the success he’s had since the AI boom got underway in late 2022 has only strengthened his grip on the company and the AI industry at large. He has become something of a celebrity in the tech world, with followers wearing leather jackets to copy him and fans pursuing him at corporate events for a selfie or a signature. He has also gotten close to the Trump administration, which has counted on him for counsel on AI and taken him on foreign trips.

Huang is Nvidia’s largest individual shareholder, with a 3.56% stake, but he doesn’t have any super-voting shares like Mark Zuckerberg has at Meta Platforms. He leads what is the world’s second most valuable company. (Its shares sank more than 4% on Monday after he admitted to the affair.) Nvidia has been estimated to control about 90% of the market for high-powered GPU computer chips used in AI data centers.

The company has also operated without a chief compliance officer. In a September 2022 staff at the Securities and Exchange Commission asked for more detail about board risk oversight, whether the company had such an officer and to whom that person reported, and about its overall structure. Nvidia has said it has a compliance committee made up of its chief financial officer, executive vice president of operations, and senior vice president of human resources, which it says “ensures communication of and adherence to all NVIDIA policies.”

There are few other cases, if any, that resemble Nvidia’s current situation. Corporate executives whose romantic liaisons have derailed their careers are common enough. In 2019, McDonald’s fired CEO Steve Easterbrook over a consensual relationship with an employee that violated company policy. The bigger scandal came afterward: the company discovered additional undisclosed relationships, sued to recover his exit compensation, and ultimately recovered cash and equity valued at $105 million. In this case however, the romantic liaison involves an alleged spy and the CEO of the dominant company building some of the U.S.’s most valuable technology.

Jason Schloetzer, an associate professor at Georgetown University who has studied CEO succession practices, told Fortune that Nvidia’s concentration of so much power and decision-making in Huang now makes it very vulnerable to what comes next.

“The board has made a mistake by not having a clearly outlined succession plan that’s been telegraphed to the market for a year or two,” Schloetzer said. “They find themselves at the day of reckoning, and it’s a sudden and perhaps forced one, rather than a relay situation where they have time to figure it out as they go.”

Hui Chen, a former federal prosecutor who served as the U.S. Justice Department’s first compliance counsel expert from 2015 to 2017, told Fortune that corporate risk efforts tend to focus on leaks from rank and file staff members, and companies don’t pay as much attention to similar risks by high-level executives.

Schloetzer and other experts said it’s plausible for Nvidia’s board of directors to appoint an outside interim CEO or have one of its directors, such as lead independent director Stephen Neal, who is chairman emeritus and senior counsel at law firm Cooley LLP, take over as interim CEO if Huang steps down. Another option for an interim could be Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress. A concern with any next-CEO plan is how the market will receive the decision, since Huang is seen as critical to Nvidia’s success.

Huang also has children who work at Nvidia and could be options to succeed him. Spencer Huang is a director of product management, and his daughter, Madison, is a senior director of product marketing. Both have reportedly worked on robotics at the company. His son-in-law, Nico Caprez, is vice president of global AI infrastructure growth.

The board could oust Huang at the end of its investigation, or Huang could have to step down before then, Burke said. He could also leave the CEO role but stay on in another capacity.

In media interviews over the years, Huang has dismissed conventional succession planning, saying his approach is to continually transfer his knowledge to colleagues. He has also said he hopes Nvidia’s next CEO already works at the company, even though Nvidia has not publicly identified a successor.

#5428. Akash’s Solana Migration Clears November 2 Vote at 97%, With Four More On-Chain Decisions Ahead

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

AKT stakers are close to approving Akash's move from Cosmos to Solana, with Mintscan projecting a pass at 97.2% yes as voting enters its final hours.

But a yes on Proposal 346 opens a door rather than completing a move. Before a single AKT reaches Solana, two independent audits and at least two more on-chain votes still have to happen.

The summary going around is simple: Akash is leaving Cosmos for Solana. The proposal itself is narrower than that, and the details matter for anyone holding AKT.

Proposal 346 on akashnet-2, titled "Migrate the Akash Protocol to Solana," closes at 15:02 UTC on November 2. A yes vote approves the migration plan and authorises AKT to launch as an SPL token through a one-way portal that stays open for two years. It does not set a cutover date, it does not move a single lease, and on its own it does not open the portal.

The technical spec for that portal was published the day after voting opened. It shows how many further steps lie between this vote and a working SPL AKT.

The proposal text in Akash's AEP repository says a yes vote does two things:

It also says plainly what it doesn't do: "it does not set a cutover date and does not move the marketplace." Live leases, staking and governance on akashnet-2 continue as normal. The marketplace moves only after audits and rehearsals pass and "a separate cutover proposal passes on this chain."

A no vote would stop the whole plan. In the proposal's words: "Nothing moves; the token does not launch and the program returns to option analysis."

At 08:43 UTC on November 2, about six hours before voting closed, Mintscan's page for Proposal 346 showed an expected result of "Will PASS":

Turnout stood at 68.80% of bonded stake, against a quorum of 33.40%. The same figures can be read from Akash's own chain API, through the proposal object and its tally endpoint.

Mintscan's 97.2% is yes as a share of all votes cast. Akash's pass threshold leaves abstentions out, and on that basis yes stands at about 98.7%, far above the 50% needed. The veto share is negligible.

The tally has barely changed since early morning. A read of the chain at 07:29 UTC showed almost exactly the same totals, with only a handful of AKT added to the yes side. With turnout and margin that large, the outcome is not in doubt. The more useful question is what happens after it passes.

The portal's design is in AEP-95, "One-Way AKT Sink to Solana,", a draft published on October 27 by core developers Artur Troian and Joseph Chalabi. It describes a "deliberately one-way" bridge with no return path. The authors say this removes "the largest class of bridge attacks."

Why supply doesn't change: every SPL AKT is backed by AKT locked on Akash, and nothing is minted independently on Solana. The token is a legacy SPL mint with six decimals and no freeze authority.

The spec's own risk table names the biggest trust point. The upgrade authority over the Solana programs could "mint without limit." That power is meant to sit with a time-locked multisig appointed by Akash governance, with monitors set to alert on every admin action.

At launch, SPL AKT has no protocol role. It will support "transfers and DEX liquidity only, with no staking or governance rights." Inflation stays on Akash. To seed trading, Overclock Labs, Akash's core developer, will send 1 million AKT through the bridge to a Solana treasury vault. That deposit follows the same rules as everyone else's.

Proposal 346 requires "two independent audits of the token and portal code before launch," with reports published within 30 days. AEP-95's launch sequence shows what that requirement means on-chain.

So Proposal 346 is the first of at least five on-chain decisions. The "2 to 3 weeks" launch estimate depends on the audits finishing and the upgrade and parameter votes passing on schedule.

For now, nothing. The proposal's disclosures set out what changes later:

Discussion of the proposal continues in GitHub Discussion #1123.

The proposal lists four items as "still open, to be settled and published before the cutover proposal":

The second item matters most to holders. The portal closes two years after launch, and the proposal doesn't yet say what happens to AKT that hasn't crossed by then. The final tally will confirm whether the plan goes ahead, but that answer, and the decisions in the votes that follow, will matter more to most holders than today's margin.

#5427. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang might hang on as CEO. But his influence on U.S. AI policy is over

Hello and welcome to Eye on AI. Jeremy Kahn here. In this edition:

Before we get to the news, can I just say, you are not going to want to miss this year’s edition of Fortune Brainstorm AI San Francisco. We have an exceptional line-up of speakers for you: OpenAI president Greg Brockman and Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman will both be onstage. Once the closest of partners, their two companies are increasingly, competitors, so I’m eager to hear how differently they see the road ahead. AI pioneers Fei-Fei Li, now of World Labs, as well as Andrew Ng, now of LearnVector, will be discussing their view of AI’s future too. Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora will talk about AI and cybersecurity. Greylock partner Reid Hoffman, CapitalG’s Jill Chase, and Kleiner Perkins’ Mamoon Hamid and Ilya Fushman will weigh in on where the money is going. Recursive Superintelligence’s Richard Socher will talk about RSI and automating AI research.Plus, we’ve got Nick Fox from Google. We’ve got Fireworks CEO Lin Qiao. We’ve got Cerebras’ Andrew Feldman, Vanta’s Christina Cacioppo, Unconventional AI’s Naveen Rao, Brex’s Pedro Franceschi, Maven Clinic’s Kate Ryder, Box’s Aaron Levie, Atlassian’s Mike Cannon-Brookes, New Work Foundation’s Clara Shih, Twilio’s Khozema Shipchandler, Rubrik’s Bipul Sinha, Harvey’s Winston Weinberg, Dynamic Creatures’ Marc Theermann, SendCutSend’s Jim Belosic, Apptronik’s Jeff Cardenas, Accenture Song’s Ndidiamaka Oteh, and Senra Systems’ Jordan Black. It’s going to be epic. So please join me and many of my Fortune colleagues at the St. Regis in San Francisco on December 7th and 8th. You can apply to attend here.

The biggest news this week in AI has been the revelation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman that U.S. intelligence reportedly believes is a Chinese spy. Whether Jensen manages to stay in his job is an open question. A lot of that will depend on exactly what Jensen knew and exactly what information he disclosed to Alice Huang, the woman at the center of the scandal. As more information comes out, it is already not looking too good for the embattled Nvidia CEO. In addition to Nvidia’s board announcing an independent investigation, House Republicans have already called the CEO to testify at a closed door hearing next week, and U.S. President Donald Trump, who initially defended Jensen, has said the FBI is now investigating the case too.There seems to be mounting evidence that Jensen knew or should have at least suspected that Alice Huang’s company, Megaspeed, was involved in supplying advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies, either allowing them to access those chips in data centers it set up in Malaysia (which would have been legal under U.S. law prior to 2025 but not since then), or by smuggling Nvidia GPUs directly into China (which would have violated U.S. export laws). If Jensen was complicit in smuggling advanced Nvidia chips into China, that would probably be enough to force his resignation.The New York Times also reported that Nvidia’s general counsel intervened in 2025 to get a Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed moved to the Justice Department, where it seems to have languished. If more emerges showing that Jensen used his clout to shield Megaspeed from federal investigators, that too could make it difficult for him to stay on as CEO. And, if it turns out that he passed Alice Huang confidential information about discussions he had with President Trump or about Nvidia’s chip designs, then he is probably toast too.If Alice Huang was, as some reporting suggests, primarily trying to influence Jensen’s position on export controls, then the picture may not be as bad for him. The Nvidia CEO’s stance on the export of chips has been remarkably consistent going back to a period before he is believed to have met Alice Huang. Plus, he didn’t exactly need convincing to oppose export regulation, given that Nvidia once made a lot of money selling its GPUs in China.

Jensen Huang’s position on exports to China hasn’t changed

When my colleague Beatrice Nolan and I sat down with Jensen in London a few weeks ago, before news of his affair broke, he told us the U.S. should want Nvidia to compete in the Chinese market. “I think the opportunity in China is large and growing, just like the AI market across the world is large and growing,” he said. “We could be of great service to the local market. We can compete and win as much of the AI market as possible for the United States, while also providing compute resources, which is really important to their economy.” Bea has more on what Jensen told us about China in a story she published earlier this week which you can read here.If Jensen does end up stepping down, that could have ramifications for the entire AI boom, although it is likely that any successor would continue to try to provide financial support to the same cluster of AI labs, startups, and neoclouds that Nvidia has funded. That said, Jensen was a singular force. He ran Nvidia as if it were a giant startup, without a clear successor, or even clear candidates, and with a remarkably flat management structure. Jensen famously had between thirty—and at one point 60—direct reports. He had, by many accounts, a direct role in almost of all the business’s key decisions. If he goes, the company could stumble and its core business could suffer.

Even if Huang stays as CEO, U.S. AI regulation is now more likely

Even if Jensen manages to hang on as Nvidia’s CEO, his influence on U.S. policy is likely to be greatly diminished. And that may have several key implications.The most obvious is that the China hawks will have removed a key opponent of more restrictive export rules on selling chips to China. In fact, this may have been the main reason that someone has leaked the U.S. government’s conclusions about Jensen and Alice Huang at this time.The less obvious policy implication is that Jensen has become a leading advocate for open source AI and was opposed to any government regulations that might impose licensing standards on these models that could effectively limit or eliminate their distribution in the U.S. With Jensen out of the way, those who believe open source AI models pose risks that cannot easily be mitigated will have a better chance at getting the federal government to enact licensing rules on all AI models.We will have to see how this story develops over the coming days, weeks, and months. But one thing is clear: the AI boom’s biggest booster has been humbled.

With that, here’s more AI news.Jeremy Kahnjeremy.kahn@fortune.com@jeremyakahn

We also discuss the Democratic sweep in the midterm elections and its impact on AI. And we talk about Google’s controversial policy on schools using, or choosing not to use, its Gemini AI models.
