A scandal is testing that bet—by Sebastian HerreraAnthropic debuts Claude Fable, Mythos 5.2 models, priced 20% below OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra—by Emily ForliniBefore news broke of his affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Nvidia’s Huang told Fortune his company “could be of great service” to China—by Beatrice NolanClaude can now join video calls as an active, visible teammate in Anthropic’s latest push to reinvent white collar jobs beyond coding—by Emily ForliniOpenAI debuts new cybersecurity-focused AI model amid growing alarm about AI-driven cyber attacks—by Wen ShaoExclusive: Publisher Spines raises $64 million in new funding to accelerate effort to automate book publishing with AI—by Jeremy KahnExclusive: In the race for robot training data, ex-Meta researchers’ startup turns to gig workers with cameras—by Wen ShaoExclusive: Alterra Labs announces $12.5 million seed round to build training environments for medical AI—by Wen Shao

METR says Anthropic is closing in on RSI, raising AI safety alarms. Anthropic’s AI models are improving nearly twice as fast as they were previously, largely because AI is increasingly helping researchers develop more powerful models, according to a new study by independent AI evaluation nonprofit METR. The researchers found that Anthropic’s models have been advancing on benchmark tasks at roughly 1.9 times their previous rate since October 2025, estimating that AI’s contributions account for much of the acceleration rather than increased computing power. The findings provide some of the strongest evidence yet of AI accelerating its own development, potentially paving the way for a milestone known as “recursive self-improvement” (RSI) in which AI systems autonomously create increasingly capable successors. However, METR cautioned that AI is not yet capable of making major autonomous contributions to the most critical stages of model training, even as the accelerating pace of progress raises concerns about whether safety evaluations can keep up. The findings have alarmed AI safety researchers, who worry that AI-driven improvements could create a feedback loop of accelerating capabilities that outpaces efforts to keep increasingly powerful systems under control. But the report also raises questions about transparency: METR said Anthropic prevented it from publishing most of the evidence underpinning its conclusions, arguing that disclosure could help competitors accelerate their own AI development. Read more from the Verge here.Anthropic strikes $3.4 billion deal for on-site gas generators for data centers. Anthropic has struck a $3.4 billion deal to acquire commitments for 1.7 gigawatts of gas-fired generators from Texas-based OnePWR Solutions, marking the largest known single purchase of power-generation equipment by an AI lab, the Financial Times reported. The deal gives Anthropic access to Caterpillar generators ordered two years ago, allowing it to bypass lengthy manufacturing delays and take greater control of the electricity supply needed for its rapidly expanding data centers. The purchase underscores how AI companies are increasingly moving directly into the energy business to secure scarce power infrastructure, as Anthropic prepares for its IPO and seeks to finance nearly $900 billion in computing commitments through 2045. But the purchase also raises environmental concerns, as the gas generators produce carbon dioxide and other pollutants, and their use is likely to increase grassroots opposition to these particular data center projects and data center construction more generally.

Microsoft winds down Oracle computing deal. Microsoft is winding down a deal to rent AI computing capacity from Oracle, declining to renew a contract for servers equipped with older Nvidia chips that no longer meet its technical requirements, Bloomberg reported. The move is part of a broader reassessment of Microsoft's more than $80 billion in commitments to rent computing power from third-party cloud providers, including CoreWeave, Nscale, and Nebius, amid concerns about high costs and data center construction delays. The decision highlights growing uncertainty around the economics of the AI infrastructure boom, particularly for Oracle, whose aggressive data center investments have driven its free cash flow into negative territory and contributed to investor concerns.

Fireworks hacked. Fireworks AI, the fast-growing startup that helps developers run and train open-source AI models, suffered a major cyberattack that exposed customer billing information, model weights, and datasets. The breach, which Fireworks said has links to a cybercriminal group involved in stealing and reselling AI access tokens, has prompted some major customers to consider switching providers and could complicate the startup’s plans to raise funding at a valuation of $30 billion or more. This is the second breach Fireworks has suffered in the past month. You can read more here from The Information.

Google DeepMind shows AI agents can produce formal verifications of software. Formal verification is a way of mathematically proving software will function according to certain specifications. The process for this has existed for decades, but as software has become more complex, people have been able to afford, in terms of both time and cost, to formally verify only a tiny fraction of software. Generally speaking, only software that runs extremely critical systems where the consequences of an error can be fatal–such as commercial airline autopilots and some industrial control systems for oil refineries or drilling rigs, or some extremely critical banking software—has been formally verified. A lot of other, still very important software, has not been subjected to such rigorous checks because it is simply too complex, time-consuming, and expensive a process.Now Google DeepMind has shown that a system built on various powerful AI models, including its most frontier AI model, Gemini Carbon, can complete a successful formal verification for a complex and important software algorithm. In this case, Google DeepMind used a system called AlphaProof Code to formally verify the reference implementation of the encryption protocol for Signal, the highly-secure messaging app. The same reference software also underpins encryption in WhatsApp, Messenger and Google Messages. The AI agents Google DeepMind used produced about 6.5 million lines of proof code in the Lean programming language, a way of expressing mathematics in code. The way Lean works is that is that if the mathematics is wrong, the code won’t properly compile. If it does, the mathematical steps are valid – which in this case also means that software adheres to whatever specifications are being tested and verified. In this case, the proofs showed that Signal’s post-quantum handshake and its “Triple Ratchet” deliver forward secrecy, authentication and post-compromise security. Every proof is machine-checked against roughly 26,000 lines of specifications that humans reviewed and approved. To make sure the specifications would catch real flaws, the researchers reinserted two bugs in the Signal code that had previously been fixed, and the system proved the resulting code was insecure.Formal verification has long been seen as the gold standard for secure software, but it has been too expensive and time-consuming to use widely: one formal verification of a complex code by humans took twenty years, another took six.

“Six months ago, if you told me that somebody could do this, I would say that you were kidding me,” Swarat Chaudhuri, a Google DeepMind research scientist and University of Texas at Austin computer science professor, told Fortune.

Chaudhuri said the work matters more now that attackers are using powerful AI models to find and exploit software flaws. Proofs offer a way out of the “cat and mouse game” of finding bugs and patching them, because they rule out whole classes of errors at once.

In Google DeepMind’s new AlphaProof Code system, humans and AI agents work together to write the specification, meaning the formal statement of what the code must guarantee. Teams of 40 to 80 autonomous prover agents then write the proofs over one to three days, and the proofs count only if Lean’s kernel checks them.

Chaudhuri said that the hard part of verification is moving from writing proofs to deciding what to prove, which still needs human expertise; the Signal effort, for instance, included cryptographers who helped write the specification that AlphaProof Code then checked.

For now the project is purely research and there is no product plan, but the specifications and proofs are public, and Google DeepMind has been coordinating with the Signal Foundation. Chaudhuri compared the moment to deep learning around 2012: an old idea that “suddenly all of the ingredients are there” to make work. You can read more about the work on Google’s blog here.

What you can learn by having frontier models play ‘Blood on the Clocktower.’ Podcaster Dwarkesh Patel has created an unusual new benchmark for frontier AI models: getting them to play Blood on the Clocktower, a social deduction game similar to Mafia or Werewolf in which players must lie, bluff, form alliances, and uncover conspiracies. In a fascinating YouTube episode explaining the experiment, Patel describes how he built a computerized version of the game that allowed competing AI models to play hundreds of matches against one another, testing their ability to reason strategically, coordinate with teammates, and sustain elaborate deceptions over time. Patel said he spent approximately $20,000 in AI API credits developing the system and running the experiments, with Claude doing much of the coding and autonomously refining the game environment through more than 20 rounds of testing.The results suggest that frontier models have become remarkably sophisticated at deception and collective reasoning, with OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra emerging as the strongest player among the models tested. Patel found that OpenAI's latest models were particularly good at detecting deception because they were more skeptical of individual pieces of evidence, whereas Anthropic's models tended to accept information too readily. But the experiment also exposed continuing weaknesses in AI models' long-term strategic planning and reasoning. Overall, Patel concluded that the AI-assisted process of building and refining the benchmark itself—which included coding the harness the AI models used—demonstrated the capabilities of frontier AI models perhaps better than their actual game play did. He said this demonstrated how AI models could be used to buidl simulated environments that could then be used to train future AI systems—an example of the steps toward recursive self-improvement, or RSI, that frontier labs such as Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google DeepMind have begun talking about.

Jeremy Kahn is the AI editor at Fortune, spearheading the publication's coverage of artificial intelligence. He also co-authors Eye on AI, Fortune’s flagship AI newsletter.

#5426. Why This CEO Rebuilt His Best-Selling Product Before Taking It to Target

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Jeff Byers already had one of the best creatines on the market. He raised the bar anyway, then took it to Target

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For years, anyone who asked me about creatine got the same answer. Buy Creapure or Creavitalis and skip everything else. I take creatine every day. I’ve written about why you might want to as well, and I’ve worked in this industry long enough to know how often a label and a scoop disagree.

So when Jeff Byers told me Momentous had moved on from Creapure, I wanted to know why.

“Creapure is amazing,” the co-founder and CEO said, and he was quick to give it credit for the role it played in building Momentous. The change came from what the company calls The Momentous Standard: keep raising your own bar, even when you’re already at the top of the category. “We believed better can be done,” Byers said. That belief is what led to Signature Spec.

I helped launch Momentous more than five years ago, and I wrote about Byers last year when he had just pulled a product bringing in $500,000 a month because the science no longer held up. He has a habit of making expensive decisions. This one may be his biggest, because he made it in the same year he took the brand into Target.

That combination is why I think every founder building a trust-based brand should pay attention. Mass retail has a way of wearing premium brands down. Margins tighten, formulas get cheaper and the marketing gets louder than the product. Momentous is trying to scale without any of that happening. I’ve watched it from the inside, and the company’s approach deserves a close look.

Creatine is one of the most studied supplements on the shelf, backed by more than 685 human clinical trials across ages, doses and durations of up to 14 years. Once a category’s science is settled, most brands compete on format, flavor and price. That’s how we ended up with creatine gummies, and with independent testing that found three of five popular gummies failed, one with less than 25% of the creatine on its label.

Byers went the other direction. “Innovation is quality. Innovation is sourcing,” he told me.

His team found a new manufacturer and wrote its own specification. The result, Signature Spec Creatine, is made in a facility to a 99.99% purity standard, with strict limits on heavy metals. It’s purified with reverse osmosis water filtration in place of the chemical wash common across the industry. It’s also screened for PFAS and microplastics, which standard certifications don’t require. Every batch moves through six stages of testing across four independent groups: Eurofins, Light Labs, NSF Certified for Sport and SuppCo.

As someone who takes creatine daily, I care about those contaminant limits. Anything you take every day for years deserves a higher bar than something you take once.

As a marketer, the line that stuck with me was about the business. Owning the spec, Byers said, “created a robustness in our business that we hadn’t had.” Buying a great branded ingredient means sharing control of quality and supply with a partner. Owning the spec puts both in your hands.

My advice to founders: If your product looks like a commodity on paper, look at the parts customers never see. Sourcing, testing and process take years and real money to build, which is exactly what makes them hard to copy. Investors should be looking there too.

Momentous landed on end caps in nearly 600 Target stores this summer, ahead of a rollout to every store in October. That came months after it entered more than 600 The Vitamin Shoppe locations. The timing lines up with Target’s own plans to grow its wellness assortment by 30% in 2026.

What struck me is how clearly Byers defines each retailer’s role. The Vitamin Shoppe carries 20 to 25 Momentous products and serves as the brand’s home base. “If Momentous had a retail location, it would be The Vitamin Shoppe,” he said. Target carries 12 products and is where new customers discover the brand for the first time.

I asked Byers whether anything changed for Target. The answer was no. The creatine on an end cap comes from the same lots sold to professional and college teams, and everything is still made domestically.

My advice to founders: Before you sign with a big-box retailer, decide what that channel is for. In my work with wellness brands heading into retail, the ones that struggle usually skipped this step and let the retailer decide their assortment for them. A discovery shelf should carry your most essential, easiest-to-understand products. A destination partner can carry the full story. If the margin only works when you water down the formula, the deal is wrong.

When I asked which product might not survive the company’s next science review, Byers said none right now. Then he talked about flavor. The team is moving to real flavors and fewer ingredients, rebuilding its chocolate protein with just cocoa, and leaning on raw ingredients like vanilla bean and cinnamon. Its sleep formula was reformulated with magnesium threonate and now costs less.

The new launches follow the same thinking. Daily Hydration has 100mg of sodium and 50mg of potassium per serving, built for work, travel and light training. Most of us are already getting plenty of sodium, and research using national survey data found 90.7% of U.S. adults exceed the 2,300mg daily limit, while fewer than 2% get the recommended amount of potassium. Many popular electrolyte mixes were built for marathons and then marketed for desk days. Byers calls that overkill for everyday life. Momentous saves the heavier dose for Fuel, its drink for long, intense training.

The brand also recently launched a Pre-Workout powder that lists every ingredient and dose, with no proprietary blends, in a category known for hiding both. It pairs 150mg of caffeine with 300mg of L-theanine, a combination studied for focus without the jitters and it’s become a go-to for me.

Then there’s fiber, the category Byers is most excited about. “Fiber feels like where we were with creatine three or four years ago,” he said. Consumers are thinking about long-term health, and he believes fiber is in its early innings. I agree, and I’d watch this space closely.

My advice to founders: Adding is easy. Cutting takes discipline. Every ingredient you remove is one less thing to source, explain and defend.

In January 2026, Momentous announced a multi-year partnership with Arnold Schwarzenegger. Byers described a three-year process in which Arnold’s team looked at suppliers, manufacturers and track record, and watched the company pull Fadogia and keep reformulating. “This was not about money,” Byers told me. “He would have picked somebody else.”

I’ve spent much of my career building partnerships between brands and the people who represent them. The ones that last look like this. The diligence runs both ways, and the decision rests on years of behavior.

Fast growth is usually where culture breaks, and Byers learned that firsthand. After an earlier merger, he spent six to nine months rebuilding a company that had lost its way.

“Teams ultimately build those standards or kill those standards,” he said. Momentous now has more red tape than ever, and Byers sees his job as protecting the scrappiness that got it here. “Don’t underestimate the values that you put in place.”

Momentous could have kept using one of the best creatines in the world, and no one would have questioned it. Byers and his co-founder, Erica Good, chose to raise their own bar instead, then put the result in front of millions of Target shoppers. Target will test whether Momentous can hold its standards at scale. After five years of watching this team make the expensive call, I’d bet on it.

For years, anyone who asked me about creatine got the same answer. Buy Creapure or Creavitalis and skip everything else. I take creatine every day. I’ve written about why you might want to as well, and I’ve worked in this industry long enough to know how often a label and a scoop disagree.

So when Jeff Byers told me Momentous had moved on from Creapure, I wanted to know why.

“Creapure is amazing,” the co-founder and CEO said, and he was quick to give it credit for the role it played in building Momentous. The change came from what the company calls The Momentous Standard: keep raising your own bar, even when you’re already at the top of the category. “We believed better can be done,” Byers said. That belief is what led to Signature Spec.

#5425. Agility Robotics co-founder on its Nasdaq debut, lessons from Amazon, and the future of work

by Todd Bishop on Nov 5, 2026 at 6:51 pmNovember 5, 2026 at 6:51 pm

Agility Robotics of Salem, Ore., made its Nasdaq debut Thursday as the first publicly traded U.S. company devoted solely to humanoid robots — offering an ambitious vision for how the technology will change work, and a cautious view of how long it will take.

“Maybe we’ll never have faster-than-light travel. Maybe we’ll never have transporters from Star Trek,” said Jonathan Hurst, the company’s co-founder and chief robot officer. “But we absolutely will have machines that can do all of the physical work that a person can do.”

However, he cautioned, “It’s not going to be next year or five years from now. It’s really a grand challenge.”

Agility went public through a merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, a special purpose acquisition company, or SPAC, led by financier Michael Klein. The deal valued Agility at $2.5 billion before the new investment and brought in about $465 million in gross proceeds. Its shares trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker AGLT.

After initially dipping below its opening price, the stock closed Thursday at $11.51, up 2.2%, bucking the trend on a day when the Nasdaq fell 5.5%, its worst day in 18 months.

Agility’s robot: The company’s main character is Digit, a two-legged robot with two arms mounted near the top of its torso that let it lift bins high and recover from falls. It moves totes and containers in warehouses and factories.

Digit 5, the latest version, was unveiled in September. Standing 5-foot-11 and weighing 284 pounds, it’s covered in sensors, with cameras and antennas in its head and safety-rated sensors in protective housings around its body. Agility says it can lift 50 pounds, reach 7.2 feet high and work more than 20 hours in a 24-hour day.

But the big advance is that Digit 5 was designed to work alongside people without a barrier. Earlier versions had to be fenced off from workers, which limited where customers could use them.

Agility learned how much that mattered at Amazon, an early investor in the company, which tested prior versions of Digit for moving and stacking bins in its warehouses.

Digit did useful work in tests there, Hurst said, but when Agility asked about scaling up, Amazon said it couldn’t deploy the robots. It showed Agility what it had taken to get its own wheeled robot through three to four years of safety certification, and said it didn’t know how a balancing robot would ever get there.

“The safety case to do this is unbelievably hard,” Hurst said. “Nobody has ever deployed a dynamically stable balancing machine, and it brings new risks.”

Getting a robot out from behind the barrier took years of engineering and standards work. Agility has been co-authoring ISO safety standards for the category and making its case to insurance companies and warehouse operators who want proof in numbers before putting a balancing machine next to a person.

Digit 5 uses AI and multiple sensors to watch for nearby people. Depending on the situation, it steers around them, stops or sits down. Visual and audio cues signal what it’s about to do, and a safety controller triggers its responses when someone gets too close.

Hurst credits the lessons from Amazon, along with ones from GXO, Toyota and Schaeffler, with shaping the design of Digit 5.

“Amazon was a huge, huge part of getting us to that point,” he said.

Amazon made an initial deposit in 2024 toward a $1.05 million purchase of five robots, according to Agility’s filings. Agility recorded about $1.04 million in net sales from Amazon in 2025, 58% of its total for the year. Hurst said he couldn’t speak to whether Amazon is a customer now.

With the safety improvements and other advancements, Hurst called Digit 5 “the scaling moment” for Agility. “That is the unlock,” he said.

One customer, which Agility has not named, has committed to a $300 million, three-year contract for 1,000 Digit 5 robots, according to its filings. The robots would be rented rather than sold, the commitment is subject to milestones and specifications, and the customer gets warrants that vest as the robots are deployed.

Agility has built about 10 Digit 5 robots, Hurst said, with the first prototypes just coming off the line. Its factory in Salem was built to eventually produce as many as 10,000 robots a year.

Financial picture: Agility’s business is still small, with revenue of $1.78 million last year and about $174,000 in the first six months of this year. It lost $362 million in the first half, up from $71.8 million a year earlier. Stock-based compensation, an accounting charge for employee equity awards, rose by about $252 million over the same period.

Agility had $14.7 million in cash at the end of June, before the deal closed, and management said in its interim financial statements that there was substantial doubt about the company’s ability to keep operating.

Hurst called the public markets his biggest unknown.

“I’m completely confident in our market path, our technological path,” he said. If public shareholders agree, he said, Agility will be able to “continue on this mission successfully and raise money when we need to.” If they doubt the company, “that’s going to make our life a lot harder.”

What Agility has that most rivals don’t is robots doing commercial work. As of May, its Digit 4 model had logged more than 65,000 hours across nine committed customer deployments, according to its filings. Digit 4 robots have moved more than 100,000 totes since June 2024 at a Georgia facility run by the logistics company GXO.

Investors have put far higher values on rivals still working largely in pilots, including Figure AI at a reported $39 billion, more than 15 times Agility’s valuation in the merger.

“Digit is doing real work in customer operations today, taking on repetitive, physically demanding tasks,” said Peggy Johnson, Agility’s CEO, in a statement. Going public, she said, gives the company more resources to put Digit into more workplaces.

Johnson became CEO in March 2024, when Hurst moved from CTO to chief robot officer. She previously ran Magic Leap, and before that spent six years as a Microsoft executive, leading business development and dealmaking under CEO Satya Nadella.

In an interview with GeekWire earlier in the week, Hurst took the long view on the stock listing, calling it a milestone on a much longer path. Treating a listing day as the achievement, he said, is a finance person’s frame: “I just don’t live in that world.”

From CMU to OSU: Hurst has been on that path for almost three decades.

He built his first walking robot in 1997, as a freshman at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh. He stayed at Carnegie Mellon for a Ph.D. in robotics, finishing in 2008, when fewer than 100 people in the world had earned one, he said.

That year he joined Oregon State University in Corvallis, planning from the start to eventually spin a company out of his research. In his Oregon State lab, Hurst’s team built ATRIAS, a two-legged robot that didn’t look like any animal because it was based on a mathematical model of walking and running. It was the first machine to reproduce the dynamics of human walking.

He started Agility in 2015 with Damion Shelton, a Carnegie Mellon classmate who was CEO until 2024, and Mikhail Jones, one of his Oregon State students, out of his lab there.

Being in Oregon helped from the start, Hurst said. Agility was almost alone in trying to build humanoid robots, and the engineers who moved to Oregon to join it were committed to that mission. The company had almost no turnover, unlike the Silicon Valley pattern of people jumping to a new job every six months.

But as it passed 400 employees, it needed experienced engineering managers, and Oregon had no robotics industry large enough to have produced them. Agility had been hiring those people in California and flying them north, so it opened an office there. Today Agility has offices in Pittsburgh and Fremont, Calif., in addition to Oregon.

Impact on jobs: For the time being, Agility pitches Digit as a way to fill jobs that are difficult to staff. Johnson told TechCrunch this week that the company has focused on “manual, very repetitive jobs, that it’s hard to find humans to do.”

Hurst calls the first commercial uses of the technology “step one” toward what he describes as the dream: “robots as part of everyday human life, doing the things people would rather not do.”

Asked what happens to the people whose work the robots replace, Hurst pointed to farming as an example of automation improving people’s lives.

“Early in American history, 90% of Americans worked in agriculture, and today 2% do,” he said. “And the only reason that’s true is because of automation.”

#5424. A tabloid scandal bankrolled a Long Island Democrat, mostly with out-of-district money. A Hollywood-linked tycoon backed a Republican who beat him.

Leaked photos were supposed to end Chris Gallant’s campaign. Instead, they bankrolled it. After the New York Post published archived images of the Democrat modeling bondage gear for a San Francisco leather retailer, his fundraising took off.

In the quarter the photos surfaced, Gallant raised more than the incumbent. His October quarterly FEC report shows $929,825 in receipts for July through September. Rep. Nick LaLota reported about $609,000 for the same period.

The money bought a close loss, not a win. LaLota won a third term in New York’s 1st Congressional District last Tuesday, 51.1% to 48.9%, a margin of nearly 7,000 votes with 560 of 561 election districts reporting. Gallant first held out for absentee ballots, then conceded Wednesday. LaLota’s margin shrank from about 11 points in 2024 to about two, in a year Democrats swept to control of Congress.

Nor was the money especially local. A Fortune review of both campaigns’ raw 2026 FEC filings through Oct. 14 found that in-district donors accounted for about 16% of LaLota’s money from named individuals and just over a third of Gallant’s.

The post-leak surge followed the same pattern. In the 32 days after the Post story ran on Sept. 13, Gallant reported $276,055 in itemized contributions. Only $65,997 of it, about 24%, came from individuals inside NY-1, and almost half of that came from 62 donors in the Hamptons. Donors in Manhattan and California gave $73,606 combined, more than every donor inside NY-1 put together.

In NY-1, the people who funded the race and the people who voted in it were often different. Both campaigns were bankrolled mostly by donors outside the district, including major Wall Street, Hollywood and tech names. Even the men on the ballot live beyond its lines: both reside near Amityville, on Long Island’s South Shore, which means neither could vote for himself.

NY-1 runs from Suffolk County’s North Shore villages to the East End, with vineyards and farms on the North Fork and the Hamptons on the South Fork. In between lie Smithtown and Brookhaven, where suburban neighborhoods give way to woods and residents are largely commuters, law enforcement and small-business owners.

Each summer, the South Fork fills with the people who run Wall Street and corporate America. That makes the district one of the country’s busiest political ATMs, where financiers and industry titans host fundraisers for both parties. Suffolk County donors gave more than $45 million to campaigns in the 2020 cycle alone, according to OpenSecrets data CNBC cited.

In August, Vice President JD Vance raised more than $5 million from young Republican donors at the Southampton home of Omeed Malik, president of 1789 Capital and a prominent Trump donor.

LaLota, a Navy veteran and former Suffolk County elections commissioner, was first elected in 2022 to succeed Lee Zeldin and was re-elected in 2024, defeating former CNN anchor John Avlon by about 11 points. In that race, LaLota criticized Avlon for his dual residency in both Sag Harbor and Manhattan.

Gallant, 37, is an Army National Guard Black Hawk pilot, a former FAA air traffic controller at JFK, a former union leader and a volunteer firefighter. He won the June primary with about 63% of the vote, defeating Lukas Ventouras, a 25-year-old law student and district resident who had raised about $124,000, mostly in unitemized small-dollar donations. Gallant later picked up endorsements from Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg.

After the Post story, Gallant’s attorney, Sara Azari, who previously represented former Rep. Eric Swalwell after misconduct allegations, confirmed the photos were authentic and consensual. Gallant told the New York Times he hoped it could be his “Kim Kardashian moment,” and the campaign began selling “Make Politics Sexy Again” merchandise. LaLota stuck to calling Gallant “weak and woke” and needling him for declining to debate.

Asked by Fortune about the surge, Gallant answered through Slingshot Strategies, a consulting firm that promises “a proven track record of shifting the conversation” for candidates facing “overwhelming odds” and “difficult fights.”

He said the Post story “backfired on them” and that the Times interview let voters see “a proud gay man who refused to be ashamed of his identity, and it resonated.” On LaLota’s outside money, he said, “I never had to rely on outside interests to try and buy this seat.” About a third of his own money from named donors came from inside the district.

LaLota cast the surge as a product of the controversy itself. “On the same days my opponent was backing out of debates, he was monetizing his BDSM and pornographic modeling past,” he said in a statement to Fortune. “Instead of boasting how kinky he is, as he did to the Times, he owes Long Islanders an explanation for choosing vanity and fundraising over debates and accountability.”

Fortune analyzed itemized contributions dated in 2026 in both campaigns’ raw FEC filings through Oct. 14, so the comparison covers the same stretch of the race for both candidates. Repeat donors were counted once, refunds subtracted and conduit entries adjusted so no gift was counted twice. The FEC does not require campaigns to name individuals who give $200 or less in a cycle, so those donors are excluded. Fortune placed donors inside or outside NY-1 based on the mailing city they listed, which may differ from where they vote. Individuals may give $3,500 per election this cycle, or $7,000 for the primary and general combined. Fortune tallied the filings by hand, then used Claude, Anthropic’s AI model, to clean the raw files and check the calculations.

LaLota had the bigger war chest. Through Oct. 14, he had raised $4.5 million and had $2.31 million in cash on hand. Gallant had raised $1.7 million and had $426,000 on hand.

The sharper contrast was where the money came from. Of the 785 named donors in LaLota’s 2026 filings, 29% listed mailing addresses in the district. Together they gave $207,161, only 16% of what he raised from named individuals. PACs and other committees supplied $1.18 million, about a quarter of his total for the cycle.

Gallant’s support was more local, but not by much. Of his 1,031 named donors in the 2026 raw file, 390 (38%) listed addresses in NY-1 and nearly $300,000, about a third of the roughly $876,000 he raised from named individuals this year. Counting gifts from 2025, his itemized individual total for the cycle is $1.15 million.

Half of that in-district money, about $159,000, came from the Hamptons and Shelter Island, the East End enclaves where wealthy New Yorkers have long kept second homes. In East Hampton Town, half of the 22,562 housing units are no one’s usual residence, according to the Census Bureau’s 2020-2024 American Community Survey, which counts second homes as vacant. In Brookhaven, the figure is only about 9%.

Outside the district, 218 Manhattan donors gave Gallant $215,600 and 85 Californians gave about $93,000. Thirteen listed San Francisco.

The photos worked as a fundraiser, just not a local one. Between Sept. 13 and Oct. 14, Gallant reported 677 itemized contributions totaling $276,055: $229,050 from 484 individual donors and $47,005 from PACs, party committees and other sources.

That haul, all in the campaign’s final month of reporting, is about 16% of the $1.7 million he raised this cycle and nearly a third of the roughly $876,000 he raised from named individuals in 2026. About a third of it arrived in the first four days after the leak.

On Sept. 15, two days after the leak, the New York State Democratic Committee transferred $25,025 to the campaign. That same day, the campaign paid Sara Azari, the celebrity attorney who specializes in crisis and media strategy.

Among the contributions that followed: $500 on Sept. 15 from Howard Sacarob, head of U.S. Tax at Royal Bank of Canada, and $3,500 on Oct. 4 from Ryan Fitzpatrick, Corcoran’s regional vice president for Downtown Manhattan.

On Oct. 7, the New York Times published its own analysis of the photo scandal. That day, Robert Saum, the World Bank Group’s regional country director for Eastern Europe, a role based in Kyiv, gave $1,000. He lists an Arlington, Va., address.

Steven Holley, COO of the New York investment manager Select Equity Group and former Sullivan & Cromwell partner, gave $1,000 on Oct. 9. Sacarob, Fitzpatrick and Holley all list New York City addresses, outside the district.

The San Francisco-based CEO of Mr. S Leather, the retailer behind the photos, gave $1,000 on Oct. 10.

Not all of Gallant’s best-known donors gave after the Post story. Fortune checked the names below against the dates in his filings.

Wall Street: Stephen Mandel, who founded the Greenwich hedge fund Lone Pine Capital, gave the $3,500 maximum on Sept. 14, the day after the story ran. Susan Mandel of Greenwich, listed as not employed, gave $3,500 the same day.

Old money and real estate: Katharine Rayner, the Cox Enterprises heiress whose fortune of about $4.9 billion (Forbes) rests on her estimated 17% stake in the family company, gave $3,500 on Sept. 15. She had also given $2,000 in July, and her cycle total is listed at the $3,500 limit.

Another maximum gift came on Sept. 26 from Michael Raynes, a developer who restores architecturally significant properties in Miami. In late 2022, he sold a historic estate in Southampton for $20 million. He lists a Miami Beach mailing address.

Wall Street: Charles Myers gave the $3,500 maximum at the end of 2025, when Gallant was still facing a primary. He is founder and chairman of Signum Global Advisors, a geopolitical research firm that advises financial institutions and touts “representation across the political spectrum.” He previously served as vice chairman at Evercore ISI and advised Hillary Clinton’s 2016 campaign.

Jason Carroll, co-founder of the high-frequency trading firm Hudson River Trading, gave $3,500 on Sept. 8, five days before the leak. Eric Knight, a senior trader at Jane Street, gave $7,000, covering both the primary and the general.

Hollywood and media: Kevin Huvane, co-chairman of Creative Artists Agency, gave $3,500 on June 30. Jeffrey Bewkes, the former Time Warner chairman and CEO who sold the company to AT&T in 2018, gave $3,500 on Aug. 12.

Local: Nancy Goroff, an organic chemist and former chair of Stony Brook University’s chemistry department, gave the maximum on June 29, days after Gallant’s primary win. Goroff lives in a modest New England saltbox overlooking Stony Brook Harbor, valued at about $1.1 million. She ran for a similarly drawn seat in 2020, losing to Lee Zeldin, now President Trump’s EPA administrator.

Goroff also backed “Team KCQ,” North Fork educator Kathryn Casey Quigley’s progressive bid to oust Suffolk County Democratic Chairman Rich Schaffer. Casey Quigley won about 43% of the weighted county committee vote on Sept. 22. Her campaign accused Schaffer of “backroom deals” with the local Conservative Party, which had harshly condemned Gallant’s photos.

Wall Street: Charles Schwab, founder of the brokerage bearing his name, a Fortune 500 company, gave LaLota $13,600 over the past two cycles, the maximum allowed. His mailing city: Palm Beach, Fla.

Crypto and defense: Faryar Shirzad, Coinbase’s chief policy officer and a deputy national security adviser under George W. Bush, gave $3,500 from a Washington, D.C., address. Palmer Luckey of Newport Beach, Calif., who founded defense contractor Anduril after selling Oculus to Facebook for about $2 billion, gave $7,000.

Global money: Leonard Blavatnik, the Ukrainian-born British American billionaire (Forbes) behind Access Industries, gave LaLota $3,500 in March. FEC reports list another $7,000 in aggregate from his wife, Emily.

“Though I have never met him, I appreciate his support,” LaLota said. His spokeswoman suggested Blavatnik may be drawn to LaLota because Russia’s Foreign Ministry put LaLota on a May 2023 list of 500 Americans barred from the country, a distinction the congressman “wears as a badge of honor.”

Blavatnik’s recent contributions also include Democratic Rep. Ritchie Torres, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham and the Equality PAC, which backs LGBTQ+ candidates.

His contribution forms give an address of 40 W. 57th St. in Manhattan, about 105 miles from the estate the press calls his.

The July 2025 sale of 408 Further Lane in Amagansett, which Behind the Hedges reported as the most expensive residential sale in Hamptons history, lists Brise Lointaine LLC as the new owner.

The seller, Terry Semel, ran Warner Bros. when Stanley Kubrick filmed his masked Long Island society for the studio. Semel had bought the property from Blackstone CEO Steve Schwarzman in 2005 for $43 million.

Property records from the real estate data service PropertyShark, reviewed by Fortune, list the arm’s-length price as $115,000, three zeros shy of the reported $115 million. East Hampton’s 2026 tax roll still billed Semel’s Windsor Digital Studio LLC. The town assessor’s office said it did not update the roll until July 2026.

The East Hampton Town Clerk’s office confirmed Brise Lointaine LLC’s ownership to Fortune and said deed updates take “very long” to process, along with the Suffolk County Clerk’s office.

Press accounts, though not the paperwork, identify the buyer as LaLota donor Len Blavatnik: Behind the Hedges, citing a source, and The Real Deal. Blavatnik owns Warner Music and holds a stake in A24, the arthouse studio behind Lady Bird (2017), Queer (2024), the gay BDSM romance Pillion (2026) and Backrooms (2026).

The tabloid framing of the race borrowed from Eyes Wide Shut (1999), but the sex and the masks were bait. Kubrick’s real horror was a gated order where wealth and power circulate in a closed circle, insulated from consequences.

In his year, the guest list was paper: electronic filing stayed voluntary for most committees until 2000, so a donor was a scanned page, not a spreadsheet. In NY-1, the circle is no secret.

In an age of metadata, AI-scanned social feeds and Flock cameras, nobody wears a mask for long. The leather shoot was archived, authenticated by an attorney and sold back to voters as merchandise. Every FEC filing is a digital fossil Kubrick’s guests would never have left behind.

The economics were another matter. LaLota raised about 84 cents of every named dollar from outside the district; Gallant, nearly two-thirds. What stayed masked on Election Day was not Gallant’s leather photos but the money, and how much of it came from outside NY-1.

#5423. Let there be LEDs: Tech upgrade helps James Turrell’s Skyspace shine again at UW art museum

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 6, 2026 at 8:01 amNovember 6, 2026 at 9:42 am

For most of the past dozen years, a James Turrell artwork on the University of Washington campus in Seattle — built to glow at sunrise and sunset — has been running on daylight alone.

That changes Nov. 14, when UW’s Henry Art Gallery relights “Light Reign,” its Turrell Skyspace, after a restoration that replaced aging lights with hundreds of new fixtures and a control system synced to the sun.

Originally installed in 2003 near the Henry’s entrance along 15th Avenue N.E., “Light Reign” is one of dozens of skyspaces by Turrell, the 83-year-old artist known for turning light itself into his medium.

Inside the artwork’s oval chamber, LEDs bathe the walls in slowly shifting color, and when the weather cooperates, a retractable lid opens to an oculus that frames the sky. From outside, the glass-paneled shell lights up with its own program — a 21st-century mood ring just steps from a bronze George Washington who has been gazing west toward the Olympics since 1909.

The relighting comes as the Henry, Washington’s first public art museum, heads into its 100th year. The museum opened on campus in February 1927, and officials are hinting that bigger changes are on the way for the centennial.

Trouble with “Light Reign” started around 2015, said Sage Sommer, the Henry’s director of exhibitions and collections. The original lights, by then more than a decade old, were reaching the end of their lifespan, and over time the museum lost the ability to run them.

Through those years, the Skyspace stayed open. Visitors could still sit inside, meditate and watch clouds and birds pass over the oculus, just without the color.

After years of planning, the Henry settled on a full lighting overhaul that also folds in ideas Turrell has used in his newer skyspaces. The exterior already ran on LEDs, but a very early generation of them, while the interior and oculus were lit by neon tubes made by Western Neon.

The museum didn’t work with Turrell directly. Instead it worked with lighting designer Ryan Pike, whose company, RHMP, works only on Turrell installations, from upgrades of existing pieces to new projects. Pike has worked on Turrell artworks since 2013.

For Pike, the toughest part was the exterior. “It’s just over 700 lights, in nine DMX universes, so each fixture can output independently of the rest,” he said in an email. DMX is the standard protocol for controlling stage and architectural lighting. Splitting the facade across multiple universes lets every fixture be programmed on its own.

Sommer said the Skyspace isn’t strictly time-based media, a museum term for art that relies on equipment and unfolds over time. But it raises the same questions. Sometimes the fix is simple, like converting a VHS tape to a digital file. Other times the hardware is integral to the work. Some artists insist a piece be shown only on a CRT TV, and some come back with a remastered version and want only that one shown.

“We work really closely with the artists to make sure that it is as they envision,” she said.

The Henry isn’t the only museum to face the problem. In 2023, Minneapolis’ Walker Art Center restored its own Turrell skyspace, “Sky Pesher,” after it became impossible to find the cold cathode tubes — a 1920s-era technology — that powered its sunrise and sunset lighting program.

Working with Turrell and his studio, the Walker switched to LEDs, which allowed more control and a much wider range of color. What had been “shades of tinted white” is now multicolored, Joe King, the Walker’s director of collections and exhibition management, said in an interview published by the museum.

The Henry’s new system uses roughly 840 LED fixtures, about 710 outside and 130 inside, Sommer said. The exterior program kicks in a half-hour before dawn and dusk. The morning show is brief, about 36 minutes, while the evening one currently runs about four hours after sunset.

“The very cool thing about this space, because we are so far north, is just how connected to sunrise and sunset it is, and how drastically different it is throughout the year,” Sommer said.

The roof has its own engineering pedigree. The Skyspace’s hydraulic lid, which lifts and slides out of the way, was designed by submarine manufacturers in Everett. It stays shut in the rain.

The museum closed the Skyspace in late July and used the downtime for physical restoration, too: repainting the interior, refinishing the teak benches, waxing floors, replacing worn locks, refitting doors that had swollen and cleaning out the gutters. Everything had to be rewired, and the project took longer than expected.

“Light Reign” is the most visible piece in the Henry’s collection of about 30,000 objects, including more than 18,000 textiles and 7,000 works on paper. Only a sliver is ever on view, so the Henry is putting its collection database online. The project was funded by UW’s Student Technology Fee. Anyone can book an appointment at its study center to see a piece up close.

Technology is also the focus of the Henry’s centennial exhibition, opening in late February. Swagato Chakravorty, associate curator, said he was surprised that no major museum had mounted a large, ambitious show on contemporary art and technology in decades, even as Seattle was transformed around it. His show looks at technology “from below,” focusing on the people and communities most directly affected rather than a “great man” story.

The exhibition is loosely organized around three threads. One is bioethics, including a work the Henry commissioned in 2002 with UW geneticist Mary-Claire King, which is being revived 25 years later. Another pairs Indigenous knowledge with tools like 3D printing and algorithms. The third is technology’s material toll, from data centers to water use.

Chakravorty said he deliberately avoids taking a side on whether technology is good or bad for art.

“Writing is a technology. Cave painting was a technology,” he said. As for AI: “It’s not going to kill art.”

The public unveiling of the refurbished “Light Reign” runs 3:30 to 6 p.m. Nov. 14, with remarks from Henry Executive Director Kris Lewis and the exterior illumination starting at 4 p.m. Admission is free, though the Henry encourages RSVPs, and interior viewing is limited to 25 people at a time for about 10 minutes each.

Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5422. The Best Leaders Never Stop Sharing the Lessons They’ve Learned. Here’s Why It Matters More Than You Think.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Decades of hard-earned business wisdom matters most when leaders are willing to share the full story behind it, not just the outcome.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Over the past few decades, leaders have lived through the Great Recession, Covid and now the rise of artificial intelligence. Each has fundamentally changed how companies operate and how leaders make decisions.

The experience of leaders who lived through those challenges — and how they pivoted in unprecedented times — contains invaluable knowledge. Too often, people think they can recapture history just by reading about it. Learning from history is useful, of course. But leadership experience isn’t something that can be replicated just by asking AI a question. Real people had to navigate real situations to keep their companies afloat, and that can’t be fully understood from the answer to a prompt.

Decades of experience are most valuable when the leaders who lived through it are willing to pass on what they learned. Not just the outcome, but the full story behind it. Here’s why.

No two business decisions are exactly alike. Looking back at what someone did in a similar situation and copying it rarely works, because the decision itself isn’t the defining factor. What mattered was the thinking behind it: the pressures, the constraints, the information available at the time. None of that gets passed down unless the person who lived it chooses to share it.

That’s why sharing the context behind a tough call, and not just the decision itself, is so important. The best leaders explain what led them down a particular path, because that reasoning is important. Without it, people start making decisions by pattern-matching to a single past example, and miss the nuance.

Frameworks offer direction, but direction isn’t the same as confidence. Confidence comes from people who have been there, done that and can give sound advice. Someone who has faced similar challenges can ask the right questions, challenge assumptions and offer a perspective that helps leaders see their decisions more clearly. That insight can give leaders the confidence to move forward.

A leader’s mettle is tested in situations they’ve never seen before and likely never will again. Leaders who share what they’ve learned give the next generation a real place to start instead of a blank page. That’s a completely different kind of value than theory can provide.

Almost every leader who’s achieved something meaningful can point to someone who helped them along the way — a mentor who believed in them, offered guidance or helped them navigate a difficult decision. All those experiences, and all the people who helped you get there, are a gift. And leaders who have benefited from that kind of support often feel a calling to pass it on to others.

It’s why some pursue business coaching as a second career when they are ready to move on from the CEO role. CEOs are builders. While they may be ready to leave the responsibilities of running a company behind, they still want to develop people, solve problems and make a meaningful impact. Looking back over long careers, many CEOs say their greatest successes involved helping others succeed.

There’s another benefit to mentoring that many experienced leaders don’t anticipate: They continue growing themselves. I’ve seen leaders leave the CEO role, begin coaching others and discover they’re developing in ways they never expected. They gain greater empathy for other people and a deeper understanding of the challenges different leaders face. After decades of making decisions and being responsible for outcomes, they find themselves learning just as much from the people they’re helping.

That’s what makes mentoring so rewarding. Mentors are not simply passing along everything they’ve learned over their careers. They’re continuing to grow as leaders and as people.

Effective mentoring means helping people see past their blind spots. Confirmation bias might be the most common one of all. It’s easy to believe an idea and then go find justification that matches it. AI is particularly good at feeding that instinct back, since it tends to reflect whatever perspective it’s given rather than challenge it.

That’s what makes outside perspectives so valuable. Experienced leaders can offer fresh perspectives, challenge assumptions and push leaders to think beyond the answer they’ve already convinced themselves is right.

None of this works if the story that a mentor passes on only includes the good parts. Most of the real wisdom comes from mistakes. When someone is vulnerable enough to admit they messed up, the real learning happens. That’s the full story, not the polished version.

Experience that never gets passed on doesn’t do anyone much good. It stays with the person who earned it. The leaders we remember are the ones who made sure what they learned — wins and losses — outlasted their own careers.

#5420. Amazon’s AI shopping agent moves into text messages, taking orders and tracking prices

by Todd Bishop on Nov 6, 2026 at 8:07 amNovember 6, 2026 at 9:35 am

Amazon is rolling out a new feature to let customers shop by text message — sending requests to its Alexa for Shopping AI agent, which will search for products, compare options and place orders on their behalf.

The idea is to make shopping work more like messaging a personal assistant. Amazon says the agent works in the background after it gets a request or a photo, and texts back when the task is done.

It’s part throwback and part hot new thing, reflecting a broader shift in how tech companies are offering AI agents for everyday use. OpenAI added texting to Dot, its personal AI agent, last month, and DoorDash rolled out text ordering in September.

The expansion of Amazon’s AI shopping assistant comes amid a larger fight over who controls online shopping when agents do the buying. Amazon has moved to block outside agents from Meta, Perplexity, Google and OpenAI from shopping its site while building its own.

The text thread is also a new place for Amazon to sell. The company says order updates, delivery notifications and deals will eventually land in the same conversation.

Digiday reports that sponsored products can appear among the options the agent texts back, free to advertisers for now, while purchases the agent completes on its own stay ad-free. Amazon reported $68.6 billion in advertising sales in 2025.

The text feature started rolling out Friday to a small group of U.S. customers by invitation, and millions more will get access in the coming weeks, the company says.

Customers who opt in get a contact called “Alexa Shopping” and can send it requests that range from a note that they’re out of dog food to a photo of a recipe they want turned into a grocery order, according to Amazon’s examples.

The agent searches, texts back with options and completes the purchase with the customer’s approval. Customers can also turn on auto-buy to have it purchase an item automatically when the price hits their target. It can also watch for price drops, reorder past purchases and check on packages, and Amazon says a conversation started by text will carry over to the Amazon app, the website and Alexa devices.

Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping in May, merging its Rufus shopping chatbot with Alexa+, the generative AI version of its voice assistant.

#5419. Stop Treating Media Coverage Like a Trophy. Put It to Work For Your Business.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Earned media shouldn’t stop working once the article is published. You get the most value from press coverage by treating it as the start.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

An agent lands a feature in a major publication. Maybe it’s a Wall Street Journal profile on luxury market trends or a Mansion Global piece showcasing a property they sold. The team celebrates, which they should. Someone posts it on LinkedIn. The logo goes on the website. And then, within about 72 hours, the whole thing gets filed away and everyone moves on to the next thing.

The publication reached its audience. The agent got their moment. Done.

Except they’ve only captured maybe one-third of the value that placement was capable of producing.

Most businesses, not just real estate, treat earned media as an event with a beginning and an end. The end is publication day, or maybe the day after when the LinkedIn post goes up. What they rarely think about is that a strong piece of coverage does something the publication’s audience only partially benefits from. It creates a transferable signal of credibility. And unlike the initial readership, which spikes and fades, that credibility doesn’t expire. It can be put to work in sales conversations, listing presentations, recruiting pitches, partnership discussions and investor meetings for as long as it remains relevant.

The publication date should be the beginning of a press hit’s useful life. Most companies treat it as the end.

When a company earns meaningful media coverage, there’s an obvious audience and a less obvious one. The obvious audience is whoever reads the publication that day. They saw it, absorbed it, formed an impression and maybe clicked through it. Some small percentage converted into something useful. That’s the audience most PR measurement focuses on, and it’s real.

The less obvious audience is everyone the company will encounter afterward who never saw the original piece. Future prospects. Potential recruits. Partners evaluating whether to work together. Investors doing background research. Sellers deciding between agents. These people didn’t read the article. But they will see what the company does with it.

Third-party credibility travels differently than self-promotion. A company saying they’re a market leader means almost nothing. A respected publication having said it, even months ago, means something different in a sales conversation, a pitch deck, or a follow-up email. The credibility is borrowed from the publication, and unlike borrowed money, you don’t have to return it. You can keep using it in every context where trust matters, which in most professional services businesses is nearly every context that matters at all.

Most companies return it anyway, unintentionally, by posting once and moving on.

Real estate is a particularly clear example of this dynamic because trust is so central to every major decision in the industry.

A luxury agent gets quoted in a piece about Central Coast market trends. That quote doesn’t just exist in the article. It can be included in the next seller presentation as third-party validation of the agent’s market knowledge. It can be referenced when following up with a prospect who went quiet. It can be sent to a past client alongside a brief note that the agent has been getting some attention for their market expertise lately. In each of those moments, the placement is doing trust work it was never credited for in any media measurement report.

A brokerage gets recognized by a real estate publication for its growth or market performance. That recognition matters on the day it runs. It also matters when a strong agent is evaluating which brokerage to join and finds it during their research. It matters when a corporate relocation client is deciding which firm to trust with their employees. It matters when a developer is choosing a listing partner. The recognition didn’t expire. It just wasn’t put back to work.

This isn’t a real estate insight specifically. Any expertise-driven business encounters the same dynamic. A founder gets a strong profile in a trade publication. A law firm gets recognized for a significant case outcome. A consultant gets quoted extensively in a piece about their industry. Each of those placements has an initial audience. Each of them also creates a credibility signal that can work across every subsequent business development interaction if the company chooses to use it that way.

There’s a structural problem in how most organizations handle earned media that helps explain why the follow-through is so consistently weak. The PR function, whether internal or external, tends to define success as placement. Coverage secured, relationship maintained, report submitted. The job is done.

But the job of making that coverage influence the business is a marketing and sales function. It belongs in listing presentations, pitch decks, email signatures and follow-up sequences. And when PR and marketing operate as separate efforts that hand off awkwardly or don’t communicate at all, the coverage falls into the gap between them. It gets celebrated briefly and then abandoned.

The practical shift here doesn’t require a new budget or a complicated system. It requires asking a different set of questions after meaningful coverage lands.

Where does trust matter in this business right now, and can this placement show up there? A listing presentation is a moment of trust evaluation. So is a recruiting conversation. So is the part of a sales process where a prospect is doing their own research to validate whether you’re worth engaging. Those moments have a before and after, and coverage that shows up before one of them does different work than coverage that never surfaces at all.

Who hasn’t seen this yet that should? Past clients who might refer based on a renewed sense that you’re doing well. Prospects who went quiet and might re-engage if the right reason appears. Investors or partners who would find the recognition relevant to a conversation already in progress.

How can the underlying idea travel beyond the placement itself? A quote about market conditions can become a social post with a different angle. A feature about a sold property can inspire a newsletter about what made that type of buyer willing to pay a premium. The article is one expression of an idea. The idea has more legs than the article does.

Most companies don’t need more press nearly as badly as they need to use the press they’ve already earned. One well-distributed placement that shows up in six different trust-critical moments over the next year is worth considerably more than six placements that each get posted once and forgotten.

Earn once. Distribute repeatedly. The press hit gets you in the door. What you do with it afterward determines whether it was worth earning in the first place.

An agent lands a feature in a major publication. Maybe it’s a Wall Street Journal profile on luxury market trends or a Mansion Global piece showcasing a property they sold. The team celebrates, which they should. Someone posts it on LinkedIn. The logo goes on the website. And then, within about 72 hours, the whole thing gets filed away and everyone moves on to the next thing.

The publication reached its audience. The agent got their moment. Done.

Except they’ve only captured maybe one-third of the value that placement was capable of producing.

#5418. Anthropic’s lower-than-expected IPO valuation: smart strategy or sign of trouble?

With a valuation that could reach $1.4 trillion, Anthropic’s initial public stock offering will represent an incredible, nearly unprecedented feat—and a disappointment.

The five-year old AI company expects to price its shares somewhere between $70 and $78 apiece on Nov. 18, and begin trading on the Nasdaq the following day under the ANT ticker. That price range, which translates to a valuation between $1.26 billion and $1.41 trillion, is significantly lower than the roughly $2 trillion projection that bullish investors and analysts were throwing around over the summer.

And it means that Anthropic would fall short of claiming the largest-IPO-in-history title, currently held by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which priced its June IPO at $1.77 trillion.

But while Anthropic may miss out on bragging rights, its lower-than-expected IPO price is not necessarily a sign that its business is in trouble, several market experts told Fortune. At a time of political and economic uncertainty, Anthropic’s conservative pricing allows it to manage expectations while leaving itself room to generate buzz if it sees a big pop in its trading debut.

“Anthropic is moving forward with its IPO at a steeper discount than market initially anticipated,” Lior Prosor, general partner at the VC firm Deep33, tells Fortune. “We think that is a smart pricing strategy. It gives nervous AI-trade investors meaningful potential upside while securing the capital Anthropic needs to take full control of its destiny and fund its compute commitments.”

Compute is among the biggest risks in Anthropic’s business. The company has nearly a trillion dollars in committed compute-related spending, according to its most recent S-1 filing, and it still might not be enough. “We expect demand for compute to continue meaningfully outpacing supply across the chain,” said Prosor.

Anthropic could raise more than $60 billion in its IPO—capital that will be vital to its efforts to secure compute and stay at the forefront of the AI race. As with every company that has an IPO however, Anthropic needs to balance the risk of leaving money on the table if it prices shares too low, with the risk of pricing too high and seeing its share price plummet when trading begins.

“Pricing an IPO to perfection doesn’t leave much excitement or positive press, especially if the stock falls after the IPO,” said Darian Shirazi, general partner at Gradient. “Anthropic is likely optimizing for positive media coverage of the IPO and to drive more upward momentum after pricing. IPOs that fall after pricing usually suffer months of negative press before recovery, so this is likely a good way to ensure a positive outcome for all investors—existing and new.”

Anthropic is one of the undisputed leaders in developing frontier AI models, with its technology widely used by businesses, particularly for software programming and cybersecurity. Whether Anthropic can make its AI tools must-have technology for a broader swath of customers however is one of the key questions facing the company as investors size it up, and compare it to competitors such as OpenAI and Google.

Anthropic’s revenue in the third quarter totaled $17 billion, up more than 1,100% from the same time one year ago. On a quarter-over-quarter basis however, Anthropic’s revenue grew 47% in the third quarter, a marked slowdown from the 144% sequential growth rate it posted in the second quarter.

Not helping matters, last week’s midterm election results could spell trouble for the data center buildout. In anticipation of more difficulty getting projects across the line, and in a bid to curry favor with the public, Anthropic’s chief rival OpenAI is attempting to rebrand data centers “compute campuses.”

Astronomical compute spending, combined with slowing third quarter revenue, has “given prospective buyers pause,” Aman Verjee, founder and general partner at Practical Venture Capital, tells Fortune. “Additionally, recent broader market sell-off related to political headwinds in Congress in key states where data centers are being built—notably Texas, Georgia, and Ohio—has dampened some enthusiasm.”

Even with these concerns, the lower valuation “reduces expectations and leaves plenty of room for upside appreciation,” Verjee said. If the IPO exceeds expectations, it sets the stage for positive press, which could have favorable downstream impacts, Gradient’s Shirazi.

As its IPO approaches, Anthropic has sought to build buzz with a blizzard of product announcements. On Monday, it debuted new models, Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, that are 20% cheaper than rival OpenAI’s flagship model, GPT-6 Astra, while claiming superior performance. On Tuesday, Anthropic released a suite of new workplace tools that could threaten Microsoft’s iron grip on white collar work for non-coding roles.

Anthropic’s lower-than-expected valuation does not signal any “weakness in Anthropic’s business,” Bastiaan Janmaat, general partner at Lithos Capital, tells Fortune. “In fact they’ve shown incredible advances recently.”

#5417. Binance’s $6.3B Hack Fix Is Coming Tomorrow: Why the ZK Math Doesn't Tell the Whole Story

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On-chain data shows the attacker behind the $6.3 billion Binance theft depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses.

At the same time, Binance's first post-hack reserve snapshot shows its biggest assets covered with buffers as small as 2.7 ETH and $6 of USDT. Binance's full zero-knowledge proof of those figures is due by Tuesday.

Some of the money stolen from Binance has started going back to Binance.

Blockchain intelligence firm Arkham has flagged the entity it tracks as "Binance Hacker" depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses. Arkham says those addresses "likely represent nested service(s)." These are third-party exchanges that use Binance for liquidity and custody, giving their own customers deposit addresses that sit on Binance's infrastructure.

If Arkham is right, the hacker isn't depositing into an ordinary Binance account. The money would be going to smaller platforms that operate through Binance. Exchanges have long known this is a weak point for stolen funds moving into normal trading. Either way, Binance is now receiving stolen funds at its own deposit addresses while it works to show customers it has replaced what was taken.

The FBI has attributed the October 29 theft to North Korea. The deposits come at a sensitive moment. Binance has just published its first reserve snapshot since the hack and has promised a full cryptographic proof of it by Tuesday.

$4 million is a small slice of a theft worth about $6.3 billion, but it matters for two reasons.

It shows how the laundering works. Nested services are a common way into the regulated financial system. A third-party platform that relies on Binance for custody may run weaker identity checks on its own users. Funds deposited there can be swapped and withdrawn without the hacker ever opening a Binance account.

Binance can act on it. Binance can't freeze bitcoin and ether sitting in wallets nobody controls, and it doesn't control the stablecoins that issuers like Tether and Circle have frozen. Deposits that land at its own addresses are different: they are on Binance's platform, so Binance can freeze them itself. One of the first tests of how Binance handles the money still in the hacker's hands is whether it freezes these funds and identifies the services that own the addresses.

While the hacker's funds move, Binance has been rebuilding its reserves. Its proof-of-reserves page now shows:

The first page covers Binance's six largest assets. Customer balances are what users hold. Reserves are on-chain wallet balances, including assets held with outside custodians.

The second page has four more assets, and two of them stand out:

Why USD1 and RLUSD matter: these are two of the stablecoins whose issuers froze stolen funds after the attack. World Liberty Financial froze $27 million of USD1, and Ripple began freezing RLUSD the same night. Both now show reserves above what Binance owes customers.

Assets with outside custodians: part of several reserves sits with outside custodians rather than in Binance's own exchange wallets:

The striking part isn't that the ratios reach 100%. It's how closely they stop there.

Compared with October's report: Binance's previous monthly report, published in early October before the hack, showed BTC at 100.35% and USDT at 103.88%. ETH was already at exactly 100.00%. After the theft:

Not every asset is that tight. USDC, ZEC and BNB carry buffers of 1.3% to 6%. The thinnest buffers are in BTC, ETH, USDT and SOL, which are among the assets the attacker took in the largest amounts.

How Binance says it got here: the pattern fits Binance's account of replacing the stolen assets in stages. It reported 80% replaced on Friday, 90% on Saturday and 95% on Sunday. The remaining 5% is in less-liquid tokens it is still buying. The money came from:

Binance confirmed taking 7,499 BTC from SAFU and has pledged to refill the fund to about $1 billion.

What the snapshot can't show: it was taken a little over a day after the theft, once the rebuild was under way. It shows the balance sheet after the replacement, not how large the gap was on October 29.

Binance says the full proof takes 40 to 50 hours to compute. Its latest update says it will be ready "by Tuesday, 2026-11-03 (UTC)." The system is open source, in Binance's zkmerkle-proof-of-solvency repository.

What the proof guarantees, according to the project's circuit design document:

The design also guards against a "dummy user attack" identified by Ethereum Foundation researcher Enrico Bottazzi. In that attack, fake accounts holding cheap tokens are used to offset debts in major assets.

What it doesn't prove: the reserve side. The project's verifier config describes the totals as information "published by CEX, it represents CEX's liability." The reserve figures are checked a different way, against the wallet addresses Binance publishes through the page's "Download All Address" option.

What customers can do: each user can get a Merkle proof for their account and check it against the published root. They can use the verifier code in Binance's repository rather than Binance's own interface. That doesn't prove Binance is solvent, but it confirms the user's balance was counted.

Binance has rebuilt its reserves to 100% across its ten largest assets, but on several of them the buffer is only a few coins. Meanwhile, stolen funds are reaching its deposit addresses through platforms that run on its infrastructure. Tuesday's proof can confirm customer balances. It can't show how Binance handles the stolen money arriving at its own door.
