#5416. Tech Moves: Fred Hutch leader goes to AWS; Temporal, Augmodo and Neuralwatt name execs

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 6, 2026 at 10:06 amNovember 6, 2026 at 10:45 am

— Amitabha “Guppy” Gupta, a Fred Hutch Cancer Center associate director who helps researchers translate their work to broader audiences, is leaving after 14 years to join Amazon. Starting Nov. 16, he will be a strategic advisor for nonprofit research and advanced AI with AWS’ Global Nonprofit Business.

Gupta said technology was often an obstacle to scientific breakthroughs at Fred Hutch.

“It’s the infrastructure, data, and tools standing between a scientist and an answer,” he wrote on LinkedIn. In his new role, “I’ll work with researchers and research institutions on using cloud, high-performance computing, and AI to remove those barriers.”

— Microsoft board member ‌Emma Walmsley has been appointed CEO of HP, effective Jan. 4. Walmsley, who led the pharmaceutical giant GSK until December 2025, succeeds Bruce Broussard. Reuters notes that her seven years serving on the Microsoft board “are her closest brush with the tech sector” prior to taking the top job at the PC maker.

— Bas Nijholt, senior staff engineer at IonQ‘s Seattle-area facility, has resigned after three years to join an AI startup that’s still in stealth mode. At IonQ, the theoretical quantum mechanics expert built MindRoom, an open-source collaboration and knowledge-sharing platform that he calls “a company brain.”

“With this new opportunity, I get to keep building and turbocharging MindRoom with a team of people who are just as excited about AI as I am,” Nijholt said, adding that the tool will remain freely available.

Before IonQ, Nijholt spent nearly four years at Microsoft.

— Bellevue, Wash., startup Temporal, whose software keeps AI agents running reliably, has named Sean Heneghan as vice president of sales for the Americas. The company ranks No. 1 on the GeekWire 200, a list of the top Pacific Northwest startups. In September it raised $550 million, putting its valuation at $12.55 billion.

Temporal is fully remote, and Heneghan is based in the Chicago area. He joins the company from MongoDB.

— Doug Heimburger, a 26-year Amazon veteran, has changed roles, shifting from chief financial officer and vice president of Worldwide Operations to CFO/VP of Worldwide Stores. In the new position, Heimburger said he’ll help oversee efforts to improve delivery speed, reduce costs and increase growth of the Stores business. His first role at the company was data mining analyst.

— Seattle startup Augmodo has named Capri Brixey as head of retail sales. The company, which sells AI-powered wearable devices with cameras, raised $21 million in July to expand from in-store applications that let workers passively track inventory into automotive, warehouse and hospital settings. Augmodo ranks No. 122 on the GeekWire 200.

Ross Finman, founder and CEO of Augmodo, called Brixey “the right leader to accelerate our expansion” given her experience selling to both retail and warehouse operations. Her past roles include leadership positions at Coca-Cola and Kroger.

— Meaghan Davison Praznik was named vice president of marketing for Neuralwatt, a Seattle-based startup that built a tool for calculating, in real time, the carbon emissions of individual AI requests. Her former employers include Clif Bar, AllTrails and Merino Energy.

Because the carbon intensity of grid power varies throughout the day and across regions, Neuralwatt’s technology can help customers run compute-intensive operations when clean energy is more abundant.

— BuyWander, an auction-based online marketplace for returned and overstocked retail items, has named Chris Holm as senior director of product. Holm spent nine years at Amazon, leaving in 2024 after managing last-mile and same-day delivery technology and working on Amazon Fresh delivery. He has since served as a consultant for carbon removal startup Lithos Carbon and as a founder-in-residence at the startup studio Foundations.

In August, BuyWander moved its headquarters across Washington from Spokane to Kent. The company announced $21 million in new funding in September.

— T-Mobile’s Kevin Lau has joined the advisory board at the University of Washington’s College of Engineering. Lau has been with the telecom giant for 22 years over two stints and serves as VP of digital experience engineering. He holds bachelor’s, master’s and doctoral degrees in electrical engineering from the UW.

— Christian Smith, an Issaquah, Wash.-based tech leader, has been named president of revenue for Cloudflare, which provides security and speed services for websites and online applications. He will oversee worldwide go-to-market operations. Smith previously served as chief revenue officer for Splunk and Nintex.

Hiring elite engineers or proven revenue leaders in 2026?

#5415. I Made a Mistake That Cost Me Everything. Rebuilding My Life and Career Taught Me These 2 Essential Leadership Lessons.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

What does it take to rebuild after your worst decision?

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I know what it’s like to have people judge you by the worst decision you’ve ever made. When I was younger, I made a mistake that followed me for years. It ended up costing me opportunities, changing the direction of my life and eventually shaping the leader I am today.

The truth is, I was 20 years old and naive. I saw an underground, unregulated industry doing things wrong and thought I could do it better, which is how I began running a gray-market peptide and steroid company.

Even though I introduced strict operational standards, like batch-testing, the reality was that it was an illicit industry. The business was shut down; I was handed a federal indictment and eventually received a felony conviction. I lost everything.

I took full responsibility, paid a heavy price and spent the best part of the next decade rebuilding my life and career. What I’ve realized is that the experience changed how I think about myself and how I treat others. I know exactly what it costs to cut corners, and I know what it means to need a second chance.

After my conviction, banks wouldn’t touch me, and institutions flagged me. I was left with a choice: I could either let my past define me or spend the rest of my life proving I was better than my worst decision.

When I began building new companies, I knew they had to operate to the highest standards. Because of my past, being “good enough” was never an option. I had to prove I was doing things the right way — that my businesses were not only legitimate but could also be successful.

I’ve now spent more than 12 years operating businesses in highly regulated medical and telehealth sectors. I expect everyone I work with to meet those same high standards. But accountability has to start with me. As a founder, I can’t expect my employees to take responsibility for their decisions if I’m not prepared to do the same with my own.

I also had to give myself a second chance. I refused to wallow in shame and failure or let the fear of being judged stop me from sticking my neck out again. I backed myself. I know firsthand how important it is to get another chance. But I also believe people have to take responsibility for what’s gone wrong.

The line between giving someone another chance and holding them accountable comes down to two things: effort and ethics. There’s a difference between someone who’s struggling with a particular job and someone who simply isn’t willing to put the effort in. If they’re trying and willing to learn, I want to support them.

But accountability is non-negotiable. If someone violates our ethical standards, that’s an immediate dealbreaker. I know that might sound harsh coming from someone who’s needed a second chance himself. I also know that getting a second chance doesn’t mean escaping the consequences of your actions. I had to accept mine before I could rebuild.

People can change. I’ve had to prove that myself. But I can’t ignore a serious breach of trust just because I believe someone deserves another chance. My advice to other leaders is to ask whether the problem is skills, effort or integrity. They’re different problems and require different responses.

If someone has the right attitude, the raw hustle and that chip on their shoulder, I want to figure out where they fit rather than simply letting them go. I call this finding the right seat on the bus for the right people.

That’s also why I hire people based on who they are, their character and potential, rather than just qualifications or professional accolades. I particularly value people who have overcome adversity. That’s a kind of determination that can’t be taught.

I employ hundreds of people, and I take their livelihoods personally. Their families depend on them, and I believe loyalty has to work both ways. Some employees who joined my businesses a decade ago are still working with me today. Seeing members of my team buy homes and support their families is one of the most rewarding parts of what I do.

I didn’t want my belief in second chances to stop with my own employees. I had grit, determination and some luck on my side when I was rebuilding my life and career after my felony conviction. But I know there are plenty of people with the same determination who don’t get the opportunity to prove themselves afterwards. I feel like it’s my responsibility to change that.

My faith has also shaped my philosophy about second chances. I believe that people can take responsibility for their past and still deserve the opportunity to build a better future. That’s why I established the Joey Stiver Foundation to support educational, entrepreneurial and second-chance opportunities.

One of its initiatives, the St. Dismas Accelerator, aims to give formerly incarcerated adults and at-risk young people access to seed capital, executive mentorship and AI training. I’ve met people who’ve been through incredibly difficult experiences and come out of them with the kind of resourcefulness and determination you need to build a business.

I know some people won’t agree with my approach. They’ll wonder how I can have such strict standards while also believing so strongly in second chances. After everything I’ve experienced, I think both are important. When you’ve been through what I have, you realize you can fail, take responsibility, get back up and build again.

I’ve met plenty of people who’ve experienced failure or hardship and started to believe that success is something that happens to other people. But if you’ve got the drive, grit and determination to build something better for yourself, why shouldn’t you get that opportunity?

It’s something I remind myself, my team and anyone else who needs a reason to keep going. Why not you? The race isn’t over.

I know what it’s like to have people judge you by the worst decision you’ve ever made. When I was younger, I made a mistake that followed me for years. It ended up costing me opportunities, changing the direction of my life and eventually shaping the leader I am today.

The truth is, I was 20 years old and naive. I saw an underground, unregulated industry doing things wrong and thought I could do it better, which is how I began running a gray-market peptide and steroid company.

Even though I introduced strict operational standards, like batch-testing, the reality was that it was an illicit industry. The business was shut down; I was handed a federal indictment and eventually received a felony conviction. I lost everything.

#5414. How to be unemployed: Glenn Kelman on life after Redfin

by Glenn Kelman on Nov 6, 2026 at 12:47 pmNovember 6, 2026 at 12:52 pm

After 20 years at Redfin, and 10 months of unemployment, I’ve co-founded a new company. My business partner and I will announce our plans after we’ve built our product, but in the meantime GeekWire asked me to explain what I learned in the transition between Redfin and this new venture.

Many of us are in transition because society is in transition, with AI hollowing out big companies and making it easier to start new companies.

In the past, my own transitions had been harrowing, because I ran out of money or lost my sense of purpose. Leaving Redfin, I thought “here we go again.” I felt self-conscious being in the grocery store at 11 a.m. on a weekday. I was ashamed when I couldn’t come up with an idea for a company. But I made it to the other side.

To do that, I had to convince myself that I was an intrepid explorer, even if what I was exploring wasn’t Mount Everest, but instead what I could be. I wanted to feel brave about encounters I otherwise would’ve found embarrassing. Over the last year, I met people about becoming a high school teacher, a Whistler bagel shopkeeper, a candidate for the state legislature, the founder of a tree-planting nonprofit, the CEO of a pre-IPO company and a project leader for Sound Transit.

The way to prepare yourself to do one thing for a long time is first to consider everything else.

At the beginning of my exploration, a CEO recruiter told me the startup scene in Seattle was “dead” and that, for all of Seattle’s talent, more companies were forming in New York and even LA. I Googled “high-growth Seattle startups” and the list included one company that went bankrupt in 2023, and Redfin, which was acquired in 2025.

Another friend told me that she was on a Discord channel with a bunch of CTOs who were miserable trying to do “AI transformations” at businesses with legacy codebases. At least for me, the logical response to all this has been to start an AI-native company in Seattle.

“The way to prepare yourself to do one thing for a long time is first to consider everything else.”

It took me months to feel ready to do that. In January, a friend told me I wasn’t allowed to make any big decisions until September. Another said I had to wait until the frenzy of my last job had subsided. “You’ll know it has happened,” he said, “because food will start tasting better” (it never happened).

At a conference, a fashion entrepreneur who’d built and abandoned vast residences in Jackson Hole and Costa Rica, and got divorced twice in the past three years, gave me a bracelet that said “we are enough.”

Since I’d often been thinking I hadn’t done enough in the morning to deserve lunch, it was a relief to feel that I didn’t have to be creative or productive in order to justify my existence. But relieving that pressure also made it easier to be creative and productive.

On a call walking through Volunteer Park, I told a friend that the bracelet reminded me I could be happy and never start a company again. She said, “YOU JUST NEED A CO-FOUNDER.”

She told me to share flawed ideas with people who could make them better. I set up meetings with potential co-founders, and we shared our ideas before they were ready, because our meetings had become deadlines. Then we used AI to turn our ideas into products, so we could see what was good and bad about each idea. Starting a company started to feel like a natural progression, instead of Athena sprouting out of Zeus’s head.

When I confessed to a friend that everything we were working on still seemed so small, she said, “What about breakfast burritos?” She outlined her vision for a shop serving breakfast burritos all day, with a line out the door. Then she started talking about inventing a nursing home “that makes everyone happy.” Rather than running a McKinsey market-sizing analysis, she just thought about what she wanted to exist in the world.

That’s something almost anyone can do. In her living room, I suddenly felt that humanity would always have an instinct — this is a bizarre word, but it’s what popped into my head — to fructify. I remember walking home from her house with my wife and hearing the thick sound of insects humming in the night as proof of life’s rich pageant. This is what I mean by surrounding yourself with good vibes.

The last step in my process maybe should’ve come first, choosing where I wanted to make a difference. I thought about all the companies that I honestly would’ve been proud to start, and they were all in the same industry. I had no experience in that industry, but a friend said I could offset that if I were willing to give it everything I have, which is what I’m now doing. I met amazing, generous investors who gave me a good idea, and a business partner who helped me think it through.

Through all of this, I depended on my wife more than any husband ever should. She works herself to the bone treating people with cancer, but she took my calls in the middle of her workday, when I would talk in detail about what to cook for dinner and then — one more thing! — what’s the meaning of my life?

Once, she was getting into our Chevy Bolt for her morning commute while I was rounding the corner with the dog, and I saw her brighten in the way many people did back when I was Redfin’s CEO.

I found myself full of anticipation. She reached into the car, as if to grab a small gift, and heaved something at me from across the street, saying it “needs reprogramming.” Before I realized it was a garage clicker, I thought she had said I was the one who needed reprogramming. “Maybe that’s true,” I said to myself, trudging past the browned lawn, and the dirty dishes, and into a world of possibilities.

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5413. Failure Is Part of Entrepreneurship. These 5 Lessons Will Help You Recover.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Most businesses stumble at some point. How you respond decides whether the failure becomes a setback or a turning point, and the research has some useful pointers.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

In 1989, I opened an Italian restaurant in Tsim Sha Tsui, Hong Kong, where the waiters sang opera arias between courses. It was a lot of fun, but it was not a good business, and it closed in 1993.

I had assumed running a restaurant was easy. It isn’t. The location was wrong, the costs were too high, and I didn’t know the trade well enough to see either problem early. Around the same time, I put money into film production and property. Both businesses struggled and were sold in the mid-1990s.

I share this because founders tend to talk about their successes and quietly bury the rest. Yet failure is a normal part of business. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, only about half of new U.S. business establishments are still operating five years later. Hong Kong is no different. In 2025, a record number of companies registered in the city, but the South China Morning Post reported that more than 99,000 were dissolved in the same year.

Here are five lessons I have learned about failing — and about recovering.

Most of my early setbacks came from businesses I entered because they looked exciting, not because I understood them. The pattern is common. CB Insights’ 2026 analysis of startup shutdowns found that 43% cited poor product-market fit. I suspect many of those founders were very capable. They had simply misread a market they didn’t know well enough.

My rule since then has been simple: Never set up a business you don’t know. If you want to enter an unfamiliar field, partner with someone who has spent years in it, and listen to them.

The hardest decision in a struggling business is often the decision to stop. CB Insights found that 70% of failed startups ultimately ran out of capital, but running out of money is usually the last symptom, not the cause. By the time the bank balance forces your hand, months or even years may have been lost.

The same analysis, as reported by Crowdfund Insider, found that nearly a quarter of these companies had been “walking dead” for three years or more after their last funding round, still operating but no longer really growing. Hanging on rarely saves a business. More often, it makes the eventual decision more expensive.

Selling the film and property businesses was painful, but it freed up time, money and attention for something better. Closing a venture is not the same as failing as a person.

Losing a business can feel like a bereavement, and research suggests we should treat it as one. Professor Dean Shepherd’s work on grief and business failure, published in the Academy of Management Review, argues that founders recover and learn faster when they move between confronting the loss and stepping away from it, rather than dwelling on it or pretending it never happened.

The emotional cost is real. In a study of 242 entrepreneurs led by Dr. Michael Freeman of the University of California, San Francisco, 72% reported being affected by mental health conditions, either directly or through their families. Talk to someone you trust, sleep properly and keep exercising. You need a clear head to make your next decision well.

I learned to look after myself early. My father died when I was 18, aged just 49, and it made me take my health seriously long before it was fashionable. In difficult periods in business, that habit has helped keep me steady.

Experience alone does not make you a better founder. Harvard research by Paul Gompers and colleagues found that venture-backed entrepreneurs whose previous company had failed had a 20% chance of success next time, barely above the 18% for first-time founders. Those who had succeeded before had a 30% chance.

It also helps to know what kind of failure you are dealing with. In her book Right Kind of Wrong, Harvard Business School professor Amy Edmondson separates basic failures, caused by avoidable mistakes, from “intelligent failures,” which happen when you test a sensible idea in new territory and keep the downside small. The first kind should be prevented. The second is the price of progress.

The lessons don’t arrive by themselves. After a setback, I now write down what I assumed, what actually happened and what I would do differently, then ask someone outside the business to challenge it. Early in a career, a setback can feel like a judgment on your ability. With practice, it becomes a source of information.

A 2019 study in Nature by Yian Yin, Dashun Wang and colleagues analyzed more than 58,000 venture-backed startups, alongside other fields. People who eventually succeeded did not fail less often than those who didn’t. The difference was that each new attempt came faster, because they built on what they had already learned instead of starting from scratch. Speed here does not mean recklessness. It means shortening the gap between learning a lesson and acting on it.

That takes courage. The Global Entrepreneurship Monitor’s 2025/2026 report found that fear of failure deters two in five adults from starting a business. It also found that people who have previously exited a business are more likely to start again.

As I once told an interviewer, all these failures are what have shaped me. If you are recovering from one now, be patient with yourself, be honest about what went wrong, and, when you are ready, go again.

In 1989, I opened an Italian restaurant in Tsim Sha Tsui, Hong Kong, where the waiters sang opera arias between courses. It was a lot of fun, but it was not a good business, and it closed in 1993.

I had assumed running a restaurant was easy. It isn’t. The location was wrong, the costs were too high, and I didn’t know the trade well enough to see either problem early. Around the same time, I put money into film production and property. Both businesses struggled and were sold in the mid-1990s.

I share this because founders tend to talk about their successes and quietly bury the rest. Yet failure is a normal part of business. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, only about half of new U.S. business establishments are still operating five years later. Hong Kong is no different. In 2025, a record number of companies registered in the city, but the South China Morning Post reported that more than 99,000 were dissolved in the same year.

#5412. How ‘Boring’ Businesses Can Turn Black Friday Into a Competitive Advantage

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Black Friday isn’t just for big retailers. Here’s how small businesses can attract customers, boost sales and stand out without big budgets.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Black Friday isn’t just for big retailers. It’s also an opportunity for the hardworking small businesses we see every day, from bakeries and hair salons to cleaning companies and accounting firms.

I affectionately call them “boring” businesses, but there’s nothing boring about the people behind them. They’re the familiar neighborhood businesses we rely on every day, run by hardworking people who often wear several hats to keep things going.

And these traditional industries continue to attract new entrepreneurs. According to internal Tailor Brands business formation data, cleaning and home service businesses saw growth ranging from 60% to more than 300% in 2026, depending on the subcategory. But whether you’re just starting out or have been serving your community for years, the challenge is the same: finding ways to attract customers and keep them coming back.

Black Friday gives small businesses an opportunity to do both. A record 202.9 million Americans shopped between Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday in 2025, up from 197 million in 2024, as reported by inBeat. While much of the attention goes to major retailers, local businesses can use the shopping season to reconnect with existing customers and give new ones a reason to try their services.

Having worked with many small businesses, I’ve learned that successful Black Friday campaigns don’t always require big budgets or massive discounts. Sometimes, a personal gesture or a clever offer can make all the difference.

Here are a few practical strategies, including examples from my own experience, to help everyday businesses make the most of Black Friday.

Whether you run a hair salon, accounting firm or neighborhood bakery, Black Friday can be an opportunity to generate sales from customers who already know and trust your business. Instead of competing for attention with another promotional email, try sending a handwritten offer.

Handwrytten’s Consumer Survey found that only 11% of consumers had recently received a handwritten note from a brand, and just 4% found them annoying. That makes handwritten outreach an interesting way to stand out during a season dominated by digital promotions.

I’ve seen this work firsthand. I once worked with a client whose cake business was on the verge of bankruptcy. With bills and taxes piling up, we asked the owner’s 10-year-old daughter to handwrite thank-you letters to existing customers, offering them a special Black Friday deal: buy cake credits now and redeem them anytime over the next 12 months.

We sold credits for 271 cakes at an average of almost €60 each, generating nearly €16,000 in Black Friday sales. That cash injection gave the business much-needed breathing room. Customers also loved the letters, and the heartwarming gesture helped turn them into even more loyal supporters.

The same idea can work for almost any local business. Hair salons can sell prepaid appointments, cleaning companies can offer service credits, and accountants can create annual packages. The trick is to combine a personal touch with an offer that brings in revenue today while giving customers something valuable tomorrow.

For hotels, Black Friday is an opportunity to sell discounted spa weekends, romantic getaways and prepaid stays during the quieter winter months. But travelers need to discover these offers before they can book them.

AI-powered travel planning creates another opportunity to reach potential guests. According to Wanderboat, 56% of active U.S. travelers used AI for some aspect of their travel experience in the previous year.

Yet ranking highly on Google doesn’t guarantee visibility in AI-generated answers. Heroic Rankings reports that Google’s AI overlooks approximately 62% of pages ranking in the top 10 traditional search results.

To improve their chances of appearing in AI-generated recommendations, hotels should make their Black Friday offers as specific as possible. Instead of simply advertising “40% off winter stays,” imagine a small hotel offering a “Two-night spa getaway for two in Asheville for $299, including breakfast and spa access, valid December 12–14.”

I’d create a dedicated page for that offer, clearly listing the price, dates, amenities, cancellation policy and booking conditions. I’d also add guest reviews and answer questions travelers might ask, such as whether parking is included or if the spa requires advance booking. Make sure the details match what’s listed on booking platforms and add appropriate structured data to help search engines understand the package.

The easier it is for AI to find and understand your offer, the better your chances of reaching travelers looking for exactly that kind of getaway.

But optimizing your own website is only part of the equation. I’d also try to get my Black Friday offer featured in local media, relevant industry websites and articles rounding up the best Black Friday deals. In its GEO research, CSP analyzed more than 70,000 AI answers across three industries in 2026 and found that 85 earned-media placements generated 5,697 AI citations. This shows why getting your offer mentioned on relevant third-party websites can be just as important as making it easy to find on your own.

Video can make even the most ordinary services more appealing. In fact, 85% of consumers say they’ve been convinced to buy a product or service after watching a video, as reported by Flova. Even less flashy businesses like accounting firms, plumbers and cleaning companies can use humor to make their Black Friday campaigns stand out.

Last year, while managing a marketing campaign for a cleaning company, I wanted to create a funny video, but the employees weren’t comfortable on camera. We used AI animation instead, creating a humorous clip about the mess after a holiday party. The video converted particularly well in paid campaigns, driving plenty of sales while also generating strong organic engagement.

What makes this approach even more attractive today is how affordable it has become to experiment. As GPTProto reports, short AI video clips can cost between $0.04 and $0.50 per generation. That doesn’t mean producing an entire campaign costs a few cents, but it does mean small businesses can test different concepts, jokes and visual styles without spending heavily on every attempt.

I’ve since started incorporating AI video into the marketing services I offer clients. For a small business with someone comfortable using AI tools, the opportunity isn’t simply to produce cheaper videos. It’s to experiment with more ideas, discover what resonates with customers and put the strongest creative into a Black Friday campaign.

Small businesses can try the same approach. Show a relatable problem, add some humor, and finish with a clear Black Friday offer. You don’t need a big budget to make an ordinary service memorable.

Organic search traffic is declining across many industries, partly because Google’s AI Overviews now answer informational queries directly. According to Get Stuff Digital, organic traffic declined by 20% to 35% in its analysis following the introduction of AI-powered search features.

But I don’t see this as a reason to panic. Small businesses don’t necessarily need more informational traffic. They need visitors who are ready to book or buy. That’s why I’d focus Black Friday SEO efforts on high-intent searches rather than trying to recover every lost click.

For example, a cleaning company could create a dedicated page targeting searches like “Black Friday cleaning deals in Chicago” or “holiday deep cleaning discounts in Chicago,” with a specific package, price and clear booking option. I’d publish that page in September, or early October at the latest, to give Google time to discover and index it before Black Friday. I’d also add a few relevant internal links from existing service pages and blog posts to help search engines find it.

The goal isn’t to attract the most traffic. It’s to make sure that when someone searches for a Black Friday deal on a service you provide, your business is there with an offer they can act on.

Black Friday isn’t just about attracting new customers. It’s also a chance to bring back shoppers who never completed their purchases.

The average cart abandonment rate is 70.22%, as reported by Knowcrunch. These shoppers have already shown interest, making them a valuable audience for Black Friday offers.

For my clients, I already use automated emails year-round to remind customers about products they’ve left in their carts. During Black Friday, I take this a step further by targeting shoppers who abandoned their carts in the past 30 to 60 days and sending them personalized emails with a limited-time discount.

AI agents can make this process even easier by helping generate messages based on the products each customer considered. Scalably reports that sales professionals expect AI agents to reduce email-drafting time by 36% once fully implemented. In my experience, automating these repetitive follow-ups can save even more time, especially when you’re managing campaigns for multiple clients.

For example, a furniture store could automatically email someone who abandoned a sofa in their cart, remind them of the exact product and offer a Black Friday discount with a direct link to checkout. The system should also exclude customers who’ve already completed their purchases, so they don’t receive unnecessary reminders.

Instead of spending your entire Black Friday budget attracting new visitors, use automated emails and timely discounts to bring interested shoppers back and turn abandoned carts into sales.

One of the first rules of marketing is to be where your customers are. And sometimes, that’s behind the wheel. Munley Law highlights that Americans spend an average of 60.2 minutes driving each day. For local businesses, that creates an opportunity to reach customers during the busy Black Friday weekend.

Run short, frequent local radio ads with one clear offer and a promo code. Leave flyers with a time-limited deal on parked cars in busy shopping areas, where local rules allow.

Extend your opening hours over the holiday weekend and add them as special hours in your Google Business Profile. Drivers searching “near me” early in the morning or late in the evening may be looking for businesses they can visit immediately, so longer hours give you more opportunities to attract them. Add your offers to the profile too, and if your business allows it, offer curbside pickup.

Plan for parking, too. Reserve a few spots near the entrance for pickups. If you need more, offer to rent a few spaces from a neighbor just for the holiday weekend. Many will say no, but a small business only needs a handful of spots, and some neighbors will gladly take a few extra dollars for them. Then tell customers where to park in your emails and Google Business Profile.

On Cyber Monday, extend the deal online for anyone who heard the ad but didn’t make it in.

Giving away a small service can be a smart Black Friday strategy when it helps customers take the first step toward a much larger purchase. A limited-time offer gives them a reason to act now rather than keep postponing their decision.

Dental practices are a good example. According to Myra, 23% of adults have delayed dental treatment because of its cost. Offering a free initial consultation during Black Friday can remove that first financial barrier and encourage patients to explore treatments they might otherwise put off.

For example, a dental practice could invite patients considering implants, veneers or orthodontic treatment to book a complimentary examination and personalized treatment plan, with clinically appropriate imaging where needed. The dentist can explain the options, discuss installment payments if available and help patients understand the costs before committing.

And it’s not always just about money. Some patients feel anxious about visiting the dentist or discovering they need extensive treatment. A free, no-obligation first appointment can make that step feel less intimidating while giving the practice an opportunity to build trust.

The appointment can take place after Black Friday, as long as it’s booked during the promotion. For treatments involving a significant financial commitment, even a few new patients could make the offer worthwhile.

If there’s one thing I’ve learned from working with small businesses, it’s that a successful Black Friday campaign doesn’t have to be complicated or expensive. Sometimes, understanding your customers and coming up with a creative offer is enough to stand out.

My advice is to pick one or two strategies that make sense for your business, test them, and learn from the results. You might be surprised by what works.

Black Friday isn’t just for big retailers. It’s also an opportunity for the hardworking small businesses we see every day, from bakeries and hair salons to cleaning companies and accounting firms.

I affectionately call them “boring” businesses, but there’s nothing boring about the people behind them. They’re the familiar neighborhood businesses we rely on every day, run by hardworking people who often wear several hats to keep things going.

And these traditional industries continue to attract new entrepreneurs. According to internal Tailor Brands business formation data, cleaning and home service businesses saw growth ranging from 60% to more than 300% in 2026, depending on the subcategory. But whether you’re just starting out or have been serving your community for years, the challenge is the same: finding ways to attract customers and keep them coming back.

#5410. JPMorgan and Mastercard back Seattle startup Firmly’s bet on AI shopping agents

by Todd Bishop on Nov 7, 2026 at 10:23 amNovember 9, 2026 at 6:47 am

Firmly, a Seattle-area startup that helps online retailers sell through AI shopping assistants, raised a $15 million Series A round led by Squarepoint Capital, with participation from J.P. Morgan Payments, Mastercard, Samsung Next and others.

The company, founded in 2019, connects retailers’ existing online stores to AI assistants, marketplaces and other shopping channels, so people can buy products inside those third-party apps and services without going to retailers’ websites. Retailers keep their own payment providers and customer relationships.

“Every new AI assistant, marketplace or shopping platform is another place to sell. But connecting to each one can take serious engineering, because catalogs, inventory, payments, and checkout all have to work together,” wrote Kumar Senthil, Firmly’s co-founder and CEO, in a blog post announcing the round.

Mastercard is a commercial partner as well as an investor. Firmly handles the merchant side of Mastercard Agent Connect, a service launched in September to link merchants, AI agents and payment providers through a single integration.

Senthil told Axios Pro that Mastercard is recruiting merchants for the service, giving Firmly a route to new customers.

Firmly charges merchants $2,000 to $15,000 a month, depending on the total value of merchandise they sell, Senthil told Axios. He said connecting a merchant took four to six weeks in 2024 and now takes a day or less, including testing.

The company lists Best Buy, Furniture.com and Backcountry among its retail customers. RetailMeNot and an AI shopping app called Wizard also use its technology.

The funding comes as AI shopping agents move into the mainstream. Meta’s Muse assistant can browse retail sites and buy items with a user’s approval. Amazon has blocked Muse from its site and is suing Perplexity over a shopping agent in the startup’s Comet browser.

Firmly takes a different approach from those agents. Instead of having software click through a retailer’s web pages, it connects directly to the retailer’s systems with its permission.

The company this week also launched Ask Agent, an AI shopping assistant for retailers’ own websites. Shoppers describe what they want, get product recommendations and can check out without leaving the chat.

Other investors in the round include Alumni Ventures, ARK Invest, Benhamou Global Ventures, Granada Funds, Hike Ventures, The Mercantile Companies and Versus Ventures.

The round brings Firmly’s total funding to about $20 million. The company had raised $5.2 million when it partnered with Perplexity in March 2025 on shopping features inside the AI search app.

Senthil spent eight years at Microsoft and later led e-commerce products at Samsung. He co-founded Firmly with Damien Balsan, a co-founder of LoopPay, the mobile payments startup acquired by Samsung, and Murali Krishnamurthy, Firmly’s CTO and a former chief technical architect for Samsung’s U.S. and global e-commerce business. Firmly is based in Issaquah, Wash., and its engineering leaders work in Seattle. The company also has engineering teams in Sao Paulo, Brazil, and Chennai, India.

#5409. This Billionaire Invested in OpenAI in 2019. Here’s What He’s Betting on Next.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

This billionaire is betting that AI will revamp websites as we know them.

He made billions betting on what’s next. Now this 71-year-old investor’s latest move reflects his conviction that AI will change how the Internet works.

Vinod Khosla’s venture capital firm, Khosla Ventures, made early investments in OpenAI, DoorDash and Instacart. His latest investment, AI startup Coframe, targets another potential shift: how websites operate. Coframe wants to rewire the Internet so every visitor to a website sees a page custom-made for them.

“The world has changed because AI has enabled extreme customization,” Khosla said in an interview with Business Insider. Forbes reported earlier this year that Khosla’s net worth is around $10 billion.

Coframe announced this week that it raised $35 million in total funding, including a $25 million Series A led by Khosla Ventures and Hanabi Capital. Executives at Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind also participated.

Coframe helps businesses improve their websites so more people buy something, sign up for something or take another desired action. The startup creates and tests different versions of a webpage, including text, images and design. It then tracks how visitors interact with the webpage to determine how to improve it.

For example, say an online store wants to sell more shoes. Coframe could help the company test different headlines, product images or page layouts and determine which versions lead to more purchases.

“For decades, the web has been frozen in place, showing every visitor essentially the same page,” Khosla said in the press release. “Coframe is building the living internet, where two people can visit the same website and have completely different experiences, personalized to who they are and what they need. These interfaces continuously learn and improve themselves. This is a huge leap beyond traditional A/B testing and the next iteration of the internet.”

Coframe claims that it can help businesses get more out of the visitors they already have and spend far less time figuring out how to capitalize on their audiences. The startup said in the press release that its AI-powered testing platform has helped customers generate more than $300 million in additional revenue, with conversion rates improving by more than 20% on average.

Coframe’s customers include Dropbox, BCG, Block, Backcountry and Sur La Table.

Speed is another part of the startup’s appeal. Coframe said it built and launched an experiment for Dropbox in 30 minutes that previously would have required four weeks of engineering, design and quality-assurance work. For an unnamed Fortune 500 customer, the company said it launched dozens of variations and increased conversions by 70% within 30 days of the contract being signed.

The idea is to let businesses try more approaches without adding weeks of production work each time. Faster testing can help teams identify promising changes and move past unsuccessful ones sooner.

Khosla sees AI as a way to deliver an experience built around each visitor to a website, like Coframe is doing.

“The alternative is to write code for every page that’s presented, but that’s too expensive and way too slow,” Khosla told Business Insider. “This idea of a customized page for every user is a really good idea.”

He made billions betting on what’s next. Now this 71-year-old investor’s latest move reflects his conviction that AI will change how the Internet works.

Vinod Khosla’s venture capital firm, Khosla Ventures, made early investments in OpenAI, DoorDash and Instacart. His latest investment, AI startup Coframe, targets another potential shift: how websites operate. Coframe wants to rewire the Internet so every visitor to a website sees a page custom-made for them.

“The world has changed because AI has enabled extreme customization,” Khosla said in an interview with Business Insider. Forbes reported earlier this year that Khosla’s net worth is around $10 billion.

#5408. Yield-Bearing eZAR Blurs the Line Between Stablecoin and Investment Product

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation. Its reserve yield is the feature that puts the stablecoin label to the test.

Most stablecoin launches promise a token that never moves. eZAR's disclosures say its holders can make money or lose it. The rand-pegged token went live to the public on November 2, and its fine print reads more like an investment product than a payments coin.

According to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to new institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations. The company says R303 million worth of tokens had been issued and were in circulation as of October 30.

The project is a partnership between eZAR Ltd, asset manager Ninety One and AVBOB Financial Services, with AVBOB acting as lead institution and liquidity partner. CEO Sean Emery said the team put "getting it right" ahead of "getting it big" during the pilot. The message now is that eZAR is ready to scale.

The model also departs from the typical single-issuer coin. Neobanks, retailers, insurers and payment firms can plug the token into their own branded wallets and share in the economics. Transfers between participating wallets settle within seconds at any hour and, according to the company, cost nothing.

The reserves backing eZAR are invested through a money market strategy run by Ninety One, mainly in the Ninety One Money Market Fund. Returns are distributed daily to partners after partnership fees, and each partner then decides on what terms its own customers receive a share.

Ninety One's head of digital assets, Adam Duxbury, described it as new rails under an old discipline. His firm has run money market strategies for 25 years, he said, and South Africa should build its own digital rand rather than import a dollar coin.

The framing is clever, since it presents the yield as a feature of "digital cash that can grow." Yet that same feature makes the classification question hard to avoid.

The risk language is the most revealing part of the launch. eZAR describes itself as a crypto asset issued by the eZAR En Commandite Partnership. It states that the token is not legal tender, not a bank deposit and not a banking product, and that it carries no guarantee.

The details that follow set it further apart. The R1 redemption value depends on available liquidity. Money market returns can be positive or negative, so capital is at risk. Holders also own no units in the underlying fund and have no direct claim on it.

"Capital at risk" rarely appears in stablecoin terms. A payments token is meant to hold its value and let users redeem at par, yet eZAR's own documents hedge on both counts. Back in March, a market survey from Blockhouse had already noted that eZAR doesn't qualify as a stablecoin under most regulations. The live launch now tests that observation against a real product.

In the major rulebooks, the yield is the sticking point. The US GENIUS Act bars permitted payment stablecoin issuers from paying holders any form of interest or yield solely for holding, using or retaining the token. The EU's MiCA framework takes a similar line on interest. The logic is that a payment token paying a return starts to function like an unregulated deposit.

The OCC issued its final GENIUS Act rules on October 21, and they confirmed that ban for covered issuers. The contested ground lies elsewhere, in who sits between the issuer and the holder. Earlier OCC proposals set a rebuttable presumption against yield arrangements run through affiliates and related third parties, whereas the statute itself names only issuers.

eZAR's design lands squarely in that gray zone. Returns flow to partners, and the partners decide how customers share in them. Whether that amounts to an issuer paying yield or a partner passing on profit is precisely the kind of question US regulators are now wrestling with, and it would be a difficult one to argue before the OCC.

eZAR doesn't operate under the US or EU regimes, so none of those rules apply to it directly. eZAR Ltd is described as an authorised financial services provider responsible for the main technology and services behind the partnership. That technology also draws on the South African Reserve Bank's Project Khokha 2, where eZAR's parent company, Block Markets Africa, was a technical contributor.

This background signals a serious, institution-backed build rather than a speculative launch. Even so, the rand stablecoin field is getting crowded. ZARU launched earlier this year as an institutional-grade rand coin, and a pattern is emerging of different models competing for the same local payments niche.

The bigger question is whether South Africa will define stablecoins narrowly, as the US and EU do, or leave room for hybrid products like this one. Because the network is permissioned, the reported circulation figure also rests on company disclosure rather than a public ledger, which makes the regulatory and disclosure framework matter even more.

For everyday users, the appeal is easy to see. A rand token that moves in seconds, costs nothing to send and might earn a daily return makes an attractive pitch. For partners, shared infrastructure with a revenue share offers a way into digital payments without building a coin from scratch.

The trade-off sits in the disclaimers. A holder who treats eZAR like a bank balance could be caught off guard by liquidity-dependent redemption, or by a money market return that dips below zero. That gap between how the product feels and how it is legally defined is where regulators tend to step in.

eZAR is best understood as a hybrid: a payments token with an investment return attached. It may well succeed on those terms. Still, as more jurisdictions tighten the stablecoin definition around no-yield, par-redemption tokens, products like this will increasingly be judged on what they are rather than what they are called. How South African regulators treat eZAR in the coming months will show which way that debate is heading.

#5406. The Great Wealth Transfer Is About More Than Money. Here’s What’s Being Overlooked.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

We’re talking about the Great Wealth Transfer too narrowly. Here’s why millions of heirs are looking to value and sell inherited jewelry.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

When economists and financial advisors talk about the Great Wealth Transfer, the conversation almost always centers on traditional financial assets: brokerage accounts, primary residences, retirement accounts and family businesses.

These numbers are massive, to be sure. Cerulli Associates estimates that $124 trillion will transfer through 2048, with $105 trillion passing directly to heirs. Nearly $100 trillion of that sum will originate with baby boomers and older generations.

Yet wealth does not sit exclusively on a balance sheet. It lives inside our homes, stored in safes, tucked into back drawers and resting quietly in velvet jewelry boxes.

It’s estimated that half of the gold ever mined in human history exists today as jewelry. Millions of families are about to inherit gold jewelry, luxury watches, diamonds, heirloom rings, coins and precious metals alongside standard investment portfolios.

We are not just approaching a Great Wealth Transfer. We are on the precipice of the Great Jewelry Transfer. Unlike a stock portfolio or checking account, heirloom pieces rarely arrive with a neat financial statement telling heirs what they own, leaving many unprepared when it’s time to evaluate, keep or sell inherited jewelry.

When people inherit jewelry, emotional value and real financial worth collide.

Most heirs can tell you the backstory without missing a beat:

What they rarely understand is the asset itself.

They’re left asking basic financial questions: Is this real? Is it worth $200 or $20,000? Does the value come from the gold, the quality of the stones, the brand or the item’s vintage status? And ultimately, what’s the right move: keep it, insure it, divide it among siblings or sell it?

Without clear answers on metal purity or stone quality, deciding whether to keep, divide or sell inherited jewelry becomes an educated guess made during an already stressful time.

Furthermore, younger generations often don’t want to inherit physical clutter. Modern estate research indicates that millennials and Gen Z heirs prefer a small, curated selection of meaningful possessions over taking custody of an entire household’s worth of heirlooms.

Inheriting an asset and understanding an asset are two completely different things.

This generational hand-off is occurring alongside a seismic shift in consumer behavior: the mainstream adoption of secondhand commerce.

Buying secondhand used to carry a subtle stigma; today it’s a mainstream consumer movement driven by younger consumers who actively prioritize circularity, sustainability and the unique appeal of vintage items. According to data from Deloitte, the broader U.S. resale market is projected to reach $73 billion by 2028, while the number of U.S. fashion brands hosting resale platforms on their own sites increased 325% between 2021 and 2025.

For the jewelry market, this shift changes everything.

A piece one generation no longer wants to wear doesn’t suddenly lose its intrinsic value. Its lifecycle can seamlessly evolve: Kept → Valued → Sold → Recycled → Worn by someone new.

This expands the concept of a circular economy beyond traditional “cash for gold” operations. The next generation doesn’t have to choose between keeping Grandma’s jewelry in a drawer forever or shipping it off to a refinery to be melted down.

When I founded Alloy, our initial premise was straightforward: The traditional process to sell gold jewelry, or any other high-value estate piece, was unnecessarily opaque and fundamentally built to favor the buyer over the consumer.

After working with thousands of consumers, one thing became clear quickly: Many customers acquired their pieces through inheritance, estate management or a major life transition. We quickly realized our main job wasn’t just facilitating a sale; it was helping people understand what they actually owned.

Solving that problem requires three foundational pillars:

That third pillar, optionality, is where the market’s future lies.

Historically, the secondary jewelry market has been deeply fragmented. A consumer sells a piece to a local business. That business flips it to another intermediary. Some pieces get resold; others are melted. Throughout the entire process, the original owner has zero insight into the asset’s true destination or value.

At The Alloy Market, we are building the infrastructure to connect these fragmented lifecycles.

By providing upfront valuation tools, real-time calculators and educational resources, we empower consumers to understand the exact value of their items before deciding. When an item is sold, our ecosystem evaluates whether to reintroduce it to the consumer market as a wearable piece, returning a portion of that resale upside to the original seller or whether to return its metals responsibly to the industrial supply chain.

We’re not merely building a better way to sell inherited jewelry; we’re building the underlying digital infrastructure that lets high-value physical assets transition smoothly from one generation to the next.

Leaving things behind isn’t new. But we’ve never seen a handoff like this, where trillions of dollars in physical items land with a generation that thinks very differently about what’s worth keeping, selling or passing along.

Some inherited jewelry will remain in families for another century. Some will be sold for financial liquidity. Some will be melted for reuse. And a growing percentage will find a second life with a new owner who appreciates its history.

The companies that win this transition won’t simply be those offering to buy these assets. They will be the trusted institutions that help heirs understand what they have and empower them to decide what happens next.

While standard wealth management focuses on paper assets and balance sheets, the Great Jewelry Transfer is about what happens to the physical history families leave behind. Trillions are at stake, but the real value is in the objects themselves.

When economists and financial advisors talk about the Great Wealth Transfer, the conversation almost always centers on traditional financial assets: brokerage accounts, primary residences, retirement accounts and family businesses.

These numbers are massive, to be sure. Cerulli Associates estimates that $124 trillion will transfer through 2048, with $105 trillion passing directly to heirs. Nearly $100 trillion of that sum will originate with baby boomers and older generations.

Yet wealth does not sit exclusively on a balance sheet. It lives inside our homes, stored in safes, tucked into back drawers and resting quietly in velvet jewelry boxes.

#5405. Trevor Noah on AI

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 8, 2026 at 9:52 amNovember 8, 2026 at 10:44 am

On Oct. 19, Trevor Noah launched Luminaries, a science conversation series at Boston’s Museum of Science. I joined him onstage, and Rana el Kaliouby moderated. Rana is a pioneer of emotion AI, software that reads human emotion, and the host of the Pioneers of AI podcast. She wrote afterward that she expected Trevor to be witty and funny, but “didn’t expect to be so blown away by his humanity and depth of ideas.”

Here are a few of his insights with his own words highlighted.

When an AI matchmaker Rana built in ChatGPT picked Trevor as her match, he pointed out that it knew very little about either of them. It assembled a plausible answer from what’s on the internet.

Trevor added that when you tell AI it made a mistake, it thanks you but often fails to correct the error: “It’s like a friend who’s been to a lot of therapy but doesn’t actually change.”

When asked how we protect ourselves from AI’s downsides, Trevor said the answer “goes back to something that is very un-technological and very un-AI.” He cited Robert Putnam’s book Bowling Alone, noting that places where communities form accrue many surprising benefits including more accountable governments.

I pushed back that communitarianism, the 1990s movement my father helped found to foster communities, had failed. Trevor responded that we hand too many ideas to intellectuals, who then “apply too much academia” to them. Communitarianism failed, he deadpanned, “because it’s called communitarianism.” An overly academic name.

He noted that nobody calls a phone a failure when the first version doesn’t sell; companies keep re-releasing it. He vowed never to stop investing in community.

Despite his concerns, Trevor has “yet to see a technology that blew up and then left everyone behind.” Cars, computers and the internet all spread to ordinary people.

AI has reached what he calls “work intelligence”: it can do the jobs we invented, but we keep inventing new ones. Salt and ice used to be precious. Now restaurants hand them out for free. What we value changes, and in Trevor’s view, we’re expendable only if we define being human by the tasks we value today.

Our conversation turned to AI’s impact on jobs.

Touring as a comic, Trevor saw towns hollowed out after Kodak and the automaker Studebaker left. Factory workers were told automation was progress. “White-collar workers are now experiencing what many blue-collar workers experienced for decades,” he said. The difference, he argued, is that white-collar workers are closer to power, so newspapers are covering it.

Trevor is confident new jobs will come, as they did after telephone exchange operators disappeared. What worries him is the gap. His analogy is the highway, where the following distance is the space that lets you stop before you hit the car ahead:

Trevor tells tech leaders that “it’s easier to be patient when you are in a position of privilege,” and added, “But ironically, they don’t have patience when it comes to quarterly earnings.”

After ChatGPT took off, show hosts kept telling him weak jokes that ChatGPT had written in a pale imitation of Trevor’s style. He rattled off four reasons AI struggles with humor: there isn’t enough comedy data, the model is a frozen snapshot while what society finds acceptable keeps shifting, comedy depends on knowing your audience (there are jokes you know are funny but you wouldn’t tell your mom), and companies have made models risk averse.

In addition to being the former host of The Daily Show, an award-winning author and a sought-after comedian, Trevor Noah is Microsoft’s Chief Questions Officer.

I reminded him of Picasso’s famous verdict on computers, “They are useless. They can only give you answers,” and joked that as Chief Questions Officer he has something rare these days: job security. He chuckled. Of course, his real job security comes from his depth and humanity, which feed his exceptional humor and wit.

Rana noted that everybody’s getting replaced by AI, but Trevor had played an AI, voicing Griot in Black Panther: Wakanda Forever.

#5403. From paper routes to fighter jets: Shield AI’s bet on Seattle is a homecoming for its co-founders

by Todd Bishop & John Cook on Nov 9, 2026 at 6:36 amNovember 9, 2026 at 6:36 am

As a kid on Mercer Island, Brandon Tseng delivered The Seattle Times and the Mercer Island Reporter for extra cash. Now he and his older brother, Ryan Tseng, are making news of their own in the Seattle region.

Shield AI, the San Diego defense tech company the brothers co-founded in 2015, announced a deal last week to buy Kirkland, Wash.-based radar maker Echodyne for up to $5.3 billion. Shield, now valued at $28.8 billion, had already unveiled plans in September to build its AI-piloted X-BAT fighter jet at a factory south of Seattle.

“I believe we will become one of the largest, or at least the fastest-growing employer in this region over the next several years,” Brandon Tseng said in an interview with GeekWire in the hours after the Echodyne acquisition was announced.

The company projects that it will employ about 4,000 people in the Seattle area by the early 2030s. It estimates the X-BAT could support about 8,000 jobs across the region in all, including jobs at Shield and its suppliers, according to an economic analysis drawing on company figures.

Tseng said Shield expects to have “well north of a million square feet” in the area before long, up from its initial 420,000-square-foot facility in Des Moines, Wash.

“That will really just be the beginning,” he said.

Brandon Tseng said the biggest reason Shield chose the Pacific Northwest for X-BAT production was the region’s “density of engineering and manufacturing talent,” pointing to Boeing, Microsoft and Amazon.

Inside the Echodyne deal: Shield believes the defense tech companies that succeed will need products that “sense, think, and act,” Tseng said. Its Hivemind autonomy software handles the thinking, and its V-BAT drone and X-BAT jet will handle the acting.

Echodyne becomes “the cornerstone of the sensing piece,” he said.

Tseng said Shield got a closer look at the market for sensors when it bought Australian optics company Sentient Vision Systems in 2024. That led the company to start looking seriously at other sensor makers, and eventually to Echodyne.

Shield and Echodyne had first crossed paths in 2016, when both were fledgling companies in the Department of Homeland Security’s Silicon Valley Innovation Program.

Nearly a decade later, the two companies’ teams were talking about working together when Echodyne began exploring a sale, Tseng said. The deal came together over several months. Tseng was at Echodyne the day it was announced last week, as the companies held all-hands meetings with their teams.

It’s an unusual deal: one venture-backed startup buying another, funded in part by a new venture round. Shield is raising $2.5 billion to help pay for the deal, including $1 billion in new funding at the $28.8 billion valuation — more than double what it was worth in March.

Echodyne has about 400 employees, after opening a $40 million radar factory in Woodinville in July. No layoffs are planned, the companies said. Eben Frankenberg, Echodyne’s co-founder and CEO, will stay in that role, reporting to Shield CEO Gary Steele. The combined company will have about 2,700 employees.

The deal is expected to close in early 2027, pending regulatory approval. Tseng said Shield plans a light touch for roughly the first year after that. Echodyne will keep selling radar to other manufacturers, many of them in counter-drone systems, while pursuing performance targets that could add $500 million to the price.

Deeper product integrations will be announced later, he said.

“They’ve been on a tear growth-wise, and we don’t want to get in their way,” Tseng said. “We don’t want to slow them down. We just want to supercharge them.”

He called the two companies’ cultures a strong match, describing both as mission-oriented and engineering-first. Echodyne’s best-selling radar, EchoShield, is designed to protect U.S. and allied service members from incoming drones.

Echodyne spun out of Intellectual Ventures, the Bellevue invention lab, in 2014 with a $15 million round led by Bill Gates and Madrona. Madrona and other Echodyne investors will become significant Shield shareholders.

Tim Porter, the Madrona Venture Group managing director who has served on Echodyne’s board since 2014, called the deal another sign of the defense tech industry’s rapid growth in the Pacific Northwest.

Echodyne “rarely, if ever, showed up on lists of the hottest defense tech companies,” he wrote. Now it’s “under the radar no longer.”

X-BAT bet: Much of Shield’s growth in the region depends on an aircraft that hasn’t flown yet. Shield unveiled its first full-scale X-BAT prototype this month and shipped it to Kansas for flight testing, with first flight targeted by the end of the year. Shield has said low-rate production will start in Des Moines in mid-2027, with the first locally built jet due in early 2028.

The Pentagon and Shield have committed a combined $400 million to X-BAT’s development, but Shield hasn’t announced any production orders.

Ryan Tseng, speaking to Breaking Defense on the sidelines of the International Fighter Conference in Munich last week, said Shield expects to announce European X-BAT orders and partnerships but declined to discuss quantities, saying only, “Watch this space.” Andrew Hawkes, Shield’s X-BAT director for Europe, told Breaking Defense the company has “several active” sales campaigns there but declined to name customers.

Asked about the X-BAT schedule in the interview last week, Brandon Tseng acknowledged the challenge but pointed to the engineering and manufacturing teams that brought the prototype together in about a year. “There was no quit in them,” he said.

“It’s hard as hell, right? Just to move out on production that fast, but you have to be confident,” he said. “I’m confident.”

Tseng, a Naval Academy graduate who deployed twice to Afghanistan as a Navy SEAL, compared Shield’s pace to that experience, when small, mission-driven groups with the right tools and resources would “do things that people didn’t think were possible.”

Ryan Tseng, an electrical engineer, previously founded wireless charging company WiPower, which was acquired by Qualcomm. The brothers started Shield with Andrew Reiter, Shield’s first CTO, who returned to the company this year.

Seattle roots: The Tseng brothers and their sister grew up on Mercer Island. Brandon Tseng spent summers swimming in Lake Washington and played water polo for Mercer Island. Ryan Tseng, who was Shield’s CEO for about a decade, graduated from Mercer Island High School, and their sister graduated from the University of Washington.

Their father, Carlos Tseng, was CEO of Seattle-based Foss Maritime from 1996 to 2001, according to Tseng and Shield. He would stop at Pike Place Market on the way home from work, and the family “probably ate salmon every other day,” Brandon Tseng said.

The family moved to Florida in 2001. None of the Tsengs live in the area anymore, but Brandon Tseng still has friends here from middle school and high school and stops by Mercer Island when he has time on his visits to the region.

Shield’s Washington state connections go further. Steele, the company’s CEO since May 2025, grew up in Yakima and graduated from Washington State University.

Brandon Tseng called Shield’s expansion in the region “a fun homecoming” for him, his brother and Steele. He is based in Washington, D.C., but expects to spend more and more time in the Seattle area.

Tseng delivered the Times, then the afternoon paper, seven days a week from age 10 to 14, making his rounds every day after school and on weekends. He credits those routes with teaching him about hard work.

“It’s always felt like home,” he said. “It’s great to be back here.”

#5402. New tax incentives give Washington’s sustainable aviation fuel industry a boost

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 9, 2026 at 9:38 amNovember 9, 2026 at 9:38 am

Washington has cleared a milestone in its effort to become a hub for lower-carbon jet fuel, unlocking tax incentives aimed at attracting production to the state.

Gov. Bob Ferguson announced Friday that Washington has reached the capacity to produce at least 20 million gallons of sustainable aviation fuel annually. That triggers incentives taking effect Jan. 1, including a tax credit starting at $1 per gallon for qualifying fuel. The credit rises to as much as $2 for fuels with greater emissions reductions.

The Department of Ecology recently surveyed potential producers and confirmed that Phillips 66’s Ferndale refinery alone has enough capacity to meet the threshold. The benchmark measures production capacity, not actual output.

Sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF, is widely seen as one of the most promising near-term options for cutting aviation’s carbon emissions because it can be blended with conventional jet fuel and used in existing aircraft. But it remains more expensive than petroleum-based fuel, and production is orders of magnitude below the industry’s needs.

“We have so many unique assets in Washington that position us to be global leaders in the SAF transition, and this tax incentive is the final element needed to really unleash the tidal wave of opportunity,” said Jake Gentry, executive director of the Cascadia Sustainable Aviation Accelerator, in a GeekWire interview.

The accelerator launched in January, bringing together airlines, SAF producers, public officials, researchers and others to promote the industry in the Pacific Northwest. Its work includes helping producers secure financing, develop feedstock supplies and connect with customers.

SAF can be produced from used cooking oil, grease and fats, plants and agricultural waste, and captured carbon. Its climate benefits depend on the raw materials and energy used to make it.

The fuel still produces carbon dioxide when burned. But unlike petroleum-based jet fuel, which releases carbon that would otherwise stay trapped underground, SAF recycles carbon already in circulation in plants, animals and the atmosphere. Washington’s per-gallon tax credit requires emissions at least 50% below those of conventional jet fuel.

Washington’s production capacity is below that of some larger facilities elsewhere. A Diamond Green Diesel plant in Texas can produce up to 235 million gallons of SAF annually, according to its partner Valero. That figure also represents capacity, not actual production.

With the minimum threshold being met, all Washington SAF producers will be eligible for the tax credit regardless of their volumes.

A startup called Twelve is already making the fuel in the central Washington city of Moses Lake. The company opened its AirPlant One facility last year and began commercially producing SAF this summer from captured carbon dioxide and water. The technology has the potential to create the most climate-friendly SAF available, potentially unlocking the largest state tax credits.

Nicholas Flanders, Twelve’s CEO and co-founder, welcomed the announcement.

“This is an extraordinary signal of support for our industry,” Flanders said via email. “Washington is building the leading foundation in the country for next-generation domestic fuel production, and Twelve is ready to build upon it.”

Twelve’s first-of-its-kind facility is designed to make up to 50,000 gallons of SAF per year. AirPlant Two, a much bigger plant that would make tens of millions of gallons a year, is in development. The company hasn’t said where it will be located.

Dutch-owned SkyNRG is building a SAF facility in Walla Walla, Wash., and plans to use renewable natural gas that’s captured at landfills and from dairy waste as a feedstock. Earlier this year, leaders said the company had secured key environmental approvals and plans to start commercial operations in 2030.

Washington’s relatively affordable hydroelectric power has historically helped attract climate tech companies. But growing electricity demand, including from data centers, is putting pressure on the region’s power supply.

Washington also faces competition from other states offering SAF tax incentives. Illinois and Minnesota already offer credits, and Nebraska’s program starts next year. Meanwhile, a federal credit was reduced from $1.75 per gallon to $1 after President Donald Trump returned to office.

Washington leaders tout other perks that could attract SAF production. It’s the only state that offers both a SAF tax credit and a clean fuel standard. Together, the policies help make cleaner jet fuel more cost-competitive by providing tax benefits and allowing SAF producers to earn credits they can sell to other fuel suppliers that need to meet the state’s emissions requirements.

The accelerator also supports efforts with Washington State University to develop regional feedstock supplies, including waste from logging and agriculture.

“Between our long history of aviation innovation, our intentional investments into the sector and our climate-forward policies, we’re making sure Washington is the best state in the country to produce sustainable aviation fuels,” Ferguson said in a statement.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.
